s.def: A part of a piece of music, such as a concerto, that is very decorative and is played by a single musician.
To become agitated or excited.

ety: Borrowed from French cadet, from Gascon capdet, from Late Latin capitellum (“small head”). Attested in English from 1634. Doublet of caddie, cadeau, cadel, capital, capitellum, and caudillo.

s.def: A student at a military school who is training to be an officer.
A younger or youngest son, who would not inherit as a firstborn son would.
Junior. (See also the heraldic term cadency.)
ex: a cadet branch of the family

s.def: A young man who makes a business of ruining girls to put them in brothels.
A young gentleman learning sheep farming at a station; also, any young man attached to a sheep station.
A participant in a cadetship.

ety: From Middle English caggen (“to tie, fasten, bind”), probably from Old Norse. Compare Old Norse kǫgurr (“quilt”), kǫgurbarn (“swaddled child”).

s.def: To tie, fasten.
To beg.
To obtain something by wit or guile; to convince people to do something they might not normally do.
ex: Are ye gannin te cadge a lift of yoer fatha?
They moved about the bar incessantly, cadging cigarettes and drinks, with something behind their eyes at once terribly vulnerable and terribly hard.

s.def: A circular frame on which cadgers carry hawks for sale.
To carry hawks and other birds of prey.
ex: For quotations using this term, see Citations:cadge.

s.def: To carry, as a burden.
ex: Another Atlas that will cadge a whole world of iniuries without fainting.

s.def: To hawk or peddle, as fish, poultry, etc.
Alternative form of qadi.
ex: The pretended cadi, directing his discourse to the feigned Ali Cogia, asked him what he had to lay to the merchant's charge.
The cadi is to give licenses for marriages, and the imam will perform the marriage ceremony accordingly.

ety: 1817, from Ancient Greek Καδμεία (Kadmeía, “calamine”), a cadmium-bearing mixture of minerals, which was named after the king Κάδμος (Kádmos, “Cadmus”).

s.def: A chemical element (symbol Cd) with an atomic number of 48: a soft, silvery-white metal.
A single atom of this element.

ety: Borrowed from French cadre, from Italian quadro (“framed painting, square”), from Latin quadrum, from quattuor (“four”).

s.def: A frame or framework.
The framework or skeleton upon which a new regiment is to be formed; the officers of a regiment forming the staff.
The core of a managing group, or a member of such a group.
ex: After the war, he was a party cadre and worked as a correspondent for the daily newspaper Zeri i Popullit (The People's Voice).
Party cadres must guard against the temptations of power, money and sex.

s.def: A small group of people specially trained for a particular purpose or profession.

ety: Via Latin cādūceus, cādūceum, adaptation of Doric Ancient Greek καρύκειον (karúkeion, “herald’s wand or staff”). This and Attic Greek κηρύκειον (kērúkeion) are derived from κῆρυξ (kêrux, “herald, public messenger”). Related to κηρύσσω (kērússō, “to announce”).

s.def: A symbol (☤) representing a staff with two snakes wrapped around it, used to indicate merchants and messengers. It is also sometimes incorrectly substituted for the rod of Asclepius as a symbol of medicine.
ex: For quotations using this term, see Citations:caduceus.

s.def: The official wand carried by a herald in ancient Greece and Rome, specifically the one carried in mythology by Hermes, the messenger of the gods, usually represented with two snakes twined around it.
ex: Caduceus the rod of Mercury, / With which he wonts the Stygian realmes inuade […]

ety: From French caducité; see caducous.

s.def: Dotage or senility.
The state of being impermanent or transitory.

ety: Borrowed from Latin caecum (“invisible, hidden”), clipping of intestīnum caecum (“blind gut”), translation of Ancient Greek τῠφλὸν ἔντερον (tŭphlòn énteron).

s.def: A cavity open at one end (such as the blind end of a duct), especially a blind pouch connected to the large intestine between the ileum and the colon.
ex: After a preliminary course in anatomy it was found that caecum and transverse colon also provided excellent sites for excitation.

ety: Inherited from Middle English Caen, Cane, Cadomy, from Old French Caem, Cahom, likely from Latin *Catumagus; the modern pronunciation is a refashioning after modern French Caen.

s.def: A city in Calvados department, Normandy, France.

ety: By extension from personal name Caesar.

s.def: An emperor of Ancient Rome.
Any emperor, ruler, or dictator.
Alternative form of Caesar.
Any agaric mushroom of the genus Amanita, section Amanita sect. Caesareae.

ety: From Latin Caesar. Displaced Old English cāsere, which would have yielded *caser, *coser, and Middle English keiser, kaiser, from Old Norse and continental Germanic languages. All ultimately from the same Latin root. (See also Kaiser and tsar.)

s.def: An ancient Roman family name, notably that of Julius Caesar.
ex: The Caesars were an ancient and aristocratic family, which for eight generations had been prominent in the commonwealth.
To the powerful, the Caesares were flattering, deferential, sincerely devoted, self-sacrificing, loyal, eagerly serving.
Five of the Caesares were killed during the years 90-85 (D. G., 3, 114).

s.def: The government; society; earthly powers.

ety: Named after (Italian-born) US restaurateur Caesar Cardini (1896–1956) who is generally thought to have invented it for his Tijuana restaurant in 1924.

s.def: Caesar salad
A type of salad, generally made from romaine lettuce, croutons, parmesan cheese, coddled or hard-boiled eggs, fresh-ground black pepper and Worcestershire sauce.
ex: Would you like some Caesar salad for lunch?
Of all the Caesar salads I've tasted, this is the finest.

s.def: A serving of such salad.
ex: Would you like a Caesar salad for lunch?

s.def: An edible mushroom, of species Amanita caesarea, with a distinctive orange cap.

ety: Learned borrowing from Latin Caesarēa. Both the Algerian and Turkish cities were named in honor of Augustus. Doublet of Kayseri and Cherchell.

s.def: any of the places called Caesarea
A port city in Israel.
Various other former cities in the Roman Empire, including:

ety: See Caesar, at caedō, and at Caesarean section § Etymology.

s.def: Delivery of a baby through an incision in the womb.

ety: From caesar + -o- + papism, probably modelled after New Latin caesaro-papia, coined by the German ecclesiastical jurist Justus Henning Böhmer (1674–1749) in his work Jus ecclesiasticum Protestantium (Ecclesiastical Law of the Protestants, 1714–1736).

s.def: The combination of state (originally imperial) power with religious authority; state authority over ecclesiastical matters.

ety: From Latin caesius (“sky-blue”), in reference to the radiation spectra, + -ium.

s.def: The chemical element (symbol Cs) with an atomic number of 55. It is a soft, gold-colored, highly reactive alkali metal.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *kh₂eyd- Proto-Indo-European *-eti Proto-Indo-European *kh₂éydeti Proto-Italic *kaidō Latin caedō Proto-Indo-European *-tew-? Proto-Indo-European *-r-eh₂? Latin -tūra Latin caesūra English caesura Latin caesūra (“cutting, hewing”), from caesus, perfect passive participle of caedō (“to cut down, hew”).

s.def: A pause or interruption in a poem, music, building, or other work of art.
Using two words to divide a metrical foot.
The caesura mark ‖ or ||.
A break of an era or other measure of history and time; where one era ends and another begins; turning point.
ex: A quiet time. A caesura. Then everything happened almost at once, and none of it was good.

s.def: Alternative form of café.
A convenience store, originally one that sold coffee and similar basic items.

ety: Unadapted borrowing from French café (“coffee; coffee shop”). Doublet of caffè and coffee.

s.def: A coffee shop; an establishment selling coffee and sometimes other non-alcoholic beverages, simple meals or snacks, with a facility to consume them on the premises.
A small restaurant of any genre.

ety: Unadapted borrowing from French café au lait (literally “coffee with milk”).

s.def: coffee with milk
A mixture of coffee and hot milk.
Coffee and hot milk served in separate jugs as a breakfast drink.
A light coffee colour.

ety: Borrowed from Mexican Spanish cafetería (“coffeehouse”), from cafetera (“coffee maker”), from French cafetière, from café, from Ottoman Turkish قهوه (kahve) (Turkish kahve), from Arabic قَهْوَة (qahwa, “coffee”). Doublet of cafetière.

s.def: A restaurant in which customers select their food at a counter then carry it on a tray to a table to eat.
A dining area in an institution where meals may be purchased (as above), provided, or brought in from elsewhere.

ety: From caffeine + -ated.

s.def: Containing caffeine naturally (e.g., coffee, tea, and cacao) or as an additive (e.g., soft drinks, sports drinks, or energy drinks).
Overly peppy or energetic; stimulated by caffeine.
ex: For most of us, to be caffeinated to one degree or another has simply become baseline human consciousness.

ety: Borrowed from French caféine, from café (“coffee”), or German Caffein, Kaffein (cp. Coffein, Koffein), from Kaffee (“coffee”) (cp. Kaffe, Koffee, Koffe), or Italian caffè (“coffee”) + -ine.

s.def: An alkaloid, C₈H₁₀N₄O₂, found naturally in tea and coffee plants, which acts as a mild stimulant on the central nervous system.
ex: For example, 0.100 grams of caffeine yield by combustion, by weight, 0.180 grammes of carbonic acid.

s.def: A region of the Philippines, composed of the provinces of Batanes, Cagayan, Isabela, Nueva Vizcaya and Quirino. Capital and largest city: Tuguegarao.

ety: From Middle English cage, from Old French cage, from Latin cavea. Doublet of cadge and cavea and related to jail.

s.def: An enclosure made of spaced bars, normally to hold animals while providing some ventilation.
ex: We keep a bird in a cage.
The tigers are in a cage to protect the public.
The most dangerous prisoners are locked away in a cage.

s.def: To confine in a cage; to put into and keep in a cage.
ex: And the row of human captors, ever leering, They who caged me, Know their power and gloat on my captivity.
The industrial practice of caging commercial laying hens has given caged housing a bad narne.
By caging chickens, farmers broke the cycle and had to busy themselves with feeding, cleaning and pest control activities.

s.def: The passenger compartment of a lift.
The goal.
Short for roll cage, a protective structure around the passenger compartment of a vehicle.
Synonym of automobile.
Something that hinders freedom.
ex: My body is a cage / That keeps me from dancing with the one I love / But my mind holds the key

s.def: A prison or prison cell.
The area from which competitors throw a discus or hammer.
A regular graph that has as few vertices as possible for its girth.

ety: From cage + -ling.

s.def: A bird that is kept confined in a cage.
ex: Am I as a child perhaps, chasing a flown cageling, who among the branches free plays and peeps at the offered cage?
Semmacherib says that he cooped up King Hezekiah of Judah in Jerusalem like a cageling.

ety: Initially US colloquial, of unknown origin. A connection with the behavior of caged prisoners (wary and closed-lipped) and caged animals (wary) has been speculated. If so, by surface analysis, cage + -y.

s.def: Uncommunicative; unwilling or hesitant to give information.
Wary, careful, shrewd.
ex: We move like cagey tigers / Oh, we couldn't get closer than this
But with both sides in the Premier League's bottom three before the game began, the three points at stake made for a cagey match.

ety: Borrowed from French cahier. Doublet of quire.

s.def: A roll of sheets of paper put loosely together, especially one of the successive portions of a work printed in numbers.
A memorial of a body; a report of legislative proceedings, etc.

ety: PIE word *ḱóm From earlier cahoot + -s (suffix forming regular plurals of nouns). Cahoot is probably borrowed: * from French cahute (“hut, shack”), from Dutch kajuit (“cabin on a ship”), from Middle Low German kajüte, probably from Middle Dutch kayhute; further etymology uncertain, possibly borrowed from Old French *cahute, chahute (whence Middle French quahute), a blend of cabane (“cabin, hut, shack”) + hute (“hut”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewH- (“to conceal, hide; to cover; h…

s.def: Chiefly preceded by in: collaboration or collusion, chiefly for a nefarious reason.
ex: Those two are definitely in cahoots.
[…] I suspected him of being in cahoots with the steward, who got the lights doused long enough for the pearls to be stolen.
They probably give it back to him; they're all in cahoots.

s.def: plural of cahoot (“a company or partnership; a group of people working together, chiefly for a nefarious reason, hence, a collaboration or collusion; an accomplice, partner”)
third-person singular simple present indicative of cahoot

ety: From Spanish caimán or Portuguese caimão, from Kari'na acayouman.

s.def: Any of the relatively small crocodilians of the genus Caiman, within the family Alligatoridae.
A crocodilian of the subfamily Caimaninae, which includes the very large black caiman.
A semi-aquatic lizard, of the genus Dracaena, found in South America. To differentiate from crocodilian caimans, they are referred to as caiman lizards.
Alternative form of kain.

ety: From Hebrew קַיִן (Káyin, “craftsman”), present since Old English.

s.def: The son of Adam and Eve who killed his brother Abel.
ex: According to the Book of Jubilees Cain got married to his sister Awan.

s.def: A male given name from Hebrew.
A surname.

ety: Borrowed from French caïque, from Italian caicco, from Ottoman Turkish قایق (kayık), from Proto-Turkic *kiayguk (“boat, oar”). Cognate with modern Turkish kayık.

s.def: A small wooden trading vessel, brightly painted and rigged for sail, traditionally used for fishing and trawling.
Any of four (previously two) species of parrot in the genus Pionites.

ety: Borrowed from French caïquejee, ultimately from Turkish kayıkçı (“boatman”).

s.def: A person who rows a caique.

ety: Borrowed from Italian Il Cairo, from Arabic الْقَاهِرَة (al-qāhira)

s.def: capital of Egypt — see also Fustat
The capital city of Egypt.
A governorate of Egypt, containing the capital city.
The Egyptian government.
Several places in the United States:
A community in the township of Dawn-Euphemia, Ontario, Canada.

ety: Borrowed from French caisson. Doublet of cassone and cajón.

s.def: A (permanent) enclosure from which water can be expelled, in order to give access to underwater areas for engineering works etc.
ex: Caissons were enclosed dry chambers built on river beds to facilitate the construction of bridge piers.

s.def: A structure with similar function that is temporary.
A coffer (sunken panel).
The gate across the entrance to a drydock.
A floating tank that can be submerged, attached to an underwater object and then pumped out to lift the object by buoyancy.
ex: Near-synonym: pontoon

s.def: A two-wheeled, horse-drawn military vehicle used to carry ammunition (and a coffin at funerals).
ex: Near-synonym: limber
Over hill, over dale / As we hit the dusty trail, / And those caissons go rolling along.

s.def: A large box to hold ammunition.
A chest filled with explosive materials, used like a mine.

ety: From Middle English caitif, from Anglo-Norman caitif (“captive”), akin to Old French chaitif (French chétif) and Middle Dutch keytyf, from a Vulgar Latin *cactīvus alteration via Gaulish influence from Latin captīvus (“captive”); compare Italian cattivo (“bad, wicked”). Doublet of captive.

s.def: A base or despicable person; a wretch.
A captive or prisoner, particularly a galley slave.
A villain, a coward or wretch.
Especially despicable; cowardly
ex: Beshrew those caitiff scouts that conspired to sully his honest name by such an imputation!
Commingled are they with that caitiff choir Of Angels, who have not rebellious been, Nor faithful were to God, but were for self.

ety: Borrowed from French cajoler, probably a blend of Middle French cageoler (“chatter like a jay”) (from gajole, dialectal diminutive of geai (“jaybird”)) + Old French gaioler (“entice into a cage”), which is from Medieval Latin gabiola, from Late Latin caveola (whence English caveola), diminutive of Latin cavea (“cage, coop, enclosure, stall”). More at cage, cave, cavum, cavus, and jail.

s.def: To persuade someone to do something which they are reluctant to do, especially by flattery or promises; to coax.
ex: If you are cajoled by the cunning arguments of a trumpeter of heresy, or the praises of a puritanic old woman, is not that womanish?
He had tried bullying, and without success. He would try cajoling and temptation.
[W]ith eloquent arts he had cajoled a young girl into a secret marriage.

s.def: The act of cajoling.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Germanic *kakǭ Old Norse kakabor. Middle English cake English cake From Middle English cake, from Old Norse kaka (“cake”) (compare Norwegian kake, Icelandic/Swedish kaka, Danish kage), from Proto-Germanic *kakǭ, of disputed origin. Likely a distant cognate with kaak. Perhaps related to cookie, kuchen, and quiche. Doublet of coca (pastry).

s.def: A rich, sweet dessert food, typically made of flour, sugar, and eggs and baked in an oven, and often covered in icing.
ex: On Monday afternoon, Ronya attends a birthday party and eats cake whenever cake is presented to her.

s.def: A small mass of baked dough, especially a thin loaf from unleavened dough.
ex: an oatmeal cake
a johnnycake

s.def: A thin wafer-shaped mass of fried batter; a griddlecake or pancake.
ex: buckwheat cakes

s.def: A block of any various dense materials.
ex: a cake of soap
a cake of sand
Cakes of rustling ice come rolling down the flood.

s.def: Ellipsis of piece of cake: a trivially easy task or responsibility.
ex: Now that I escape, sleepwalk awake / Those who could relate know the world ain't cake

s.def: Synonym of money.
Ellipsis of have one's cake and eat it too.
ex: "It looks like the cake philosophy is still alive." Quote attributed to Donald Tusk.

s.def: Synonym of buttocks, especially a pair that are exceptionally plump or full.
ex: Since I started doing squats, I've built up some serious cake.

s.def: A multishot fireworks assembly comprising several tubes, each with a fireworks effect, lit by a single fuse.
Synonym of pie, the whole of a wealth or resource, to be divided into parts.

ety: From cake + walk. Originally an African-American form of dance and music that developed after the Civil War, later popularised by minstrel shows. It was danced at social events, with the best dancers often receiving cake as a prize. It derives from dance competitions by plantation slaves in which the style of dance lampooned the ballroom dances of the slaveowners. Slaveowners seem to have found the competitions entertaining and the habit of offering cake may originate from this period. The name…

s.def: A contest in which cake was offered for the best dancers.
The style of music associated with such a contest.
The dance, or strutting style of dance, associated with such a contest.
Something that is easy or simple, or that does not present a great challenge.
ex: Just as common as she is, a cakewalk sort of a name.
Nah. The first step’s a cakewalk. We can beat the hell out of a developing infant, in any case.

s.def: To perform the cakewalk dance.

ety: From French calebasse, from Spanish calabaza (“gourd; pumpkin”), possibly from Arabic قَرْعَةٌ يَابِسَةٌ (qarʕatun yābisatun, “dry gourd”) or directly from its etymon Persian خربزه (xarboze, “melon”), possibly ultimately from Sanskrit त्रपुस (trapusa, “colocynth fruit”) (compare Persian تربزه (tarboze, “watermelon”)). The English word is cognate with Catalan carabassa (“pumpkin; orange colour”), Galician cabaza (“gourd, pumpkin, squash; calabash (container)”), Occitan calebasso, carabasso, carb…

s.def: The bottle gourd (calabash vine, Lagenaria siceraria), believed to have originated in Africa, which is grown for its fruit that are used as a vegetable and to make containers (sense 3); the fruit of this plant.

A tree (known as the calabash tree; Crescentia cujete) native to Central and South America, the West Indies, and southern Florida, bearing large, round fruit used to make containers (sense 3); the fruit of this tree.
ex: There was a teacher who taught children to read under a calabash tree, and this teacher's name was Goso.

s.def: A container made from the mature, dried shell of the fruit of one of the above plants; also, a similarly shaped container made from some other material.
ex: [...] we would pour water from the tank over ourselves with a calabash and finish by splashing on the Agua Florida from Lanman & Kemps […]

s.def: A calabash and its contents; as much as fills such a container.
ex: It was dusk by the time Yandi reappeared, carrying a calabash of parboiled rice and a peanut and chili sauce on his head.

s.def: A musical instrument, most commonly a drum or rattle, made from a calabash fruit.
The head.
ex: ‘What d’ye say about rewardin’ this yer young gent, as walloped his chum on the callybash to help us?’ Ben called after them.

ety: From Cajun French calabousse, from Spanish calabozo. Doublet of calabozo.

s.def: A prison or jail/gaol.
ex: Bogator: (Still unbelieving) And you turned the calaboose over?
[…] he had but recently come out of Calaboose, where he had been serving a term for debt […]

ety: From French Calais and Middle English Caleys (from Anglo-Norman Caleis), from the Roman name, Latin Caletum, named after the Caleti, a Gaulish tribe in the area, from Proto-Celtic *kaletos, from Proto-Indo-European *kal- (“hard”). The placename is cognate with Breton calet, Middle Irish calath, and calad.

s.def: A city in Pas-de-Calais department, Hauts-de-France, France.
A city in Washington County, Maine, United States.
A town in Washington County, Vermont, United States (both states have a Washington County).

ety: From Sinhalese [script needed] (kaḷu-madīriya), perhaps from Coromandel ebony (see coromandel), changed by association with Sinhalese කළු (kaḷu, “black”); or perhaps a metathetic variant of coromandel via Dutch kalamanderhout.

s.def: A wood from India and Sri Lanka, of a hazel-brown color, with black stripes, very hard in texture. It is a kind of ebony obtained from species of Diospyros, especially Diospyros quaesita, used to make furniture.

ety: Borrowed from Italian calamari, plural of calamaro, from Latin calamarius, from calamus, from Ancient Greek κάλαμος (kálamos, “reed, ink pen”).

s.def: Squid as food, especially cooked in the form of calamari rings.
Squid, the mollusk.

ety: From Middle French calamité, from Latin calamitās (“loss, damage; disaster”).

s.def: An event resulting in great loss.
ex: And the village was deserted, the huts gaped black, rotting, all askew within the fallen enclosures. A calamity had come to it, sure enough.

s.def: The distress that results from some disaster.

ety: Learned borrowing from Latin calamus (“reed, cane”). Doublet of culm, haulm, helm (Etymology 4, stalk), qalam, and shawm.

s.def: Sweet flag (Acorus calamus).
Synonym of fistula (“tube for sucking Eucharist wine”).
A quill; the hard, horny, hollow, and more or less transparent part of the stem or scape of a feather.
ex: In follicles late in feather growth, after rupture of the feather sheath, this canal contained the upper part of the calamus.
Chapin asserted that the calamus is firmly fixed in the wing

s.def: A fish of genus Calamus in family Sparidae; certain porgies.
A palm in genus Calamus, of rattan palms.
A fistular stem without an articulation.
Any bird in the genus Melanocorypha, but especially in the species Melanocorypha calandra of the Mediterranean region and central Asia.

ety: From Tagalog Calapan.

s.def: A city, the provincial capital of Oriental Mindoro, Mimaropa, Philippines.

ety: From French calèche.

s.def: Alternative form of calèche (“type of carriage with low wheels”).
A silk and whalebone hood worn by ladies to shade the face.

ety: From Latin calcāneus (“heel”), rare form of calx (“heel”).

s.def: The large bone making up the heel of the human foot, the heel bone.

ety: Learned borrowing from Latin calcārius (“of or pertaining to lime”), derived from calx (“lime”). Similar to calcium.

s.def: Resembling, containing, or composed of calcium carbonate or limestone; chalky.
Growing in a chalky habitat.

ety: From translingual Calceolaria, the genus of slipperworts, from Latin calceolus (“slipper, little shoe”) + -āria (“-ary: forming plant names”), from calceus (“calceus, footwear”) + -olus (“-ole: forming diminutives”), , from calx (“heel”) + -eus (adjective-forming suffix).

s.def: Any plant of the genus Calceolaria.

ety: From calci- + -ic.

s.def: Of, pertaining to, or derived from calcium or lime.
ex: The echostructure is mixed, cystic with more or less echogenous zones that are connective, fatty, or calcic structures.

ety: Etymology tree Pre-Greekbor.? Ancient Greek χᾰ́λῐξ (khắlĭx)bor.? substratebor.? Latin calx Proto-Indo-European *-om Proto-Italic *-om Latin -umder. English -ium English calcium English calci- Proto-Indo-European *bʰer- Proto-Indo-European *-eti Proto-Indo-European *bʰéreti Proto-Italic *ferō Latin ferō Proto-Indo-European *h₃ed- Proto-Indo-European *-os Proto-Indo-European *h₃édosder.? Proto-Italic *-ŏ̄dsos? Old Latin -ōssus Latin -ōsus Old French -usbor. Middle English -ous English -ous Englis…

s.def: Yielding or containing calcium, calcium carbonate or calcite.

ety: Etymology tree English calcify Proto-Indo-European *-tis Proto-Indo-European *-Hō Proto-Indo-European *-tiHō Proto-Italic *-tiō Latin -tiō Latin -ātiōlbor. Old French -ationbor. Middle English -acioun English -ation English calcification From calcify + -ation.

s.def: The process of change into a stony or calcareous substance by the deposition of lime salt; normally, as in the formation of bone and of teeth; abnormally, as in the calcareous degeneration of tissue.
ex: An examination of the tooth shows a beautiful specimen of calcification of the dental pulp.

ety: From French calcifier, or from English calcium + -ify.

s.def: To make or become hard and stony by impregnating with calcium salts.
ex: calcify tissue
calcify rapidly
calcify with age

s.def: To make or become rigid or inflexible; to ossify.

ety: Alteration of kalsomine, after Latin calcis, genitive of calx (“lime”).

s.def: A form of whitewash (inexpensive white paint) made from calcium carbonate, glue and water, used to coat wooden or plaster surfaces.
To coat with this substance.

ety: The verb is derived from Late Middle English calcinen (“(alchemy, medicine) to heat (something) until it turns to powder; to change the nature of (something) by heating”) [and other forms], from Old French calciner (modern French calciner (“to calcinate; to calcine”)) and from its etymon Medieval Latin calcināre (“(alchemy) to burn like lime; to reduce to calx”), from Late Latin calcīna (“inorganic material containing calcium, lime”) + -āre (suffix forming present active infinitive forms of ver…

s.def: To heat (a substance) to remove its impurities and refine it.

To heat (a substance) without melting in order to drive off water, etc., and to oxidize or reduce it; specifically, to decompose (carbonates) into oxides, and, especially, to heat (limestone) to form quicklime.
To heat (something) to dry and sterilize it.
To purify or refine (something).
To burn up (something) completely; to incinerate; hence, to destroy (something).
ex: It nothing skills: I cannot help my case: / The Judgment's fire alone can cure this place, / Calcine its clods and set my prisoners free.

s.def: Of a substance: to undergo heating so as to oxidize it.
Something calcined; also, material left over after burning or roasting.

s.def: Synonym of teneral (“of certain insects or other arthropods such as spiders: lacking colour or firmness just after ecdysis (“shedding of the exoskeleton”)”).
Of land: having no vegetation; bare.
Synonym of teneral (“an insect or other arthropod such as a spider which has just undergone ecdysis (“shedding of the exoskeleton”) and so lacks colour or firmness”).
An alluvial flat.
The upper layer of rubble in a quarry which has to be removed to reach the material to be mined.

ety: Borrowed from Latin callum (“hard skin”). Displaced Old English wearr.

s.def: A hardened area of the skin (especially on the foot or hand) caused by repeated friction, wear or use.

The material of repair in fractures of bone; a substance exuded at the site of fracture, which is at first soft or cartilaginous in consistency, but is ultimately converted into true bone and unites the fragments into a single piece.
The new formation over the end of a cutting, before it puts out rootlets.
In orchids, a fleshy outgrowth from the labellum.
In grasses, a hardened extension from the base of a floret, which may or may not elongate and is often covered in hairs or bristles.
A shining area on the frons of many species of Tabanomorpha (horse flies and relatives).
To form such hardened tissue.

ety: From Middle English calm, calme, from Middle French calme, probably from Old Italian calma, of uncertain origin. Calma may derive from Late Latin cauma (“heat of the midday sun”), from Ancient Greek καῦμα (kaûma, “heat, especially of the sun”), from καίω (kaíō, “to burn”), or possibly from Latin caleō. Compare also Lombardic *chalm, *chalma (“frozenness”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *kalmaz (“frozenness, cold”). Displaced native Middle English smilte (“quiet, still, gentle”) from Old Englis…

s.def: Peaceful, quiet, especially free from anger and anxiety.
Free of noise and disturbance.
ex: Calm is the morn without a sound, ⁠Calm as to suit a calmer grief, ⁠And only thro’ the faded leaf The chestnut pattering to the ground: […]

s.def: with few or no waves on the surface; not rippled.
Without wind or storm.
Good; alright; cool; OK.
ex: Been living my life as a Kingpin. I'm calm with the heat of the kitchen.
I really hit for the long ting, calm (Ha, ha). Who would've thought you woulda heard Yung Filly on drill (Filly on drill).

s.def: The state of being calm; peacefulness; absence of worry, anger, fear or other strong negative emotion.
The state of being calm; absence of noise and disturbance.
The absence of wind; a period of time without wind.
ex: The wind ceased, and there was a great calm.
It was a calm ; so, forming a tandem of three boats, we commenced the slow business of towing the trophy to the Pequod.

s.def: To make calm.
ex: to calm a crying baby
to calm the passions
to calm the tempest raised by Aeolus

s.def: To become calm.
A period of peace before a disturbance or crisis; an unnatural or false calm before a storm.
ex: The meeting may be peaceful now, but this is only the calm before the storm.
Calm before the storm, Marines. Enjoy it.

s.def: To become less excited, intense, or angry.
ex: Calm down before you hurt somebody.

s.def: To cause to become less excited, intense, or angry.

ety: From Caló caló.

s.def: a mixed language or dialect spoken by the Spanish and Portuguese Romani.
an argot spoken by pachuco Chicanos in the United States in the early 20th century.

ety: From French calomel.

s.def: Mercurous chloride Hg₂Cl₂, formerly used as a laxative and disinfectant and to treat syphilis.
ex: “Where am I?” said the little spectre, in a pathetic voice. “And why was I born in the Calomel days, and why did I have all that Calomel given me?”

ety: From calorie + -ic. From French calorique, coined by French chemist Antoine Lavoisier, from Latin calor (“heat”).

s.def: Relating to calories.
ex: caloric intake

s.def: Containing calories.
ex: Milk is a caloric beverage.

s.def: Synonym of calorific (“high in calories and thus likely fattening”).
ex: a dry, caloric food

s.def: Synonym of calorific (“relating to or producing heat or other energy”).
The hypothetical medium of heat.
ex: The fluid matter of heat, or Calorique, in which all bodies are immersed, is as necessary to vegetable as to animal existence.
Caloric expands all bodies.
I offered apologies to her beautyship, but she grew furious; and the fiery spots on her face became red-hot with the caloric of anger […]

ety: Borrowed from French calorie, formed from Latin calor. It was originally defined as the large calorie in the early 19th century, with the small calorie being defined some decades later.

s.def: A non-SI unit of energy, equivalent to 4.184 joules, that can raise the temperature of a gram of water by one degree Celsius. This unit was formerly widely used in chemistry and physics.
ex: Holonyms: kilocalorie, calorie (large-calorie sense), large calorie, Calorie (capital C) < megacalorie < gigacalorie

s.def: A non-SI unit of energy, equivalent to 4.184 kilojoules, that can raise the temperature of a kilogram of water by one degree Celsius. This is the unit normally used in food labeling.
ex: Holonyms: megacalorie < gigacalorie
Meronyms: calorie (small-calorie sense), small calorie, gram calorie, thermochemical calorie

der: a calorie is a calorie is a calorie

ety: From French calorifique or Latin calorificus, from calor + -i- + -ficus.

s.def: Relating to calories.
Relating to or producing heat or other energy.
High in calories and thus likely fattening.
The amount of energy produced by the complete combustion of a material or fuel. Measured in units of energy per amount of material, e.g. kJ/kg.
The amount of energy available from an item of food when digested, mostly from carbohydrates and fats

ety: From Latin calor (“warmth, heat”) + -meter.

s.def: An apparatus for measuring the heat generated or absorbed by either a chemical reaction, change of phase or some other physical change.

ety: Borrowed from French calotte.

s.def: A skullcap worn by Roman Catholic priests.
The vertical central area of the crown of a bird's head.

A round cavity or depression, in the form of a cup or cap, lathed and plastered; used to diminish the rise or elevation of a moderate chapel, alcove, etc. which would otherwise be too high for other pieces of the apartment.
The upper (superior) or lower (inferior) half of the globe of the eye.

ety: From Ottoman Turkish قلپاق (Turkish kalpak), from Proto-Turkic or from Middle Persian kwlʾp̄k' (kulāfak, “little cap; calyx”), diminutive of kwlʾp̄ (kulāf, “cap, bonnet”), (Persian کلاهک (kolâhak), diminutive of کلاه (kolâh, “hat”)), or from Proto-Common Turkic *kalpak. Doublet of kolpik.

s.def: A kind of cap from Turkic countries, with a high crown.

ety: From French calque (“calque”, literally “copy, tracing”), from calquer (“to copy, trace”) (whence also calk), itself borrowed from Italian calcare, from Latin calcāre (“to tread”). Doublet of calcate and calcation.

s.def: A word or phrase in a language formed by word-for-word or morpheme-by-morpheme translation of a word in another language.
ex: One of the primary benefits of calque is its ability to enhance cross-cultural communication.

ety: From Middle English calketrappe, from Old English calcatrippe, from Medieval Latin calcatrippa (“thistle”), from Latin calx or calcare (“to tread”) + trappa (“trap”).

s.def: A metal object, usually small, with spikes arranged so that, when thrown onto the ground, one always faces up as a threat to pedestrians, horses, and vehicles (also used as a heraldic charge).
ex: […] her father, the emperor Alexius, who reigned AD 1081-1118, ordered caltrops to be cast in front of his archers […]
By Sung times, several different types of caltrops had been developed. As in earlier times, both caltrops could be made from both wood and iron...
Caltrops, tetrahedrons, and similar devices are designed to puncture vehicle tires or limit foot traffic. The standard design has four points.

s.def: Any of a number of flowering plants in the family Zygophyllaceae, including several members of the genus Kallstroemia and the species Tribulus terrestris, native to warm temperate and tropical regions.
The starthistle, Centaurea calcitrapa, a plant with sharp thorns.

ety: First attested in 1554; borrowed from Latin calumniātus, perfect passive participle of calumnior (“to blame, cavil at; to accuse falsely”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

s.def: To make hurtful untrue comments about.
To levy a false charge against, especially of a vague offense, with the intent to damage someone's reputation or standing.

ety: Etymology tree English calumniate Proto-Indo-European *-tis Proto-Indo-European *-Hō Proto-Indo-European *-tiHō Proto-Italic *-tiō Latin -tiō Latin -ātiōlbor. Old French -ationbor. Middle English -acioun English -ation English -ion English calumniation From calumniate + -ion.

s.def: A false accusation, or a malicious statement, about someone.

ety: From Late Latin calumniōsus.

s.def: Possessing the traits of calumny.

ety: From Late Middle English calumnīe (“false accusation, slander; (law) objection raised in bad faith”), borrowed from Old French calomnie (“slander, calumny”) (modern French calomnie), or directly from its etymon Latin calumnia (“false statement, misrepresentation; false accusation, malicious charge”), perhaps also related to calvor (“to deceive”). The English word is a doublet of challenge. The verb is derived from French calomnier (“to slander”), from Late Latin calumniāre, from Latin calumpniā…

s.def: A false accusation or charge brought to tarnish another's reputation or standing.
Falsifications or misrepresentations intended to disparage or discredit another.
ex: Accusations of abuse were pure extortive calumny in a malicious bid to make money.
Stephen, the first martyr of the Church, was a victim of calumny. And calumny is worse than a sin; calumny is a direct expression of Satan.

s.def: To make false accusations or levy false charges against a person with the intent to tarnish that person's reputation or standing; to calumniate.
ex: His [Dominieus Dietrich's] memory has been basely calumnied by many German historians.
He rails, he piles on the abuse, he calumnies without any sense of decency or restraint, and his gloomy character makes him see everything as black.

ety: From Late Latin calvāria (“skull”). Doublet of calavera and calvaria.

s.def: A life-size representation of the crucifixion of Jesus Christ on a piece of raised ground.
A series of representations of Christ’s Passion in a church.
A type of monumental public Christian cross, sometimes encased in an open shrine.
ex: Calvaries are typical of Galicia (Spain) and Portugal.

s.def: A strenuous experience.
Misspelling of cavalry.

ety: From Middle English calven, from Old English *calfian, cealfian, from Proto-West Germanic *kalbōn, from Proto-Germanic *kalbōną (“to calve”), from *kalbaz (“calf”). Cognate with Saterland Frisian koolvje, Dutch kalven, German Low German kalven, German kalben, Swedish kalva, Icelandic kálfa.

s.def: To give birth to a calf.
ex: The farmer could tell Bessie was about to calve.

s.def: To assist in a cow’s giving birth to a calf.
ex: The farmer calved Bessie for almost two hours.

s.def: To give birth to (a calf).
To shed a large piece.
ex: The glacier was starting to calve even as we watched.

s.def: To break off.
ex: The sea was dangerous because of icebergs calving off the nearby glacier.

s.def: To shed (a large piece); to set loose (a mass of ice).
ex: The glacier was starting to calve an iceberg even as we watched.

ety: From French calvinisme, equivalent to Calvin + -ism.

s.def: The Christian religious tradition based upon the doctrines and forms of Christian practice of several Protestant reformers, especially John Calvin, in contrast to Catholicism, Lutheranism, Anabaptism, and Arminianism. One distinctive trait of the system is its Augustinian doctrine of predestination…

ety: Borrowed from Latin calvitiēs (“baldness”).

s.def: Baldness, the condition of being bald.
plural of calvity

ety: From Latin calx (“lime”). Doublet of cauk and chalk.

s.def: The substance which remains after a metal or mineral has been thoroughly burnt, once seen as being the essential substance left after the expulsion of phlogiston, but now recognised as being the metallic oxide (or, in some cases, the metal in a state of sublimation).
In the Eton College wall game, an area at the end of the field where a shy can be scored by lifting the ball against the wall with one's foot.

ety: From Latin calyculus (“small flower bud, calyx”), diminutive of calyx. See calyx and compare calicle. By surface analysis, calyc- + -le.

s.def: calyculus

ety: Originally Trinidad English, an alteration of kaiso, perhaps ultimately of African origin; Allsopp 1996 suggests Ibibio ka iso (“come on”), used to urge dancers on. The spelling reflects a later folk-etymological assimilation with the mythological name Calypso.

s.def: A style of Afro-Caribbean music that originated in Trinidad and Tobago during the early to the mid-19th century and spread to the rest of the Caribbean Antilles and Venezuela by the mid-20th century.
A song in this style of music.
To perform calypso.
A light blue color.
A bulbous bog orchid of the genus Calypso, Calypso bulbosa

ety: From Ancient Greek καλύπτρα (kalúptra, “covering or veiling”).

s.def: In bryophytes, a thin hood of tissue that forms from the archegonium and covers the developing sporophyte and is shed as it ripens.
ex: (b) sporophyte with foot reduced, the entire sporophyte enveloped by the calyptra, which is ± stipitate at the base.

s.def: any cap-like covering of a flower or fruit, such as the operculum over the unopened buds of Eucalyptus flowers
Any of various coverings at the tips of structures, in the terminology of various authors; for example rootcaps and the apical cells of trichomes.

In flies such as the housefly, Musca, in the taxonomic order Diptera, zoological section Schizophora, subsection Calyptrata, the calyptra is a membranous rearward extension of the forewing; it covers the haltere.

ety: From Latin calyx, from Ancient Greek κάλυξ (kálux, “case of a bud, husk”). Doublet of chalice and kelch.

s.def: The outermost whorl of flower parts, comprising the sepals, which covers and protects the petals as they develop.
Any of various cup-like structures.

ety: Unadapted borrowing from French camaraderie. Recent American pronunciations such as /ˌkɑməˈɹɑdəɹi/ and /ˌkɑmˈɹɑdəɹi/ are influenced by the cognate comrade.

s.def: A close friendship in a group of friends or teammates.
ex: Moreover, a spirit of camaraderie exists between the staff of the railway and its regular patrons.
And regardless of their differences, they always act with such camaraderie and complicity among themselves.

s.def: A spirit of familiarity and closeness, especially when expressed somewhat boisterously.

ety: Borrowed from Spanish camarilla, from cámara (“chamber”) and the diminutive suffix -illa.

s.def: A secret, usually sinister, group of conspiring advisors close to the leadership; a cabal.

ety: From Old French cambre (“bent”), from Latin camurum, from camur (“arched”).

s.def: A slight convexity, arching or curvature of a surface of a road, beam, roof, ship's deck etc., so that liquids will flow off the sides.
ex: The track was stony with a grassy camber up the middle.

s.def: The slope of a curved road created to minimize the effect of centrifugal force.
ex: Even a small camber one way caused the whole outfit to list alarmingly.

s.def: An upward concavity in the underside of a beam, girder, or lintel; also, a slight upward concavity in a straight arch.
The alignment on the roll axis of the wheels of a road vehicle, where positive camber signifies that the wheels are closer together at the bottom than the top.
The curvature of an airfoil.
A small enclosed dock in which timber for masts (etc.) is kept to weather.
To curve upwards in the middle.
To adjust the camber of the wheels of a vehicle.
ex: Because he cambered the tires too much, he had less control on the turns.

ety: From French cambiste, Italian cambista, from Latin cambire (“to exchange”). See change.

s.def: A banker; a money changer or broker; one who deals in bills of exchange, or who is skilled in the science of exchange.

ety: Borrowed from Late Latin cambium (“a change”), from Gaulish. Doublet of change.

s.def: A layer of cells between the xylem and the phloem that is responsible for the secondary growth of roots and stems.
ex: During winter we perceive no change in the cells of the cambium layer, which are filled with nutritive matter […].

s.def: Periosteum, a membrane that covers the outer surface of bones
One of the humours formerly believed to nourish the bodily organs.

ety: Borrowed from French Cambodge and Portuguese Camboja. Doublet of Kampuchea and gamboge.

ety: Of unclear origin, inspired by George Gaylord Simpson's description of "explosive" evolution. The earliest known use is in a BSCS high school biology textbook written in 1961 under the direction of paleobotanist Wilson Steward.

ety: From Cambrai, a French commune where it was manufactured.

ex: Scotch cambric, now largely manufactured, is a kind of imitation cambric, made from fine hard-twisted cotton.
His upper tunic was of white cambric, as fine as a handkerchief, so that the bright red tunic beneath it showed through.

ety: From Middle English camel, through Old English camel and Old Northern French camel (Old French chamel, modern French chameau), from Latin camēlus, from Ancient Greek κάμηλος (kámēlos), from a Semitic source, ultimately from Proto-Semitic *gamal-; compare Arabic جَمَل (jamal), Hebrew גמל (gamál), Aramaic ܓܡܠܐ (gamlā), Coptic ϭⲁⲙⲟⲩⲗ (čamoul). ex: Returne our Mules and emptie Camels backe, That we may trauell into Siria, […]
Achilles! a drayman, a porter, a very camel.

A vessel or tank, typically paired, used to make an object more buoyant.
ex: Near-synonym: pontoon

A fairy chess piece that is moved three squares in one direction and one at right angles to that direction in a single move, leaping over any intervening pieces.

a camel is a horse made by a committee

ety: With reference to the New Testament, Mark 10.25, Mat. 19.24 and Luke 18.25. See the Citations page for those texts.

ex: Getting George to wake up before 7 o'clock is harder than getting a camel through the eye of a needle.

ety: Borrowed from translingual Camellia, named after Moravian botanist Joseph Kamel (‘Camellus’) (1661–1706). The Czech surname Kamel is a variant of Kamil.

ety: Learned borrowing from Latin camēlopardus, variant of camēlopardalis, from Ancient Greek καμηλοπάρδαλις (kamēlopárdalis, “giraffe”).

s.def: Synonym of giraffe.
Alternative form of camlet.

ety: From Dutch kameeldoorn, Afrikaans kameeldoring. Equivalent to camel + thorn.

Vachellia erioloba, formerly Acacia erioloba, a tree native to southern Africa.

ety: From camel + toe, from a reference to the visual similarity in appearance to the two toes of a camel’s hoof.

s.def: The pudendal cleft itself.

ety: From Camembert, the Normandy village where it originated.

s.def: A soft, creamy cheese from France made from cow's milk.

ety: Borrowed from Italian cammeo, from Medieval Latin camaeus, of unknown origin. The movie sense is short for “cameo role” referring to a famous person who was playing no character, but him or herself. Like a cameo brooch — a low-relief carving of a person’s head or bust — the actor or celebrity is instantly recognizable. More recently, it has come to refer to any short appearances, whether as a character or as oneself. Doublet of camaieu.

s.def: A piece of jewelry, etc., carved in relief.
ex: SIMONE: And he tracked down Mom's cameo—the one Dad pawned? He outbid fourteen other buyers on eBay.

s.def: A single very brief appearance, especially by a prominent celebrity in a movie or song.
ex: As they turned into Hertford Street they startled a robin from the poet's head on a barren fountain, and he fled away with a cameo note.
Dr. Helen O’Connell, Australia’s first female urologist, recalled that in her own medical training, the clitoris barely made a cameo.

s.def: To appear in a cameo role.

ety: Learned borrowing from Latin camera (“chamber or bedchamber”), from Ancient Greek καμάρα (kamára, “anything with an arched cover, a covered carriage or boat, a vaulted chamber, a vault”), of Old Iranian origin, from Proto-Iranian *kamarā- (“something curved”), from *kamárati, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *kmárati, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kh₂em- (“to bend, curve”). A judge's private chamber, where cases may be heard in camera.

A light jacket with sleeves.
To straitjacket.
ex: He believes it better to camisole a patient than to seclude him.

ety: From Middle English chamelet, chamelot, chamlot via Old French chamelot, suffixed + -ot from Arabic خَمْلَة (ḵamla, “velvet”).

ex: She was richly clad in a bodice of gold-coloured camlet and a skirt of gray silk trimmed with gold and silver lace.

Ellipsis of camomile tea.
A beverage made by infusing the leaves of the camomile plant (either Matricaria recutita or Chamaemelum nobile) in hot water.

ety: Adopted in 16th century from Spanish canoa, from Taíno *kanowa (“dugout canoe”) (compare Lokono kanoa (“canoe”), Wayuu anuwa, anua (“boat, canoe”)), from Proto-Arawak *kanawa.

s.def: A small long and narrow boat, propelled by one or more people (depending on the size of canoe), using single-bladed paddles. The paddlers face in the direction of travel, in either a seated position, or kneeling on the bottom of the boat. Canoes are open on top, and pointed at both ends.
ex: The canoe is of pure black oak, and is in excellent preservation.
He and Gerald usually challenged the rollers in a sponson canoe when Gerald was there for the weekend; […]

s.def: An oversize, usually older, luxury car.
Any of the deflectors positioned around a roulette wheel, shaped like upside-down boats.
To ride or paddle a canoe.
ex: Car drivers were helicoptered to safety from nearby roads. There were photographs of people canoeing down streets.

s.def: To split someone's head with a round.

ety: From canoe + -ing.

s.def: A water sport involving travelling or racing in canoes or kayaks.
ex: Their adventures are much more thrilling than your summer hikes and canoeings.

s.def: When a cigar, cigarette, or joint burns unevenly, burning more on one side.

ety: From Middle English canoun, from Old French canon and Old English canon, both from Latin canōn, from Ancient Greek κανών (kanṓn, “measuring rod, standard”), akin to κάννα (kánna, “reed”), from Semitic (compare Hebrew קָנֶה (qane, “reed”) and Arabic قَنَاة (qanāh, “reed”)). Doublet of qanun. See also cane, cannon, canyon, canal.

s.def: A generally accepted principle; a rule.
ex: The trial must proceed according to the canons of law.
Or that the Everlasting had not fixed His canon 'gainst self-slaughter.

s.def: A group of literary works that are generally accepted as representing a field.
ex: Russo had been working as a salesman, selling Great Books of the Western World, hawking the canon to the rubes.
the durable canon of American short fiction

s.def: The works of a writer that have been accepted as authentic.
ex: the entire Shakespearean canon

s.def: A eucharistic prayer, particularly the Roman Canon.
A religious law or body of law decreed by the church.
ex: We must proceed according to canon law.

s.def: A catalogue of saints acknowledged and canonized in the Roman Catholic Church.
In monasteries, a book containing the rules of a religious order.
A piece of music in which the same melody is played by different voices, but beginning at different times; a round.
ex: Pachelbel’s Canon has become very popular.

s.def: A rent or stipend payable at some regular time, generally annual, e.g., canon frumentarius
ex: The lessees of public lands had to pay a perpetual rent or "canon" at some periodical time.

s.def: The officially recognized continuity, events, characters, relationships, etc. of a work of fiction.
ex: A spin-off book series revealed the aliens to be originally from Earth, but it's not canon.

ety: From Middle English canonycal, from Medieval Latin canōnicālis. By surface analysis, canon + -ical.

s.def: Present in a canon, religious or otherwise.
ex: The Gospel of Luke is a canonical New Testament book.

s.def: According to recognised or orthodox rules.
ex: The men played golf in the most canonical way, with no local rules.

s.def: Stated or used in the most basic and straightforwardly applicable manner.
ex: the reduction of a linear substitution to its canonical form

s.def: Prototypical.
In conformity with canon law.
In the form of a canon.
Of or pertaining to an ecclesiastical chapter.
In canonical form.
Distinguished among entities of its kind, so that it can be picked out in a way that does not depend on any arbitrary choices.
Related to or part of the canon of a fictional universe; officially part of a fictional work’s established continuity.
plural of canonical

ety: From canon + -ist.

s.def: An expert in canon law; canon lawyer.

s.def: To declare (a deceased person) as a saint, and enter them into the canon of saints.
ex: Thomas Becket was canonized in 1173.
Prospective candidates for sainthood normally need to have two miracles attributed to them before they can be canonized.

s.def: To regard as a saint; to glorify, to exalt to the highest honour.
ex: I am no mediæval maid, / Of saints obscure to brag on, / But one there is I canonize— / St. George who killed the dragon.

s.def: To formally declare (a piece of religious writing) to be part of the biblical canon.
ex: Not all psalms that claim Davidic authorship were included in the canon, but those that were canonized frequently had this association.

s.def: To regard (an artistic or written work or its creator) as one of a group that are representative of a particular field.
Especially of a church: to give official approval to; to authorize, to sanction.

ety: The origin of the verb is uncertain; the following possibilities have been suggested: * From a blend of ca(ress) + noodle (“to engage in frivolous behavior; to fool around or waste time; to mess around, to play”). * From German knuddeln (“to cuddle; (originally) to embrace tightly”); or related to Low German knuddle (“a clump, a knot”), a diminutive of knude, related to Old High German knodo, knoto (“a knot”) (modern German Knoten (“knot”)); ultimate etymology unknown. s.def: Of a person: to caress, fondle, or pet another person; of two people: to caress, fondle, or pet each other; also, to have sexual intercourse; to make love.
ex: Young Robin and my daughter. / ‘Canoodling’ too. This must lead to manslaughter.
Gerald Arbuthnot sat with her in the library all the time Jim was upstairs dying and they canoodled together on the sofa in front of the fire.
You may have been a classy, demure teenager, but I was a pragmatist, a hedge-better. And it was often hedges in which I canoodled.

s.def: To caress, fondle, or pet (someone); also, to have sexual intercourse with (someone); to make love with.
ex: He’s got a big smile on his face—who’s he been canoodling recently?

s.def: To cajole or persuade (someone).
ex: “There,” she cried triumphantly, when her labours were finished, “it [the drawing-room] looks different now, really quite effective and ‘canoodling’.”
He canoodled my husband into believin' that the end of the world was comin' and it was his duty to give all his property away.

ety: From Middle English canapy, canepie, canapee, canape, canope, from Old French conopé, Medieval Latin canapeum, canopeum, from Latin cōnōpēum (“mosquito net, canopy”), from Ancient Greek κωνωπεῖον (kōnōpeîon, “mosquito net”), from Ancient Greek κώνωψ (kṓnōps, “mosquito”), of uncertain origin. More at Ancient Greek κώνωψ (kṓnōps). Doublet of canapé and conopeum.

s.def: A high cover providing shelter, such as a cloth supported above an object, particularly over a bed.

s.def: Any overhanging or projecting roof structure, typically over entrances or doors.
The zone of the highest foliage and branches of a forest.
In an airplane, the transparent cockpit cover.
In a parachute, the cloth that fills with air and thus limits the falling speed.
To cover with or as if with a canopy.
ex: Away before me to sweet beds of flowers: Love-thoughts lie rich when canopied with bowers.
I sat me down to watch upon a bank With ivy canopied, and interwove With flaunting honeysuckle […]

ety: From Latin cantō, probably via Old Northern French canter (“sing, tell”). Doublet of chant.

ety: From French cantaloup, from Italian Cantalupo (a place name), from Italian canto + lupo, literally "howl of the wolf". Named after Cantalupo in Sabina, a former Papal summer estate near Rome, where the melons were first grown after being introduced to Europe.

Cucumis melo Cantalupensis Group, a cultivar group melon with sweet aromatic orange flesh, including two main types:
ex: Trevor, like an Aussie outbacker, eats snacks and a pickup meal of bread, cantaloupe, olives, mangoes, and melon.

s.def: An orange colour, like that of cantaloupe flesh.
A woman's breasts, particularly large breasts.
ex: "Suzie that one with the pair of cantaloupes?" Freddy holds his palms out from chest.

ety: Perhaps derived from earlier contenkerous, from contentious + rancorous.

s.def: The person lawfully in command of a ship or other vessel.
ex: The captain is the last man to leave a sinking ship.

s.def: An army officer with a rank between the most senior grade of lieutenant and major.
A chief or leader.
ex: For out of the shal come a captaine, whych shall govern my people israhel.
Stand up-stand up, Northumberland! / I bid you answer true, / If England's King has under his hand / A Captain as good as you?

s.def: A naval officer with a rank between commander and commodore.

A commissioned officer in the United States Navy, Coast Guard, NOAA Corps, or PHS Corps of a grade superior to a commander and junior to a rear admiral (lower half). A captain is equal in grade or rank to a United States Army, Marine Corps, or Air Force colonel.
A rank qualifying an airline pilot to act as pilot in command of a two-pilot flight crew.
One of the athletes on a sports team who is designated to make decisions, and is allowed to speak for his team with a referee or official.
ex: Captain's supposed to be the leader, right?

s.def: The leader of a group of workers.
ex: John Henry said to the captain, "A man ain't nothing but a man."

s.def: The head boy of a school.
A maître d', a headwaiter.

ety: Coined by a team of researchers at Carnegie Mellon University in 2000 as a loose acronym of “completely automated public Turing test to tell computers and humans apart”.

s.def: A computerized test requiring the human user to perform a task deemed to be difficult to automate, such as entering a displayed series of distorted characters or describing images, to demonstrate that they are a human and not a computer program.
ex: A CAPTCHA is a quick check to make sure that an actual person, rather than a computer program, is using the website. Web applications use CAPTCHA […]

ety: Borrowed from Latin captiō (“deception, fraud”), from the past participle of capiō (“to take, to seize”) (English capture). Compare Middle English capcioun (“seizure, capture”).

s.def: The descriptive heading or title, of a document or part thereof.
A title or brief explanation attached to an illustration, cartoon, user interface element, etc.
ex: Some of the photographs are new and interesting, but many captions are amateurish, uninformative or simply careless.

s.def: The section on an official paper (for example, as part of a seizure or capture) that describes when, where, and what was taken, found or executed, and who authorized the act.
A seizure or capture, especially of tangible property (chattel).
A story that is embedded in a pre-existing image (sometimes with image manipulation)
A piece of text appearing on screen as a subtitle or other part of a film or broadcast, describing dialogue (and sometimes other sound) for viewers who cannot hear.
ex: (theater, performance production) By analogy, text in a similar system used in a performance venue for transcription of a live event.

s.def: To add captions to a text or illustration.
ex: Only once the drawing is done will the letterer caption it.

s.def: To add captions to a film or broadcast.

ety: From Middle English capcious, from Middle French captieux, or its source, Latin captiōsus, from captiō.

s.def: Having a disposition to find fault unreasonably or to raise petty objections; cavilling, nitpicky.
That captures; especially, (of an argument, words etc.) designed to capture or entrap in misleading arguments; sophistical.

ety: Learned borrowing from Late Latin captīvātus, the perfect passive participle of captīvō (“to capture”), from Latin captīvus (“captive, prisoner”) (ultimately from capiō (“to capture, seize”), from Proto-Indo-European *kap- (“to hold; to seize”)) + -ō (suffix forming first-conjugation verbs). Equivalent to captive + -ate (verb-forming suffix).

s.def: To make (a person, an animal, etc.) a captive; to take prisoner; to capture, to subdue.
To capture or control (the mind, etc.); to subdue, to subjugate.
ex: 'Tis a greater credit to know the ways of captivating Nature, and making her subserve our purposes, than to have learned all the intrigues of policy.

s.def: To attract and hold (someone's) attention and interest; to charm, to entrance, to fascinate, to enchain.
Made captive; taken prisoner; captured, subdued.

ety: Inherited from Middle English captif; derived from Latin captīvus, probably through a borrowing from a Middle French intermediate. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kap- (“seize, hold”). Doublet of caitiff.

s.def: One who has been captured or is otherwise confined.
ex: I envy not in any moods ⁠The captive void of noble rage, ⁠The linnet born within the cage, That never knew the summer woods: […]

s.def: One held prisoner.
One charmed or subdued by beauty, excellence, or affection; one who is captivated.
A captive insurance company, a subsidiary of a company used as its internal insurer.
Held prisoner; not free; confined.
ex: A poor, miserable, captive thrall.

s.def: Subdued by love; charmed; captivated.
ex: Even in so short a space, my woman's heart / Grossly grew captive to his honey words.

s.def: Of or relating to bondage or confinement; serving to confine.
ex: captive chains; captive hours

s.def: To capture; to take captive.

ety: From Middle English captivite, from Latin captīvitās. By surface analysis, captive + -ity. Entered into the English lexicon around the 14th century.

s.def: The state of being captive.
ex: held in captivity
escape from captivity
The animals lived in captivity at the zoo.

s.def: A group of people/beings captive.
The state or period of being imprisoned, confined, or enslaved.
ex: long captivity

ety: Borrowed from Late Latin captor, from Latin capiō. English usage began around 1688.

s.def: One who is holding a captive or captives.
One who catches or has caught or captured something or someone.

ety: Borrowed from Middle French capture (noun), from Latin captūra. Displaced native Old English fenġ (noun) and ġefōn (verb).

s.def: To take control of; to seize by force or stratagem.
ex: to capture an enemy, a vessel, or a criminal

s.def: remove or take control of opponent’s piece
An act of capturing; a seizing by force or stratagem.
ex: even with regard to captures made at sea

s.def: The securing of an object of strife or desire, as by the power of some attraction.
ex: the capture of a lover’s heart

s.def: Something that has been captured; a captive.
The recording or storage of something for later playback.
ex: video capture

s.def: A particular match found for a pattern in a text string.
ex: After the match […], the text matched within the named capture is available via the Match object's Groups(name) property.

s.def: To take hold of.
ex: The paintings in the gallery really captured my imagination.

s.def: To store (as in sounds or image) for later revisitation.
ex: She captured the sounds of a subway station on tape.
She captured the details of the fresco in a series of photographs.

s.def: To reproduce convincingly.
ex: His film adaptation captured the spirit of the original work.
In her latest masterpiece, she captured the essence of Venice.

ety: First use appears c. 1589, from French capuchin, from earlier capucin, from Italian cappuccino, ultimately from Late Latin cappa (“cape, hood”).

s.def: A monk in the Order of Friars Minor Capuchin; (generally) a Franciscan.
ex: “That is something,” said the capuchin, “but not the most essential. Are you certain that he is a Christian?”

s.def: A garment consisting of a cloak and hood, made in imitation of the dress of Capuchin monks.
ex: Of Ermine is his doublet — / His Capuchin gay —

s.def: A capuchin monkey.
A hooded pigeon.

ety: From the resemblance to the dress of a Capuchin monk.

s.def: Any New World monkey of the subfamily Cebinae.

ety: From Spanish capibara, from Portuguese capivara, from Old Tupi kapi'iûara (literally “grass eater”).

s.def: A large semi-aquatic South American rodent of the genus Hydrochoerus.
The greater capybara (true capybara).
ex: It was tenanted by the small caymans and by capybaras—the largest known rodent, a huge aquatic guinea-pig, the size of a small sheep.

ety: Inherited from Middle English carre, borrowed from Anglo-Norman carre, from Old Northern French (compare Old French char), from Latin carrus (“two-wheeled baggage wagon”), from Gaulish *karros, from Proto-Celtic *karros (“wagon”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱr̥sós (“vehicle”). Doublet of carrus and horse.

s.def: A wheeled vehicle that moves independently, with at least three wheels, powered mechanically, steered by a driver and mostly for personal transportation but relatively smaller than a truck/lorry and a bus.
ex: He drove his car to the theatre.
He was thinking about buying a brand new car.
I'm a stunt; ride in the car with some bump in the trunk.

s.def: The moving, load-carrying component of an elevator or other cable-drawn transport mechanism.
ex: Fix the car of the express elevator - the door is sticking.

s.def: A wheeled vehicle, drawn by a horse or other animal.
ex: He has deserved it [armour], were it carbuncled Like holy Phoebus’ car.
In a poem by Sappho, Aphrodite is represented as riding in a car drawn by sparrows.

s.def: Any vehicle designed to run on rails, especially an unpowered one towed by being connected to others.
ex: The conductor coupled the cars to the locomotive.

s.def: The passenger-carrying portion of certain amusement park rides, such as Ferris wheels.
ex: The most exciting part of riding a Ferris wheel is when your car goes over the top.

s.def: The part of an airship, such as a balloon or dirigible, which houses the passengers and control apparatus.
ex: Everything being apparently in readiness now, I stepped into the car of the balloon, […]

s.def: A sliding fitting that runs along a track.
ex: On boats 25 feet or more, it is best to mount a mast car and track on the front of the mast so you can adjust the height of the pole above the deck.

s.def: A floating perforated box for living fish.
A clique or gang.
Deliberate misspelling of cat.

A radio receiver fitted in a car, typically on or just below the dashboard, sometimes with specific features for use while driving, such as traffic alert interrupts and alternative frequency functions (switching frequencies as one moves in and out of range of transmitters).
An on-board entertainment system in a car, usually including a radio receiver as well as the capability to play audio from recorded media.
A place at which a car is washed, usually for a fee and often mechanically by driving the car through a tunnel.
ex: I'm going to take the car to the car wash.

s.def: An event at which people (often students) wash cars, often for a small fee or donation
An instance of washing a car, especially such a place.
ex: I'm going to take the car in for a car wash.

ety: Borrowed from French carabinier, from carabine (“carbine”). By surface analysis, carabine + -eer.

s.def: A cavalry soldier.

ety: Shortened from German Karabinerhaken (“carbine hook”), reflecting that such a link was used for gear slinging even before it was used for rock climbing.

s.def: A metal link with a gate that can open and close, generally used for clipping ropes to anchors or other objects or for slinging gear (equipment) on one's person.
ex: A carrabeener (metal clasp used in rock climbing) inside the pipes was devised as a release out, a tactic lent to them by Greenpeace.

ety: Etymology tree French carabin French carabinebor. Italian carabina Italian -iere Italian carabinierebor. English carabiniere Borrowed from Italian carabiniere.

s.def: A member of the carabinieri.

ety: From French caracal, from Ottoman Turkish قره قولاق (kara kulak, literally “black ear”), a calque of Classical Persian سیاهگوش (siyāh-gōš). Compare modern Turkish karakulak.

s.def: A type of cat native to Southern Africa, West Asia, and parts of Central and South Asia, Caracal caracal.

ety: Borrowed from Spanish Caracas. Named after the Caraca tribe.

s.def: The capital city of Venezuela.
The Venezuelan government.

ety: Borrowed from French caracole (noun, literally “snail's shell”), caracoler (verb).

s.def: A half-turn performed by a horse and rider in dressage.
A combat maneuver where riders of the same squadron turn simultaneously to their left or to their right.
ex: How the chargers neigh and champ, / (Their riders weary of camp,) / With curvet and with caracole!
The caracole played a role well into the Thirty Years' War.

s.def: A spiral staircase.
To execute a caracole.

ety: First attested 1786, from French carafe, from Italian caraffa, probably from Arabic غُرْفَة (ḡurfa, “cup or dipper”), from غَرَفَ (ḡarafa, “to ladle”). Doublet of carboy.

s.def: A bottle, usually glass and with a flared lip, used for serving water, wine, or other beverages.
ex: Amongst the scattered letters and papers, there stood a claret jug, a large carafe of water, and an empty glass.
[…]I ask if he'd like something to drink besides the carafe of tap water that has materialised on the table while we've been talking.

s.def: A glass pot with a spout for pouring, used both for serving coffee and as a receptacle during the brewing process.
ex: Emma brings out the carafe of dark coffee.

ety: Borrowed from French caramel, from Spanish caramelo, from Portuguese caramelo, dissimilated from Late Latin calamellus, diminutive of calamus (“reed”) (and a doublet of chalumeau and shawm). Alternatively from Medieval Latin cannamellis, which is a compound of canna + mellis.

s.def: confection
A smooth, chewy, sticky confection made by heating sugar and other ingredients until the sugars polymerize and become sticky.
ex: The usual technique for making caramel is to mix table sugar with some water, then heat until the water has boiled off and the molten sugar colors.

s.def: A (sometimes hardened) piece of this confection.
A yellow-brown color, like that of caramel.
Of a yellow-brown color.
To caramelize.

ety: From caramel + -ization.

s.def: The process that converts sugars into caramel; the process of caramelizing.
The browning of sugars by heat.
ex: Slowly cooking the onions will cause caramelization which will bring out the sweetness and give them a brown color.

ety: Etymology tree English caramel Proto-Indo-European *-id- Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-idyéti Proto-Hellenic *-íd͏̌d͏̌ō Ancient Greek -ῐ́ζω (-ĭ́zō)bor. Late Latin -izōder. Middle French -iserbor. Middle English -isen English -ize English caramelize From caramel + -ize.

s.def: To convert (sugar) into caramel.
To brown (sugar, or a foodstuff containing sugar) by means of heat.
ex: Slowly cooking the onions will caramelize them, which brings out the sweetness and gives them a brown color.

s.def: To undergo this kind of conversion or browning.

ety: Etymology tree substrateder.? Spanish carapachobor. French carapacebor. English carapace Borrowed from French carapace (“tortoise shell”), from Spanish carapacho, of unknown origin, but likely from an extinct Ibero-Mediterranean substrate language. Compare Catalan carabassa, Ancient Greek κάραβος (kárabos, “beetle”), Latin scarabaeus (the source of scarab); also Spanish galápago (“kind of turtle”). Doublet of calipash.

s.def: A hard protective covering of bone or chitin, especially one which covers the dorsal portion of an animal.
That which protects.
ex: So, little by little, youth loosens the hard carapace of confining custom their elders have built over the human heart.
This is all a massive failure of science to pierce the carapace of public ignorance.

ety: From Middle French carat, from Italian carato, from Arabic قِيرَاط (qīrāṭ, “carat, similarly small units such as inches”), from Ancient Greek κεράτιον (kerátion, “hornlet, carob seed”), from κέρας (kéras, “horn”) + -ιον (-ion, diminutive suffix). Doublet of quilate and keratin.

s.def: Any of several small units of mass used for measuring precious stones and pearls, equivalent to 189–212 mg.
A 24-point scale used to measure the purity of gold.
ex: 18-carat gold is 75% gold by mass. 24-carat gold is pure.

s.def: A metric unit of mass equal to exactly 200 mg, chiefly used for measuring precious stones and pearls.

ety: From Middle French caravane, from Old French carvane, from Persian کاروان (kârvân), from Middle Persian kʾlwʾn' (kārawān), from Old Persian 𐎣𐎠𐎼 (k-a-r, “people, subjects”). The word was used to designate a group of people who were travelling by camel or horse on the Silk Road. Doublet of Kairouan.

s.def: A convoy or procession of travellers, their cargo and vehicles, and any pack animals, especially camels crossing a desert.
ex: To the left the caravan animals, securely picketed, at regular distances of some fifteen yards apart, occupied an area of several acres.
The caravan of skilled and experienced designers, tunnellers and builders follows these projects around the world.

s.def: A furnished vehicle towed behind a car, etc., and used as a dwelling when stationary.
A group of camels, especially when used as beasts of burden carrying people and merchandise.
ex: Twice, however, we encountered a caravan of camels-about seventy strong in one instance, and about thirty in the other.

s.def: To travel in a caravan (procession).
ex: The wedding party got in their cars and caravaned from the chapel to the reception hall.

s.def: To travel and/or live in a caravan (vehicle).
ex: When my parents retired they really got back into caravanning.
Norm writes, ‘My wife and I did a lot of caravaning and it certainly didn′t pull the car out of shape, although lots of people thought it would!’

ety: Borrowed either: * from Middle French carvansera, carvassera (modern French caravansérail, carauanserrail (obsolete), caravansara (obsolete)); or * directly from its etymon Ottoman Turkish كاروانسَرای (karvanseray), كَروانسَرای (kervanseray) (modern Turkish kervansaray), from Old Anatolian Turkish [script needed] (kārvān-serā); or * directly from its etymon Persian کاروانسرای (kârvânsarây), from کاروان (kârvân, “caravan; convoy”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ker- (“army”)) + سرای (sarâ…

s.def: A roadside inn, usually having a central courtyard where caravans (see sense 3) can rest, providing accommodation for travellers along trade routes in Asia and North Africa.
ex: But not in sumptuous Caravansary / The adventurer idles there, / Nor satiates wonder with her pomp and wealth; […]

s.def: A place resembling a caravanserai (sense 1) as being a place for resting temporarily, or a meeting place (especially one that is busy, or where people of different cultures encounter each other).
Synonym of caravan (“a convoy of travellers, their cargo and vehicles, and pack animals”).
A hostelry, an inn; also (humorous), an (upscale) hotel.

ety: From Middle French caravelle, from Old French caruelle, carvelle (“caravel”), from Old Galician-Portuguese caravela (“caravel”), a diminutive of caravo, carabo (“type of small vessel”), from Late Latin carabus (“small wicker boat decked with hide”), from Ancient Greek κᾱ́ρᾰβος (kā́răbos, “type of light ship; kind of beetle, probably a longhorn beetle; kind of crustacean, probably a crayfish”).

s.def: A light, usually lateen-rigged sailing ship used by the Portuguese and Spanish for about 300 years from the 15th century, first for trade and later for voyages of exploration.
ex: Thus the brand-new caravel which took [Alvise] Cadamosto to Senegambia in 1455 was a vessel of some fifty-four tons capacity.

ety: From Middle English caraway, carewey, carwey, from Medieval Latin carui, from Arabic كَرَاوِيَا (karāwiyā), via Aramaic from Ancient Greek καρώ (karṓ), κάρον (káron, “caraway”).

s.def: The seed-like fruit of the caraway plant.
A biennial plant of species Carum carvi, native to Europe and Asia, mainly grown for its seed to be used as a culinary spice.
ex: Caraway has a reputed aphrodisiac virtue. It is frequently mentioned in Oriental love manuals.

s.def: A cake or sweetmeat containing caraway seeds.
ex: I'll eat her marchpane and her caraways
the housewife of today can surely match the skill of those of three centuries ago and make "caraways” or cheesecakes

s.def: Any binary compound of carbon and a more electropositive element
The polyatomic ion C2−2, or any of its salts.
The monatomic ion C⁴⁻, or any of its salts.
A carbon-containing alloy or doping of a metal or semiconductor, such as steel.
Tungsten carbide.
trivial name for calcium carbide (CaC₂), used to produce acetylene in bicycle lamps in the early 1900s.

ety: Ca. 1600, from French carabine. Doublet of carabine.

s.def: A rifle with a short barrel.
ex: The lock-up was upstairs, a cage surrounded by six-inch wooden bars, guarded by a constable armed with a carbine.
The man who fired the carbine, who fired the gun with the scope, who brought the lead horse down, was discovered sitting cross-legged in a cargo van.

s.def: Methanol
The compound methanol.
Any substituted methanol.
