s.def: A sugar, starch, or cellulose that is a food source of energy for an animal or plant.
ex: These microbes are primarily responsible for breaking down cellulose and other carbohydrates into volatile fatty acids (VFAs).

s.def: Any food rich in starch or other carbohydrates.
ex: I'm cutting down on carbohydrates like bread and pasta.

s.def: Modified by the addition of carbolic acid

ety: From carbolic + -ize.

s.def: To wash or treat with carbolic acid; to phenolize.

ety: Borrowed from French carbone, coined by Antoine Lavoisier, from Latin carbō, carbōnem (“charcoal, coal”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *kerh₃- (“to burn”).

s.def: The chemical element (symbol C) with an atomic number of 6. It can be found in pure form for example as graphite, a black, shiny and very soft material, or diamond, a colourless, transparent, crystalline solid and the hardest known material.
ex: Carbon is the most common element in our bodies—indeed, in all living things on earth.

s.def: A fossil fuel that is made of impure carbon such as coal or charcoal.
An atom of this element, in reference to a molecule containing it.
ex: A methane molecule is made up of a single carbon with four hydrogens.

s.def: A sheet of carbon paper.
ex: He stepped back and opened his bag and took out a printed pad of D.O.A. forms and began to write over a carbon.

s.def: A carbon copy.
ex: Please provide me with a carbon of your form.
Press firmly: you are making a carbon.

s.def: Soot.
ex: Every morning she cleaned the carbon from the lamp chimneys.

s.def: Ellipsis of carbon dioxide.
ex: carbon neutral
carbon capture

s.def: A carbon rod or pencil used in an arc lamp.
ex: To trim an arc lamp, first remove the old carbons and carefully and thoroughly wipe the carbon rods, holders, &c. with a clean, dry rag.

s.def: A plate or piece of carbon used as one of the elements of a voltaic battery.
Ellipsis of carbon fiber (reinforced polymer).
ex: carbon bike frame

s.def: The normal oxide of carbon, CO₂; a colorless, odorless gas formed during respiration and combustion and consumed by plants during photosynthesis.
ex: There were dozens of presentations in 2008, including: […

ety: Coined in a 1999 BBC Vegetarian Good Food article and after the 1990s term ecological footprint and popularized by a 2005 advertising campaign for fossil-fuel company BP in order to shift blame for climate change onto individual consumers. Modelled after the ecological footprint concept developed in the 1990s.

s.def: A measure of the amount of carbon dioxide produced by a person, organization or state in a given time.
ex: House insulation is another way of reducing energy consumption and carbon footprint, as well as double glazing and draught-proofing.

ety: In mainstream usage since the early 2000s.

s.def: Having an overall zero carbon footprint after carbon emissions trading has been taken into account.
ex: We must accelerate the switch from coal and oil to clean, carbon-neutral power. Such a shift will bring new jobs and growth.

s.def: Paper with one of the faces impregnated with carbon, used to make carbon copies.
The halogenated hydrocarbon tetrachloromethane; a toxic, nonflammable liquid, used as a solvent, formerly used in dry cleaning and in fire extinguishers.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *kerh₃-der.? Latin carbōnemlbor. French carbonebor. English carbon English -aceous English carbonaceous From carbon + -aceous.

s.def: Of, relating to, rich in, or yielding carbon, or a compound of carbon.

ety: The noun is derived from Spanish carbonada (“carbonized”) (from carbonar (“to carbonize”)) + -ado (suffix forming past participles of regular verbs ending in -ar). Carbonada appears to have been modelled after Italian carbonata (“coal pile; stew of beef in red wine”), from carbone (“coal; charcoal”) (from Latin carbō (“coal; charcoal”), from Proto-Indo-European *ker- (“to burn”)) + -ata. The verb is derived from the noun.

s.def: Meat or fish that has been scored and broiled.
To make a carbonado of; to score and broil.
To cut or hack, as in combat.
ex: In Moscow, a Count carbonadoes / His ignorant serfs with the knout; / […] / But Eton has crueller terrors / Than these,—in the Windsor Express.

s.def: A dark, non-transparent, impure form of polycrystalline diamond (also containing graphite and amorphous carbon) used in drilling.

ety: From the Italian carbonara, shortening of alla carbonara (literally “in the manner of charcoal burners”, or “in the manner of the Carbonari”), ultimately from carbone (“coal”).

s.def: A thick Italian pasta sauce, made with guanciale, grated cheese, beaten egg yolks and pepper.
A spaghetti dish made using such a sauce.
A spaghetti dish made using a similar sauce made from a different type of cured pork than guanciale (such as bacon, pancetta, lardons, gammon or ham).

ety: From French carbonate, equivalent of carbon + -ate (“suffix used for salts of acids ending in -ic”).

s.def: Any salt or ester of carbonic acid.
To charge (often a beverage) with carbon dioxide.
Containing carbon dioxide gas under pressure, especially pertaining to beverages, as natural mineral water or man-made drinks.
ex: Soda pop, lemon soda and soda water are carbonated drinks. Champagne and beer are naturally carbonated through fermentation.

s.def: Containing calcium carbonate, often as a result of mineral carbonation.

s.def: The state of having carbon dioxide gas dissolved in a liquid; the act or process of creating that state.
ex: Soda pop is basically sugar water with a little bit of flavoring and added carbonation.

s.def: The amount or level of dissolved carbon dioxide remaining in solution.
ex: Celia didn't eat at the diner anymore because she thought the carbonation in their fountain drinks was off.

s.def: The replacement of calcium hydroxide with calcium carbonate triggered by a chemical reaction.
Synonym of carbonization.

A weak unstable acid, H₂CO₃, known only in solution, and as carbonate salts; it is present in carbonated drinks, and sparkling wine, but decomposes to form carbon dioxide and water.
Carbon dioxide.

ety: From Middle English cas, from Old French cas (“an event”), from Latin cāsus (“a falling, a fall; accident, event, occurrence; occasion, opportunity; noun case”), perfect passive participle of cadō (“to fall, to drop”).

ex: Near-synonym: custos

s.def: A word or expression repeated until it becomes representative of a particular group or time; a slogan or buzzword.
The last word of a speech, serving as a cue for the next speaker.
A word printed (often in large or bold type) at the head of a page or other section of text, serving to draw a reader's attention or summarise contents, especially in a reference work; a heading.

s.def: Instantly appealing and memorable.
ex: Eric wrote a catchy tune to play on his acoustic guitar while Alyssa plays the drums.
This hook is so catchy that I can't stop listening to it!
Because in today's 2,000mph technological freefall, he who coins the catchiest buzzword generally wins the debate by default.

s.def: Tending to catch or ensnare; entangling.
ex: a catchy question

s.def: Consisting of, or occurring in, disconnected parts or snatches; changeable.
ex: a catchy wind
Encyc. of Sport It [the fox's scent] is […] flighty or catchy, if variable.

s.def: Contagious; catching.
ex: The catchy cold which has been transmitted to you directly or indirectly might have been avoided had you been in better physical condition.

ety: From Late Latin catechismus, from Ancient Greek *κατηχισμός (*katēkhismós), from κατηχίζω (katēkhízō, “to catechize”), a later extended form of κατηχέω (katēkhéō, “to catechize, instruct, teach by word of mouth”), from κατά (katá, “down”) + ἠχέω (ēkhéō, “to sound, resound”).

s.def: A book, in question and answer form, summarizing the basic principles of Christianity.
A basic manual in some subject.
A set of questions designed to determine knowledge.
ex: Miss Taylor kept by his side, and resumed her catechism. “Is it a long time since you saw your friend?” “Just over seven years.”

ety: Derived from Latin catēchizāre, from Ancient Greek κατηχίζω (katēkhízō), from κατηχέω (katēkhéō, “to teach (orally)”), from κατά (katá, “down”) + ἠχέω (ēkhéō, “to sound, to resound”).

s.def: To give oral instruction, especially of religion; (specifically) by the formal question-and-answer method; in the Church of England and Roman Catholic Church, to teach the catechism as preparation for confirmation.
To question at length.

ety: Probably a corruption of the Malay kacu.

s.def: A gummy extract of any of several species of Acacieae, but especially Senegalia catechu, produced by boiling the wood of the tree in water and evaporating the resulting liquid.
ex: The pale catechus are usually sweeter and more pleasant for chewing.

ety: From Middle English cathecumynys pl, from Middle French cathecumin (modern French catéchumène) or Ecclesiastical Latin catēchūmenus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek κατηχούμενος (katēkhoúmenos, “being instructed”), present participle passive of κατηχέω (katēkhéō, “sound through, instruct orally, catechise”), from κατά (katá, “down”) + ἠχή (ēkhḗ, “sound”).

s.def: A student of Christian doctrine who studies it for the purpose of adopting it: either a convert to Christianity under instruction before baptism or a young or recent Christian preparing for confirmation.

ex: First, categorize incoming messages according to the needed actions.

s.def: A group, often named or numbered, to which items are assigned based on similarity or defined criteria.
ex: This steep and dangerous climb belongs to the most difficult category.
I wouldn’t put this book in the same category as the author’s first novel.

s.def: A collection of objects, together with a transitively closed collection of composable arrows between them, such that every object has an identity arrow, and such that arrow composition is associative.
ex: One well-known category has sets as objects and functions as arrows.

s.def: A branch of mathematics which deals with spaces and maps between them in abstraction, taking similar theorems from various disparate more concrete branches of mathematics and unifying them.
ex: Holonyms: math, maths, mathematics

ety: From Medieval Latin catena, from Latin catēna (“chain”). Doublet of chain.

s.def: A series of related items.
A series of distinct soils arrayed along a slope.
ex: The changes in soil characteristics from the crest to the foot of a slope are together known as a catena.

ety: Borrowed from Latin catēnātus (“chained”), from catēnāre, from catēna (“chain”).

s.def: To connect things together, especially to form a chain.

ety: From Middle English catour (“acater, provisioner”), aphetic form of acatour (“acater”), from Old French acater (“to buy, to purchase”). Equivalent to cate + -er.

s.def: To provide, particularly
ex: Noe widdowes curse caters a dish of mine.

s.def: To provide
ex: I catered for her bat mitzvah.
His company catered our wedding.

s.def: Synonym of acater: an officer who purchased cates (food supplies) for the steward of a large household or estate.
ex: I am oure Catour and bere oure Alther purse.
Rec. for iij calvys off þe cater of Crystis Cherche.

s.def: Synonym of caterer: any provider of food.
ex: Of his diete catour was scarsite...

s.def: Synonym of purveyor: any provider of anything.
ex: The eye is loues Cator.

s.def: To place, set, move, or cut diagonally or rhomboidally.
ex: The trees are set checkerwise, and so catred [Latin: partim in quincuncem directis], as looke which way ye wyl, they lye leuel.
‘Cater’ across the rails ever so cleverly, you cannot escape jolt and jar.

s.def: Diagonally.
Four.
ex: The auditour... cometh in with sise sould, and cater denere, for vi.s. and iiii.d.

s.def: The four of cards or dice.
ex: Cater is a very good caste.

s.def: A method of ringing nine bells in four pairs with a ninth tenor bell.
ex: The very terms of the art are enough to frighten an amateur. Hunting, dodging... caters, cinques, etc.

s.def: Alternative form of cater-corner.

ety: Apparently from cater + cousin; further etymology uncertain. The following derivations of the first element cater have been suggested: * Stephen Skinner (1623–1667) proposed a derivation from French quatre (“four”), used in place of quatrième (“fourth”) to refer to a fourth cousin. Samuel Johnson (1709–1784) agreed, saying that the term alluded to the “ridiculousness of calling cousin or relation to so remote a degree”. The Oxford English Dictionary (“OED”) states that this “seems very unlikely…

s.def: A person who, while not being a blood relation, is regarded as close enough to be called a cousin; a (very) close or good friend; a bosom friend.
ex: Out rushed sighs and groans by dozens, / Forth by scores oaths, curses flew: / Proving you were cater-cousins, / Kith and kindred, king and you!

s.def: A thing which is closely associated with or related to another thing.

ety: From Scottish Gaelic ceatharn (“troop”), ceathairne (“peasantry, yeomanry”).

s.def: A Highlander working as a professional fighter; a mercenary attached to a Scottish clan.
ex: And the great-grandson of Cospatric, he joined the English against the cateran Wallace […].
They found the hire of lawyers more cost-effective than the maintenance of caterans.

ety: From Middle English catirpel, catirpeller, probably from Old Northern French catepeluse (Modern French chatte + pileuse (“hairy cat”)), from Late Latin catta + pilōsa. The sense "rapacious, extortionate person" arose by association with obsolete piller (“plunderer”). See Modern Norman cattepeleuse. Displaced native kaleworm, from Middle English cowle worm, cale worme (“caterpillar, corn weevil”), from Old English cawelwyrm, cawelwurm (“caterpillar”).

s.def: The larva of a butterfly or moth; leafworm.
ex: The bird just ate that green caterpillar.

A rapacious, extortionate person preying upon the community.
A set of subtrees of a tree.
To move along slowly, drawing one's body up, in the manner of a caterpillar.

A generic trademark name for a continuous track in the form of a steel or rubber belt fitted around the wheels of crawlers, bulldozers, excavators, loaders, backhoes, tanks and similar off-road vehicles in such a manner as to spread the load on the ground surface and thereby improve traction and re…

ety: From Middle English caterwrawen, from cater (“cat”) + wrawen, wrawlen (“cry like a cat”), equivalent to cat + waul. Compare Low German katerwaulen (“to cry like a cat”) and Middle Dutch cater (“tomcat”) (Dutch kater).

s.def: To cry as cats in heat; to make a harsh, offensive noise.
To have a noisy argument, like cats.
A yowling.
A noisy quarrel.

ety: From cat + fish. Likely so named for its prominent barbels like a cat's whiskers. Compare West Frisian katfisk (“catfish”), Dutch katvis (“catfish”). Compare also German Seekatze (“catfish”, literally “sea-cat”).

s.def: Any fish of the order Siluriformes, mainly found in fresh water, lacking scales, and having barbels like whiskers around the mouth.
The meat of such a fish, popular in the Southern U.S. and Central Europe.
To fish for catfish.
ex: I only use this rod for catfishing.

s.def: Such a false profile.
Someone who creates a false profile on a social media platform in order to deceive people.
To create and operate a fake online profile to deceive (someone).
ex: [to Abed] You made a profile for a fake dude and lured her into an online relationship. [to Annie] He's catfishing you.

ety: Possibly an abbreviation of the word cattlegut. Alternatively, it may derive by folk etymology from kitgut or kitstring — the word kit, meaning fiddle, having at some point been confused with the word kit for a young cat.

s.def: A cord of great toughness made from the intestines of animals, especially of sheep, used for strings of musical instruments, racquets, sutures etc.
ex: Eventually they carved small paddles to strike the ball and refined this implement with a mesh of catgut.

s.def: The material from which such cords are made.
A sort of linen or canvas, with wide interstices.
Tephrosia virginiana (goat's rue, devil's shoestring).

ety: From Ancient Greek κάθαρσις (kátharsis, “cleansing, purging”), from καθαίρω (kathaírō, “I cleanse”). Coined in the dramatic-emotional sense by Aristotle.

s.def: A therapeutic technique to relieve tension by reestablishing the association of an emotion with the memory or idea of the event that first caused it, and then eliminating it by complete expression (called the abreaction).
drama: release of emotional tension
A release of emotional tension after an overwhelming vicarious experience, resulting in the purging or purification of the emotions, as through watching a dramatic production (especially a tragedy).
Any release of emotional tension to the same effect, more widely.
A purification or cleansing, especially emotional.
A purging of the digestive system.
ex: Saline catharses deplete the system of body fluids and are particularly harmful in pregnancy.

s.def: China, specifically medieval northern China as reached by the overland Silk Road to Xi'an or Beijing, not known at the time to be related to southern China as reached by the maritime routes to Guangzhou.
A settlement in North Dakota.
Ellipsis of Cathay Pacific.

ety: From Cathay + -an.

s.def: Of or relating to Cathay.
A native or inhabitant of Cathay.

ety: Borrowed from Latin cathedra (“seat”), from Ancient Greek καθέδρα (kathédra, “chair of a teacher, throne”), from κατά (katá, “down”) + ἕδρα (hédra, “seat”). Doublet of chair and chaise.

s.def: The chair or throne of a bishop.
The rank of bishop.
The official chair of some position or office, as of a professor.

ety: From Middle English cathedral, chathedral, cathiderall, from Old French [Term?], from Latin cathedrālis, from cathedra + -ālis, from Ancient Greek καθέδρα (kathédra, “chair of a teacher, throne”).

s.def: Relating to the office of a bishop or an archbishop.
The principal church serving as the office (and some as place of residence) of an archdiocese's/a diocese's archbishop/bishop which is symbolized by an episcopal throne known as the cathedra.
ex: The bishop presided over the ceremony from his seat in the cathedral.

s.def: A large or important church building.
A large, impressive, lofty, and/or important building or place of some other kind.
ex: a cathedral of commerce

s.def: A large buttressed structure built by certain termites.

ety: Borrowed from French cathéter, from Late Latin cathetēr, from Ancient Greek καθετήρ (kathetḗr, “surgical instrument for emptying the bladder”), from καθίημι (kathíēmi, “to descend, let down”) + -τήρ (-tḗr, suffix forming masculine nouns from verbs).

s.def: A small tube inserted into a body cavity to administer a drug, create an opening, distend a passageway, or remove fluid.

ety: From Ancient Greek κάθεξις (káthexis, “holding, retention”). The term entered the English language as a translation for the common everyday German word Besetzung, which in the context of psychoanalysis means "occupation" in the sense of a position or something being occupied or filled, and not a military occupation of a place or the filling of job positions (although it can also mean either of these in other contexts). (In English translations, a Greek word was used to be more scientific.)

s.def: The concentration of libido or emotional energy on a single object or idea.
ex: How contemporary artistic performances elicit cathexis on the part of the audience and promote unifying social rituals.

ety: From Ancient Greek κατα- (kata-, “down”) and ὁδός (hodós, “journey, way”), equivalent to Ancient Greek κάθοδος (káthodos, “way down, descent”). Coined by English polymath William Whewell in 1834 for Michael Faraday, who introduced it later that year. By surface analysis, cath- (alternative form of cata-) + -ode.

s.def: An electrode, of a cell or other electrically polarized device, through which a positive current of electricity flows outwards (and thus, electrons flow inwards). It can have either a negative or a positive voltage with respect to anode of the same polarized device (depending on whether the device…
The electrode at which chemical reduction of cations takes place, usually resulting in the deposition of metal onto the electrode.
The electrode from which electrons are emitted into a vacuum tube or gas-filled tube.
That electrode of a semiconductor device which is connected to the n-type material of a p-n junction.

A vacuum tube that displays still or moving images (such as for a television), by controlling the direction of a cathode ray emitted towards the front of the tube. The front is coated by a layer of fluorescent material, so that it emits light when struck by the beam.

ety: From Old French catholique, from Latin catholicus, from Ancient Greek καθολικός (katholikós, “universal”), from κατά (katá, “according to”) + ὅλος (hólos, “whole”).

s.def: Universal; all-encompassing.
ex: The church is catholic, universal, so are all her actions; all that she does, belongs to all.
Newton Heath depot has lately been catholic in its choice of power for the 6.10 p.m. Manchester-Southport and the 9 p.m. back via Bolton.

s.def: Alternative letter-case form of Catholic.
Common or prevalent; especially universally prevalent.
All-embracing.
ex: "I've got catholic tastes. Catholic with a small "c", of course."
He was omnivorous in his appetite for knowledge, quite catholic in his range of interests […]

s.def: Universally applicable.
Of universal human interest or use.
The Catholic Church, which consists of 24 particular churches in full communion with the Pope as the Bishop of Rome.
ex: The Catholic Church is the largest Christian church, comprising almost half of all Christians in the world.
The “Catholic Church” or “Roman Catholic Church” is the world's second largest single religious body after Sunni Islam

s.def: Literally "universal church", the whole body of Christendom, especially before the division into Western and Eastern churches.
Any of the independent Catholic Churches, such as the Old Catholic Church, the Polish National Catholic Church, or the Orthodox Catholic Church.
Any Christian denomination that identifies explicitly as "Catholic" based on its affirmation of the Nicene Creed, such as any of the Anglican Churches.

ety: From catholic + -ism.

s.def: The state or quality of being catholic or universal; catholicity.
ex: 1664-1667, Jeremy Taylor, Dissuasive from Popery this broken consent is not an infallible testimony of the catholicism of the doctrine

s.def: Liberality of sentiment; breadth of view.

ety: Compare French catholicisme.

s.def: The faiths, practices and doctrines of the Catholic Church, usually the Roman Catholic Church.
ex: Catholicism is the second largest religious body after Sunni Muslims

ety: Etymology tree English catholic Proto-Indo-European *-teh₂ Proto-Indo-European *-ts Proto-Indo-European *-teh₂ts Latin -itāsder. Old French -itebor. Middle English -ite English -ity English catholicity From catholic + -ity.

s.def: The quality of being catholic, universal or inclusive.
Alternative spelling of Catholicize.

ety: Late Middle English, via Medieval Latin from Ancient Greek καθολικόν (katholikón, “that which is universal”), the neuter substantive form of καθολικός (katholikós).

s.def: A supposed universal remedy.
A large urban church used for large gatherings.

ety: From Ancient Greek καθολικός (katholikós). Doublet of catholic.

s.def: A high-ranking bishop or patriarch in certain Eastern Christian traditions.

ety: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek κᾰτῐόν (kătĭón), neuter present participle of κᾰ́τειμῐ (kắteimĭ, “to go down, come down”), from κᾰτᾰ- (kătă-, “downwards, down, cata-”) + εἶμῐ (eîmĭ, “to go, come”). Coined by English polymath William Whewell in 1834 for Michael Faraday, who introduced it later that year. By surface analysis, cat(a)- + ion.

s.def: A positively charged ion: one that would be attracted to the cathode in electrolysis.

ety: From Middle Dutch katteken (“catkin”, literally “little cat”). So named due to the resemblance of lengthier kinds to a kitten's tail, or, perhaps more probably, the fine fur found on some catkins (compare the pictures). Cognate with German Kätzchen, modern Dutch katje; compare French chaton (“kitten”; “catkin”). By surface analysis, cat + -kin.

s.def: A type of inflorescence, consisting of an axis with many unisexual apetalous flowers along its sides, as in the willow and poplar.

ety: From cat + -ling. Compare kitling, catkin. According to the OED, the sense of a surgical knife may be an independent word.

s.def: A little cat; a kitten.
ex: For never cat nor catling I shall find, / But mew shall they in Pluto's palace blind.
Abel was a lover of the worst type: when he was with a catling he hardly ever laughed . If the catling came back again, he never did.
"Have you seen the ship's catling, Little Mistress?" he called, crossing to Hisvet, the kitten almost hidden in his big hands.

s.def: catgut; a catgut string
ex: but, I am sure, none, unless the fiddler Apollo get his sinews to make catlings on.
Festing's bill suggests that a catling could be used to make or improve the handle of a bow.

s.def: A double-edged, sharp-pointed dismembering knife.

ety: A historical illustration of countryfolk and townsfolk catnapping with their pets. A farrier taking a midday catnap. From cat + nap. Named in reference to the feline habit of taking multiple, brief, and light naps throughout the day to conserve energy, rather than sleeping for one long, uninterrupted block.

s.def: A brief, light sleep, usually during the daytime.
ex: By 9 A.M., however, all but the most insomniac of the night owls were taking a catnap.

ety: Compound of cat + nep, nip (“catnip”), from Middle English nep, from Old English nepte, from Proto-West Germanic *nepetā, from Latin nepeta (“catnip”). Compare earlier catmint (“catnip”), from Middle English catt mynte, which very likely existed in Old English (as *cattes minte) as well.

s.def: Any of the about 250 species of flowering plant of the genus Nepeta, family Lamiaceae, certain of which are said to have medicinal qualities.
ex: Some cats go bonkers over catnip; others ignore it.

s.def: Something that causes excitement or interest.
ex: Near-synonym: crack

Unlike IPOs, however, ICOs are catnip for scammers.

ety: From Middle English cattal, cattyle (also as cattestail), equivalent to cat + tail.

s.def: Any of several perennial herbs, of the genus Typha, that have long flat leaves, and grow in marshy places.
A cat-o'-nine-tails.

ety: From Middle English catel, from Anglo-Norman catel (“personal property”), from Old Northern French (compare French cheptel, Old French chetel, chatel, also English chattel) from Medieval Latin capitāle, from Latin capitālis (“of the head”) (whence also capital, from caput (“head”) + -alis (“-al”)). Resembling or characteristic of a cat.

To limit team members' consumption, it issued food stamps to the villagers and allowed everyone to eat one catty of rice a day.

s.def: A catapult.

ety: From cat + walk.

The business of making clothes for fashion shows.

ety: From Latin Celtae (singular Celta) from Ancient Greek Κελτοί (Keltoí). English Celts is from the 17th century. Until the mid 19th century, /sɛlt/ is the only recorded pronunciation. A consciously archaizing pronunciation /kɛlt/ was advocated during Irish and Welsh nationalism beginning in the 1850s.

s.def: A member of one of the ancient peoples of Western Europe called Celtae by the Romans.
A member of any of the (modern, Celtic) peoples who speak Celtic languages.

ety: Borrowed from French celtique or Latin celticus, equivalent to Celt + -ic. First attested in the 17th century.

s.def: A branch of the Indo-European languages that was spread widely over Western and Central Europe in the pre-Christian era.
Any of several sports teams. See Wikipedia for a list.
A player for any of several teams named the Celtics.
ex: After the draft, Brown became a Celtic for six years.

s.def: Celtic F.C., a football club from Glasgow, Scotland.

A sea in British Isles, Europe in the Atlantic The area of the Atlantic Ocean off the south coast of Ireland bounded by Saint George's Channel, the Bristol Channel, the English Channel, and the Bay of Biscay.
the academic discipline occupied with the study of any sort of cultural output relating to a Celtic people

The paste-like substance resulting from mixing such a powder with water, or the rock-like substance that forms when it dries.
Any material with strong adhesive and cohesive properties such as binding agents, glues, grout.
A bond of union; that which unites firmly, as persons in friendship or in society.

The use of a cement join of the parts of a broken bone to aid in the healing process.
The use of a cement or adhesive to fasten orthodontics or to restore chipped or broken teeth.
Bonded by cement or a similar substance.

ety: From Middle English cimiterie, from Old French cimitiere, from Medieval Latin cimitērium, from Late Latin coemētērium, from Ancient Greek κοιμητήριον (koimētḗrion), from κοιμάω (koimáō, “I put to sleep”); compare cœmeterium. Displaced Middle English charnel (“mass grave, cemetery”) and Old English līctūn (“cemetery”).

[…] the cemetery – which people of shattering wit like Sampson never tired of calling ‘the dead centre of town’ […]

ety: Inherited from Middle English censer, from Anglo-Norman censier, from Old French encensier, from encens (“incense”).

s.def: An ornamental container for burning incense, especially during religious ceremonies.
ex: Then, methought, the air grew denser, perfumed from an unseen censer / Swung by Seraphim whose foot-falls tinkled on the tufted floor.

s.def: A person who censes, a person who perfumes with incense.

ety: The noun is borrowed from Latin cēnsor (“magistrate; critic”), from cēnseō (“to give an opinion, judge; to assess, reckon; to decree, determine”) + -sor (variant of -tor (suffix forming masculine agent nouns)). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱens- (“to announce, proclaim; to put in order”). The English word is cognate with Late Middle English sensour, Proto-Iranian *cánhati (“to declare; to explain”), Sanskrit शंसति (śaṃsati, “to declare”). The verb is derived from the noun.

s.def: One of the two magistrates who originally administered the census of citizens, and by Classical times (between the 8th century B.C.E. and the 6th century C.E.) was a high judge of public behaviour and morality.
ex: The Ancient Roman censors were part of the cursus honorum, a series of public offices held during a political career, like consuls and praetors.

s.def: A high-ranking official who was responsible for the supervision of subordinate government officials.

An official responsible for the removal or suppression of objectionable material (for example, if obscene or likely to incite violence) or sensitive content in books, films, correspondence, and other media.
A college or university official whose duties vary depending on the institution.
One who censures or condemns.
An algorithm that approves or rejects something on grounds of taste or morality etc.
ex: I tried using a dirty word as my user name for the online game, but the censor rejected it.

s.def: To review for, and if necessary to remove or suppress, content from books, films, correspondence, and other media which is regarded as objectionable (for example, obscene, likely to incite violence, or sensitive).
ex: The people responsible for censoring films have seen some startling things in their time.
Occupying powers typically censor anything reeking of resistance
Ganley is in hourly dread of every message that comes into your wireless-room. He insists on censoring anything that might betray him.

s.def: To partially obscure an observation.
ex: Early dropout is one cause of right-censoring.

s.def: A hypothetical subconscious agency which filters unacceptable thought before it reaches the conscious mind.

ety: From Latin cēnsōrius (“of or pertaining to a censor; severe”). In sense 3 ("tending to engage in or support censorship"), reanalyzed as censor + -ious.

s.def: Addicted to censure and scolding; apt to blame or condemn; severe in making remarks on others, or on their writings or manners.
Implying or expressing censure.
ex: censorious remarks

s.def: Tending to engage in or support censorship.
ex: Is there something in the California water that makes Silicon Valley's censorious dweebs so damned shameless?

ex: […] such a curious thing — it is the only thing left of the old censorship of the press."

s.def: The role of the censor (magistrate) in Ancient Rome.

ety: From 1350–1400 Middle English censure, from Old French, from Latin censūra (“censor's office or assessment”), from censēre (“to consider, to assess, to value, to judge, to tax, etc.”).

ex: Both the censure and the praise were merited.

s.def: To formally rebuke.
To form or express a judgment in regard to; to estimate; to judge.

ety: Borrowed from Latin cēnsus, from cēnseō. See censor.

s.def: An official count or enumeration of members of a population (not necessarily human), usually residents or citizens in a particular region, often done at regular intervals.
The people being treated in a healthcare facility, clinic or program.
Count, tally.

s.def: A type of tax levied by feudal lords on peasants.
A count of the number of individual patterns within a larger pattern, most often the ash of a soup or a methuselah.
To collect a census.
To conduct a census on.
ex: Each page of the schedule was crossruled with 8 lines, capable of censussing 8 individuals.

A subunit of currency equal to one-hundredth of the main unit of currency in many countries. Symbol: ¢.

One of a number of icy planetoids that orbit the Sun between Jupiter and Neptune.
A chess-playing team comprising a human player and a computer who work together.
A human and an AI who work together.

ety: From Latin centaurus, from Ancient Greek κένταυρος (kéntauros, “centaur”). Doublet of centaur.

ety: From Middle English centaure, from Old English centaurie, from Medieval Latin centaurēa, centauria, from Latin centaurēum, centaurion, from Ancient Greek κενταύρειον (kentaúreion, “several plants related to Centaurea”), from κένταυρος (kéntauros, “centaur”) (due to the mythological discovery of its medicinal properties by Chiron the Centaur). ety: From New Latin centrifugālis, coined by Christiaan Huygens from Latin centrum (“center”) + fugiō (“to flee”) + -al.

s.def: Tending, or causing, to recede from the center.
Expanding first at the summit, and later at the base, as a flower cluster.
Having the radicle turned toward the sides of the fruit, as some embryos.
A rotating machine used to separate massecuite into sugar crystals and molasses.
ex: Modern practice favours warming the massecuite in pug mills, placed above the centrifugals.

s.def: Centripetal force.
In everyday understanding, the effect that tends to move an object away from the center of a circle it is rotating about (a consequence of inertia).

In a rotating reference frame, the apparent force that seems to push all bodies away from the centre of rotation of the frame and is a consequence of the body's mass and the frame's angular speed. It works in conjunction with the Coriolis force to give correct motion.
In circular motion, the 'reactive' centrifugal force is a real force applied by the accelerating body that is equal and opposite to the centripetal force that is acting on the accelerating body.
In polar coordinates, the apparent radial force that acts away from the center and is a consequence of the body's angular speed around the origin.

ety: From French centrifuge, from Latin centrum (“center”) + fugiō (“to flee”). Equivalent to centri- + -fuge.

An apparatus in which humans are spun to simulate acceleration in an aircraft or spacecraft.
By extension, any device which rotates in order to produce artificial gravity (in the form of centrifugal force)

ety: From Latin centriolum, diminutive of centrum. English equivalent centri- + -ole.

ety: From New Latin centripetālis coined by Sir Isaac Newton, from Latin centrum (“center”) + petō (“to seek, aim”) + -al. Analysable as centri- + -petal.

s.def: Directed or moving towards a centre.

s.def: Directed towards the central nervous system; afferent.

ety: From centro- + -some.

A pilot in the United States Navy who has performed one hundred night landings on an aircraft carrier.

ety: From Middle English centurie (“a count of one hundred (of anything); a division of the Roman army; century; a division of land”), from Old French centurie, from Latin centuria, from centum (“one hundred”). The most common modern use is an ellipsis of century of years.

s.def: A period of one hundred consecutive years; often specifically a numbered period with conventional start and end dates, e.g., the twentieth century, which stretches from (strictly) 1901 through 2000, or (informally) 1900 through 1999. The first century AD was from 1 to 100.
ex: In 16th and 17th century Britain, for example, women’s alopecia was sometimes interpreted as retribution for sins, including adultery.

s.def: A unit in ancient Roman army, originally of one hundred army soldiers as part of a cohort, later of more varied sizes (but typically containing sixty to seventy or eighty) soldiers or other men (guards, police, firemen), commanded by a centurion.
ex: Holonyms: maniple, cohort, legion

s.def: A political division of ancient Rome, meeting in the Centuriate Assembly.
A hundred things of the same kind; a hundred.
ex: 'tis the subject of whole books: I might cite a century of authors pro and con.

s.def: A hundred runs scored either by a single player in one innings, or by two players in a partnership.
ex: He has scored 44 limited-overs centuries.
They put on a century stand to help their team recover from 57–4 to 198–4.

s.def: A score of one hundred points.
ex: That was his tenth professional century.

s.def: A race a hundred units (as meters, kilometres, miles) in length.
A banknote in the denomination of one hundred dollars.
A Chinese delicacy made by preserving a duck, chicken or quail egg in a mixture of clay, ash, salt, quicklime and rice hulls for several weeks to several months.
ex: There are many varieties of congee but the most common is this salted pork with century egg.

s.def: Initialism of chief executive officer.
ex: CEOs who once made 50 times the average worker’s salary made more than 500 times as much in 2001.

s.def: Initialism of civil enforcement officer.
Acronym of current engine option.
Initialism of city engineering office.

ety: From Middle French céphalique, from Latin cephalicus (“head”), from Ancient Greek κεφαλικός (kephalikós, “capital”), from κεφαλή (kephalḗ, “head”).

s.def: of or referring to the head
Of or relating to the head.
Toward the head; in bipeds such as humans, this direction corresponds to superior.
Headlike; cephaloid.
A remedy that benefits the head or brain.
ex: […] recover their Sight […] by the use of Bleeding, Purging, Blistering and Cephalics.

ety: From French céphalopode, from Ancient Greek κεφαλή (kephalḗ, “head”) + ποδός (podós), genitive singular of πούς (poús, “foot, leg”). By surface analysis, cephalo- + -pod.

s.def: Any mollusc of the class Cephalopoda, which includes squid, cuttlefish, octopus, nautiloids etc.

ety: From Ancient Greek κεφαλή (kephalḗ, “head”), with the suffix -ous.

s.def: Having a head; applied chiefly to the former division of mollusks Cephalata, or Cephalophora (mollusks with a head).

ety: From Latin cēra (“wax”) + -aceous.

s.def: Waxy.

ety: Borrowed from Translingual Cerambycidae.

s.def: Any member of the family Cerambycidae of longhorn beetles.

ety: From Ancient Greek κεραμικός (keramikós, “potter's”), from κέραμος (kéramos, “potter's clay”), perhaps from a pre-Hellenic word or from Proto-Indo-European *kerh₂- (“to heat, burn, fire”).

s.def: Made of material produced by the high-temperature firing of inorganic, nonmetallic rocks and minerals.
ex: A ceramic vase stood on the table.

s.def: An object made of this material.
ex: Joe had dozens of ceramics in his apartment.

s.def: material
A hard, brittle, inorganic, nonmetallic material, made by firing a material such as clay at a high temperature.
ex: Joan made the dish from ceramic.

s.def: plural of ceramic
The art or science of making ceramic objects.
Ceramic objects as a group.

ety: Etymology tree English ceramic Proto-Indo-European *-ikos Proto-Italic *-ikos Latin -icuslbor. Old French -iquebor. Middle English -ik English -ic Old English -as Middle English -es English -s English -ics English ceramics From ceramic + -ics.
Blend of cerebroside + amide, or from Latin cēra (“wax”) + amide.

s.def: Any of various lipids formed by linking a fatty acid to sphingosine and found widely but in small amounts in plant and animal tissue

ety: From Middle English cerate, cerote, from Latin cērātum, from cēra (“wax”), see -ate (noun-forming suffix)

s.def: An unctuous preparation for external application — mainly wax (or resin or spermaceti) mixed with oil, lard, and various medicinal ingredients — of a consistency between ointment and plaster, so that it can be spread upon cloth without the use of heat, but does not melt when applied to the skin.
The anion CeO₃²⁻ of cerium.

ety: From cerato- + -oid.

s.def: Having a horn-like shape or structure.

ety: From Middle English sere, from Old French cire, from Latin cēra (“wax, cere”), or via Latin cērō (“to smear or coat with wax”).

s.def: A fleshy, waxy area at the base of the upper beak in certain birds.
To wax; to cover or close with wax.
ex: a strong twisted Thread cered

ety: Borrowed from French céréale (“having to do with cereal”), from Latin Cerealis (“of or relating to Ceres”), from Ceres (“Roman goddess of agriculture”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱer- (“grow”), from which also Latin sincerus (English sincere) and Latin crēscō (“grow”) (English crescent). The adjective is equivalent to Cere(s) + -al.

s.def: A type of grass (such as wheat, rice or oats) cultivated for its edible grains.
The grains of such a grass.
Breakfast cereal.
ex: Would you like some cereal?
Which cereal would you like for breakfast?
a bowl of cereal

s.def: Of or relating to cereal.
ex: Wheat .. is, of all the cereal seeds, the best adapted to the making of bread.
Millet, the smallest of all the cereal seeds cultivated for food, grows on arid soils, where rice and maize cannot be successfully cultivated, […]
The species printed in small capitals are Corn-producing or Cereal Grasses, called Cereals, from Ceres, the Roman goddess of Corn.

ety: Learned borrowing from Latin cerebellum, diminutive of cerebrum.

s.def: Part of the hindbrain in vertebrates. In humans it lies between the brainstem and the back of the cerebrum and is formed of two lateral lobes and a median lobe. It plays an important role in sensory perception, motor output, balance and posture.
ex: Although the cerebellum occupies just 10 per cent of the cranial cavity, it has more than half the brain’s neurons.

ety: Borrowing from French cérébral, from Latin cerebrum (“a brain”); equivalent to cerebrum + -al.

s.def: Of or relating to the brain, cerebrum, or cerebral cortex.
Intellectual rather than emotional or physical.
ex: Certainly, “Capital” is a cerebral read and the dangers of the world Marx lived in are not all the same as ours.

s.def: Retroflex.
The grey, folded, outermost layer of the cerebrum that is responsible for higher brain processes such as sensation, voluntary muscle movement, thought, reasoning, and memory.
A group of nonprogressive, noncontagious conditions, caused by brain damage before birth or during infancy, characterized by impairment of muscular coordination.

ety: First attested in 1874; from Latin cerebrum (“brain”) + -ate (verb-forming suffix); likely a back-formation from cerebration.

s.def: To think or cogitate, especially so as to make inferences or decisions or to solve problems.
Any salt of cerebric acid (cerebrin).

ety: From Latin cerebrum (“brain”) + -ation.

s.def: The act of cerebrating; reflection, thinking, thought.
ex: Duncan himself, however, seems to have alpine cerebrations embedded in his very molecules.

ety: From cerebro- + spinal.

s.def: Of or relating to brain or spine (particularly the spinal cord).
ex: There was an infection of the cerebrospinal fluid.

s.def: A clear bodily fluid in the form of a very pure saline solution with microglia that occupies the subarachnoid space in the brain (between the skull and the cerebral cortex), and which acts as a cushion or buffer for the cortex.
A bodily fluid filling the third ventricle and surrounding the interthalamic adhesion.

ety: From cerebro- + vascular.

s.def: Relating to the blood vessels that run to or from the brain.

ety: Inherited from Middle English cerebrum, from Latin cerebrum (“a brain; a skull”); see there for more.

s.def: The principal and most anterior part of the brain in vertebrates, which is located in the front area of the skull and divided into two hemispheres, left and right, separated by a fissure. In humans it is the largest part of the brain and is responsible for the integration of complex sensory functio…

ety: From cere + cloth, from Latin cera (“wax, cere”).

s.def: Cloth coated with wax so that it is waterproof, used for covering the dead.
ex: ’Twere damnation To think so base a thought; it were too gross To rib her cerecloth in the obscure grave.

ety: From French cirement (“waxing, wax dressing”), from cirer (“to wax, wrap”).

s.def: A burial shroud or garment.
ex: "Who is the woman in the cerements?", she inconsequently wondered.
The cerements still cling to their wasted frames, but will soon be exchanged for a gayer garb in their passage from the tomb to the temple.

s.def: Cerecloth.

ety: From Middle English cerymonial, from Latin caerimōniālis. Morphologically ceremony + -al or -ial.

s.def: Of, relating to, consisting of, or used in a ceremony.
ex: What mockery will it be / To want the bridegroom when the priest attends / To speak the ceremonial rites of marriage!
[T]his change in ceremonial observances and outward show was trifling when compared to that in the objects of worship […]
Philomena Guinea's black Cadillac eased through the tight, five o'clock traffic like a ceremonial car.

s.def: Used only for the purpose of ceremony; symbolic.
Synonym of ceremonious (“of a person: fond of ceremony or ritual, or of observing strict etiquette or formality; punctilious”).
ex: Oh monstrous, superstitious puritan, / Of refin’d manners, yet ceremoniall man, […]
[W]ith dumb Pride, and a set formal Face, / He moves, in the dull Ceremonial track, […]

s.def: A ceremony, or series of ceremonies, prescribed by ritual.
ex: I have been in favour of ceremonial and patterns all my life, and I have no desire to break the funeral pattern.

ety: Learned borrowing from Middle French cérémonieux (modern French cérémonieux) or directly from its etymon Latin caerimōniōsus + English -ous (suffix forming adjectives from nouns, denoting the presence of a quality in any degree (typically an abundance)). Caerimōniōsus is derived from Latin caerimōnia (“awe, reverence, veneration; sacredness, sanctity; religious ceremony, ritual”) (possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kʷer- (“to build, make; to do”)) + -ōsus (suffix meaning ‘full of, ov…

s.def: According to the required or usual ceremonies, formalities, or rituals; specifically (Christianity, obsolete), to ceremonial laws in the Bible.
Involving much ceremony; ostentatious, showy.
ex: He descended to the cabin to bid a ceremonious, and, it may be, tacitly rebukeful adieu.

s.def: Of a person: fond of ceremony or ritual, or of observing strict etiquette or formality; punctilious.
ex: Ancient and oriental cultures are in many ways more conventional, more ceremonious, and more courteous than our own.

s.def: Synonym of ceremonial (“of, relating to, consisting of, or used in a ceremony or rite”); formal, ritual.

ety: From Middle English cerymonye, from Latin caerimonia or caeremonia, later often cerimonia (“sacredness, reverence, a sacred rite”).

s.def: A ritual, with religious or cultural significance.
ex: Under certain circumstances there are few hours in life more agreeable than the hour dedicated to the ceremony known as afternoon tea.

s.def: An official gathering to celebrate, commemorate, or otherwise mark some event.
ex: a graduation ceremony, an opening ceremony

s.def: A formal socially established behaviour, often in relation to people of different ranks; formality.
ex: They went into the bars and interrupted the drinking, hustling the men out without ceremony.

s.def: Show of magnificence, display, ostentation.
An accessory or object associated with a ritual.
ex: […] his ceremonies laid by, in his nakedness he appears but a man […]

s.def: An omen or portent.
ex: For he is superstitious grown of late, Quite from the main opinion he held once Of fantasy, of dreams, and ceremonies.
Caesar, I never stood on ceremonies, Yet now they fright me.

s.def: plural of cere

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *ḱer- Proto-Indo-European *ḱerēs Proto-Italic *Kerēs Latin Cerēslbor. English Ceres Learned borrowing from Latin Cerēs, goddess of the bounty, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱer- (“to grow, to nourish”). More at create.

s.def: An asteroid orbiting between Mars and Jupiter, the innermost dwarf planet; officially called (1) Ceres.
The Roman goddess of agriculture; equivalent to the Greek goddess Demeter.
A city in Stanislaus County, California, United States.

A locality in the City of Greater Geelong, south western Victoria, Australia.

ety: Borrowed from French cerise (mid 19th century), itself from Vulgar Latin ceresia, from Latin cerasium. Doublet of cherry and kirsch.

s.def: A deep, bright red colour tinted with pink.
ex: Before us lay the autumn tinted woods glimmering in gold, purple, green, and cerise.

s.def: Cherry-colored; a light bright red.

ety: From Ceres (a famous asteroid and dwarf planet), + -ium. The element was discovered and named in 1803. It was named after the asteroid, which had been discovered recently (1801) and had been named after Ceres, the Roman goddess of agriculture. s.def: A chemical element (symbol Ce) with an atomic number of 58, a very soft, ductile, silvery-white metal that tarnishes when exposed to air.

A method of making stereotype plates from inscribed sheets of wax.

ety: From Middle English certeyn, certein, certain, borrowed from Old French certain, from a Vulgar Latin unattested form *certānus, extended form of Latin certus (“fixed, resolved, certain”), of the same origin as cretus, past participle of cernere (“to separate, perceive, decide”). Displaced native Middle English wis, iwis (“certain, sure”) (from Old English ġewiss (“certain, sure”)) and alternative Middle English spelling sertane (“some, certain”).

s.def: sure, positive, not doubting
not specifically named, indeterminate, indefinite
Having been determined but not specified.
ex: Certain people are good at running.
One saint's day in mid-term a certain newly-appointed suffragan-bishop came to the school chapel, and there preached on “The Inner Life.”

s.def: Sure in one's mind, positive; absolutely confident in the truth of something.
ex: I was certain of my decision.
[…] I think, nay, I may say that I'm sartain, we'll have a hurricane afore morning. It's not the first time I've cruised in these latitudes.

s.def: Not to be doubted or denied; established as a fact.
ex: Now that more experiments have been run, the theory is certain and the argument is settled.

s.def: Sure to happen, inevitable; assured.
ex: It is certain that Spain will reach the finals. / Spain is now certain to reach the finals. / Spain is now certain of a place in the finals.
Bankruptcy is the certain outcome of your constant gambling and lending.

s.def: Unfailing; infallible.
ex: I have often wished, that I knew so certain a remedy in any other disease

s.def: Fixed; regular; determinate.
ex: at certain intervals

s.def: Particular and definite, but unspecified or unnamed; used to introduce someone or something without going into further detail.
ex: Every wine has a certain distinctive character which sets it apart from all others.
Each morning, she would see a certain man rush past her window on his way to work.
About everything that he wrote, serious or sportive, there was a certain natural grace and decorum[…]

s.def: Used to denote that the speaker is referring to a specific person or thing that they do not want to name directly, implying that the listener should infer the identity of the referent.
ex: I would have been here on time, but a certain someone lost the car keys!

ety: From Middle English certeynly; equivalent to certain + -ly.

s.def: In a way which is certain; with certainty.
ex: The torque was "built up" in the special back axle and the car crawled tankwise but very certainly over the obstacles without a jar or hesitation.

s.def: Without doubt, surely.
ex: The accident was certainly caused by human error.
That was certainly sweet of him.
'I'm all grown up now' -'You certainly have (grown)!'

s.def: An emphatic affirmative answer; of course.
ex: Would you like it with ice? Certainly, and with lemon please.

ety: From Middle English certes, from Old French [Term?], from Latin certus (“certain”).

s.def: Certainly, indeed.
ex: This was very unpleasant, at least to myself; though, certes, it did not prey upon the minds of the others.
Here, certes, was no lost soul, but one who had gone joyfully to meet her Lord.

ety: The noun is from Middle English certificat, certificate, sertyfycat, from Middle French certificat or its etymon Medieval Latin certificātum. The verb is from the noun. The adjective is a learned borrowing from Latin certificātus.

s.def: A document containing a certified statement.
A document evidencing ownership or debt.
A document serving as evidence that a person has completed an educational course, issued either by an institution not authorised to grant diplomas, or to a student not qualifying for a diploma.
The information needed in order to verify a positive answer to a problem.
Ellipsis of public key certificate.
A motion picture age rating.
ex: The film is certificate 15.

s.def: Synonym of certification.
To supply with a certificate, especially following certification.
Certified, assured.
The act of certifying.
The granting of a certificate.
A professional qualification that certifies a person's ability.
ex: You do not possess the certifications required for this post.

s.def: Having met an official standard.
ex: a certified organization
a certified product

s.def: Authenticated or verified in writing.
simple past and past participle of certify

ety: From Old French certefier (“confirm, assure, make certain”). Compare French certifier.

s.def: To attest to (a fact) as the truth.
To authenticate or verify in writing.
To attest that a product, service, organization, or person has met an official standard.
ex: These blankets have been certified as fireproof.

s.def: To inform; to tell (a person) that something is true.
To assure (oneself) of something; to ascertain.
ex: After having certified himself of her own good health, he very kindly inquired about her mother and Miss Sophy […].

ety: From Middle French certitude, from Late Latin certitūdō, from Latin certus.

s.def: Sureness, certainty.
ex: I have absolute certitude about that.

s.def: Something that is a certainty.
ex: Taxes are obviously certitudes.

ety: From Latin caeruleus (“blue”) + -an, from caelum (“sky, heaven”) + -uleus (diminutive suffix).

s.def: A greenish-blue color.
ex: For our blues we have the azures and ceruleans, lapis lazulis, the light and dusty, the powder blues, the deeps: royal, sapphire, navy, and marine […]

s.def: Any of various lycaenid butterflies of the genus Jamides.
Sky-blue.
ex: Oh Ramona, if there was only some kind of future / And these cerulean skies / Something in our skies, something in our skies

ety: From Medieval Latin caerūmen, from cera + -men. The appearance of the u is unexplained, but may have been influenced by words like albūmen and bitūmen.

s.def: Earwax.

ety: From French céruse, from Latin cērusa, variant of cērussa, q.v.

s.def: Synonym of white lead, a hydrate of lead mixed with carbonate, particularly as used to whiten skin or in early medicine.

ety: Etymology tree Latin cervīx Proto-Indo-European *h₂el- Proto-Indo-European *-is Proto-Indo-European *h₂élisder.? Proto-Italic *-ālis Latin -ālis New Latin cervīcālislbor. French cervicalbor. English cervical Borrowing from French cervical, from New Latin cervīcālis, from cervīx (“the neck, nape”) + -ālis (“-al”, adjectival suffix). By surface analysis, cervic- + -al.

s.def: Of or pertaining to the neck.
ex: cervical pain

s.def: Of or pertaining to the cervix.
ex: cervical cancer

s.def: Ellipsis of cervical vertebra.

A type of cancer of the cervix of the uterus which can afflict some female mammals including humans. The term usually does not refer to cancer of the neck or other parts of the anatomy which use the term cervix.
Any of the seven vertebrae of the neck.

ety: By anglicisation from Latin cervīnus; by surface analysis, Latin cerv(us) (“deer”) + -ine.

s.def: Of, pertaining to, or characteristic of deer (in the broad sense).
ex: Near-synonym: cervid (in attributive use)

s.def: Any cervid/true deer.

ety: Borrowed from Latin cervīx (“neck”), see below.

s.def: The cervix uteri, or lower, narrow portion of the uterus where it joins with the top end of the vagina.
ex: Screening involves taking a small sample of cells from the cervix and looking for high-risk HPV that could develop into cancer if left untreated.

s.def: The neck.
ex: I put my hands on Madeleine's hot cheeks, making a prize cup of my hands and her cervix, and tilted her head to one side.

s.def: The necklike portion of an organ or part of the body.

ety: From Caesar + -ean, but see also Caesarean section § Etymology.

s.def: Alternative letter-case form of Cesarean.
Alternative letter-case form of Cesarean.
Alternative form of caesium.

ety: Borrowed from Middle French cessation, itself a borrowing from Latin cessātiō. By surface analysis, cease + -ation. Compare cession < cede.

s.def: A ceasing or discontinuance, for example of an action, whether temporary or final.
ex: it might be advisable to permit the temporary cessation of the papal inquisition
The day […]was […]yearly observ'd for a festival Day by cessation from Labour.

ety: From Middle French cession, from Latin cessionem, from past participle of cēdere (“to yield”). By surface analysis, cede + -sion.

s.def: That which is ceded.
ex: The reinsurance company accepted a 25% cession from the direct insurer.

s.def: The giving up of rights, property etc. which one is entitled to.

ety: From Latin cedere (“to yield”).

s.def: The person who receives transfer or cession of a personal obligation from the cedent.

ety: Uncertain. The first part, cess-, is undoubtedly the same as for cesspool, whose origin is likewise uncertain. The second part is pit, a hole in the ground.

s.def: A cesspool; a pit or covered cistern used to collect sewage and waste water.
A place or situation characterised by corruption, filth or immoral activities.
ex: Politics devolved into a cesspit of lies and deceit.

ety: From earlier sesspool. Origin uncertain. Perhaps from Italian cesso (“privy, a toilet”) + English pool. Alternatively, an alteration of English dialectal suspool, from suss, soss (“a puddle; mire”) + pool. Another possible derivation is from a folk etymology (influence from pool) from earlier cesperalle, alteration of Middle English suspiral, from Middle French souspirail (“an air hole”), from soupirer, souspirer (“to sigh, breathe”), from Latin suspirare.

s.def: An underground pit where sewage is held.
A filthy place.

ety: From New Latin Cestoda, from cestus (“girdle, belt”), from Ancient Greek κεστός (kestós, “of Aphrodite’s charmed girdle”).

s.def: A parasitic flatworm of the class Cestoda; a tapeworm.

ety: From Latin caestus.

s.def: A leather fighting glove, frequently weighted with metal.
ex: 'Cestus': This includes all sorts of fist wrappings and brass knuckle weapon types.

s.def: A girdle, especially that of Aphrodite (or Venus) which gave the wearer the power to excite love.
Whale-like mammals.
ex: But here we give no such extracts, but content ourselves with four short skits, having the cetacea for their subject.
--Acalephae[1] are plentiful, so much so, indeed, that they occasionally tempt the larger cetacea into the Gulf of Manaar.
PORPOISES AT MORETON BAY. Among the marine animals of Moreton Bay are two cetacea of great interest.

ety: From translingual Cetacea, from Latin cētus (“whale”), + -an.

ex: The poached blubber was definitely cetacean in origin, but the particular species could not be identified.

s.def: Resembling or relating to large aquatic mammals.
ex: The obese woman, ungainly on land, moved with a kind of cetacean grace in the water.

s.def: A marine mammal belonging to the infraorder Cetacea, including dolphins, porpoises, and whales, characterized by a streamlined body, one or two blowholes, tail flukes, and fin-like forelimbs without hind limbs.
ex: The tour promised spiritual experiences with humpback whales and other cetaceans, but all we saw were seagulls and a dead sea otter.

s.def: A city and municipality of Montenegro; the former capital of Montenegro, from 1878 to 1918.

ety: Borrowed from Spanish Ceuta.

ety: Borrowed from Spanish cebiche, of uncertain origin; see that entry for more. Cf. escabeche.

A river in Anatolia, in southern Turkey, also known as the Pyramus, flowing 509 km from the Taurus Mountains to the Mediterranean Sea.

ety: Borrowed from Portuguese Ceilão, from Old French Seilan (Marco Polo), from Persian سیلان (saylān), ultimately from Pali sīhaḷa, from Sanskrit सिंहल (siṃhala). Doublet of Sinhala.

s.def: Former name of Sri Lanka: an island country in South Asia .
A male given name transferred from the place name.
An object-oriented, strongly statically typed programming language with an emphasis on immutability.

plural of cg (“center of gravity”)

ety: From French chaconne, from Spanish chacona, likely from Basque txukun (“pretty”).

s.def: A slow, stately Baroque dance.
The music for such a dance, often containing variations on a theme.

ety: Uncertain; possibly from the English slang term chat (“louse”). The word predates the chadless punch, which therefore cannot be its origin, and a derivation from Scots chad (“river gravel”) stated in some dictionaries is now thought to be nothing more than guesswork.

s.def: Small pieces of paper punched out from the edges of continuous stationery, or from ballot papers, paper tape, punched cards, etc.
ex: The keypunch wasn't named after a Mr. Chadless; it was so named because, as expected, it punched tape while producing little or no chad.

s.def: One of these pieces of paper.
ex: The small hinged discs of paper, called ‘chad’, remain attached to the body of the tape.

s.def: I had
ex: Chad et in my meend, and zo chave still. Bet chawnt drow et out bevore tha begen'st agen, and than chell.

s.def: Alternative spelling of Chad (“alpha-male; a virile man”).

ety: Believed to be from Kanuri tsade (“lake”). The country is named after the lake.

ety: From Middle English chaffynch, chaffynche, caffynche, equivalent to chaff + finch. However, more recently the first element has been argued to derive from the same root as Old English cæfed (“ornamented”) and cæfing (“hair-ornament”), thus meaning "ornamented finch, colourful finch".

s.def: A small passerine bird, Fringilla coelebs, of the finch family, found throughout Europe and eastward to Iran and eastern Mediterranean coastlands.

ety: Transliteration of Russian Чагата́й (Čagatáj), from Uyghur چاغاتاي (chaghatay), from Chagatai چغتای (čaġatay), from Middle Mongol ᠴᠠᠭᠠᠲᠠᠶ (čaɣatay).

An extinct literary Turkic language used in Central Asia and Bashkortostan between the 15th and the 20th century.
An ethnic group of Uzbekistan.

ety: From French chagrin (“sorrow”), from Middle French chagrin (“pain, affliction”) (compare Middle French chagriner, chagrigner (“to experience sorrow”), Old French chagrin (“painful, afflicted”)), probably derived from Old Northern French chagreiner, chagraigner (“to sadden”), of uncertain origin. ety: ] From Middle English Chauntecleer, from Old French Chantecler (modern French Chanteclair), the proper name of the cock in the literary cycle of Reynard the Fox, that also gave origin to chantecler, the name of a chicken breed; from chanter (“to sing, to crow”) + cler (“clear, clearly”). To crow in exultation.

ety: From Middle English chaunterie, from Old French chanterie, from chanter (“to sing”).

s.def: An endowment for the maintenance of a priest to sing a daily mass for the souls of specified people.
A chapel set up for this purpose.

One of the two metaphysical forces of the world in some fantasy settings, as opposed to law.
A vast chasm or abyss.
A given medium; a space in which something exists or lives; an environment.

ety: From Late Latin chaoticus (“of or pertaining to the primordial state of the universe”), from Latin chaos (“chaos”) + -ticus (suffix forming adjectives from nouns); analysable as chaos + -otic. Doublet of gassy.

ex: Yes, there is death in this business of whaling—a speechlessly quick chaotic bundling of a man into Eternity.

s.def: Filled with chaos.
Highly sensitive to starting conditions, so that a small change to them may yield a very different outcome.
Aligned against following or upholding laws and principles.
A character having a chaotic alignment.

ety: Clipping of chapman (“dealer, customer”) in 16th-century English.

ex: Who’s that chap over there?

A child.
Of the skin, to split or flake due to cold weather or dryness.
To cause to open in slits or chinks; to split; to cause the skin of to crack or become rough.
ex: Then would unbalanced heat licentious reign, / Crack the dry hill, and chap the russet plain.
whose fair face neither the summer's blaze can scorch nor winter's blast chap.

The jaw.

He unseamed him from the nave to the chaps.

ety: From Spanish chaparral, from chaparro (“evergreen oak”) + -al, from Basque txaparro, from txapar, from sapar.

ex: Have you ever been south of Monterey? / Barrancas carve the coastline / And the chaparral flows to the sea / 'Neath waves of golden sunshine
“Look at all the chaparral on California’s coast — it’s all about surviving that kind of fire cycle.”

ety: Formerly sold by chapmen; see the etymology there, and book.

s.def: A small book, usually made from a single sheet, folded several times, containing poems, ballads or religious tracts.
ex: For Haines’s chapbook. No-one here to hear.

ety: From Middle English chape, from Old French chape (“a churchman's cope, a cover, a chape”), from Latin cappa, itself derived from Latin caput (“the head”). Doublet of cap, cape, and cope.

s.def: The lower metallic cap at the end of a sword's scabbard.
ex: The scabbard ended in a chape, which took two forms: sometimes it terminated in a ball, and sometimes in a crescent or fish-tail.

s.def: Alternative form of chappe (“rainguard”) (piece fitted to a sword's crossguard).
The piece by which an object is attached to something, such as the frog of a scabbard or the metal loop at the back of a buckle by which it is fastened to a strap.
ex: At the end of each point a buckle is attached by means of a leather chape, and it is to these buckles that the two […]

s.def: The tip of a fox's tail.

ety: From Middle English chapele, chapel, from Old French chapele, from Late Latin cappella (“little cloak; chapel”), diminutive of cappa (“cloak, cape”). Doublet of capelle. Displaced native Old English bēdhūs. (printing office): Said to be because printing was first carried on in England in a chapel near Westminster Abbey.

s.def: A place of worship, smaller than or subordinate to a church.
A place of worship in another building or within a civil institution such as a larger church, airport, prison, monastery, school, etc.; often primarily for private prayer.

s.def: A place of worship of a denomination not in conformity with the Church of England, usually Protestant; for example, of Nonconformist or Dissenter congregations.
A funeral home, or a room in one for holding funeral services.
A trade union branch in printing or journalism.
A printing office.
A choir of singers, or an orchestra, attached to the court of a prince or nobleman.
Describing a person who attends a nonconformist chapel.

To deposit or inter in a chapel; to enshrine.
ex: give us the bones Of our dead kings, that we may chapel them!

ety: From French chaperon (“hood”), from Middle French, "head covering", from Old French chape.

s.def: An adult who accompanies or supervises one or more young, unmarried men or women during social occasions, usually with the specific intent of preventing some types of social or sexual interactions or illegal behavior.
A type of hood, often ornamental or official, with an attached cape and a tail, later worn as a hat with the face hole put over the top of the head instead.
ex: His head and face cover'd with a chaperon, out of which there are but two holes to look through.

s.def: A device placed on the foreheads of horses which draw the hearse in pompous funerals.
To accompany; to escort.
To mother.

ety: See chaperon.

s.def: A protein that assists the non-covalent folding/unfolding and the assembly/disassembly of other macromolecular structures, but does not occur in these structures when the latter are performing their normal biological functions.
An older person who accompanies other younger people to ensure the propriety of their behaviour, often an older woman accompanying a young woman.
An employee sent by a British company to the European Union to work with a client there, to circumvent restrictions imposed after Brexit.

ety: From chap + fallen; see chap (“jaw”).

s.def: Crestfallen, dejected.

ety: From Middle English chapitre, from Old French chapitre, from Latin capitulum, diminutive of caput (“head”). Doublet of chapter and capitulum.

The capital or uppermost part of a column, upon which the roof and its decorations are supported.

ety: From Middle English chapeleyn, from Old French chapelain, from Medieval Latin, Late Latin cappellānus, from cappella. Doublet of capelin. Displaced Old English handprēost.

s.def: A member of a religious body (who is often, although not always, of the clergy) officially assigned to provide pastoral care at an institution, group, private chapel, etc.
ex: The Railway Mission's regionally based chaplains perform the role of impartial 'friend' to anyone working on the railway, regardless of their faith.

s.def: A person without religious affiliation who carries out similar duties in a secular context.

ety: From Middle English chapelet, from Old French chapelet. Doublet of chapelet.

s.def: A garland or circlet for the head.
A molding in the form of a string of beads; a bead molding.
A metal support for a cylindrical pipe.
A headdress in the form of a wreath made of leaves, flowers or twigs woven into a ring.
A string (of beads), especially when making up five decades of the rosary.

s.def: A set of repetitive prayers, other than the Rosary, typically prayed with a string of beads.
ex: The Chaplet of the Seven Sorrows of Mary consists of seven sets of Hail Marys.

s.def: A series of spores or other objects arranged like beads on a string.
A bent piece of sheet iron, or a pin with thin plates on its ends, for holding a core in place in the mould.
Alternative form of chapelet.
A small chapel or shrine.

ety: From Middle English chapman, chepman, from Old English ċēapmann (“dealer, merchant”), from Proto-West Germanic *kaupamann, equivalent to cheap (noun) + man. Cognate with synonymous West Frisian keapman, Dutch koopman, German Low German Koopmann, German Kaufmann, Swedish köpman.

s.def: A dealer or merchant, especially an itinerant one.

When chapmen billies leave the street, / And drouthy neibors, neibors meet, / As market days are wearing late, / An' folk begin to tak the gate

s.def: A purchaser.

third-person singular simple present indicative of chap
Protective leather leggings attached at the waist.
ex: If you are going to use that chainsaw, why don't you put on a pair of chaps?
Chaps were a costume staple of Westerns.

ety: From Middle English chapitre, from Old French chapitre, from Latin capitulum (“a chapter of a book, in Medieval Latin also a synod or council”), diminutive of caput (“a head”); see capital, capitulum, and chapiter, which are doublets of chapter.
