s.def: One who claps; a person who applauds by clapping the hands.
An object so suspended inside a bell that it may hit the bell and cause it to ring; a clanger or tongue.
A wooden mechanical device used as a scarecrow; bird-scaring rattle, a wind-rattle or a wind-clapper.
ex: "Sir, sir! folks' tongues go like the clappers in the fields to drive away the blackbirds. A very little wind makes 'em rattle wonderfully."

s.def: A clapstick (musical instrument).
A pounding block.
The chattering damsel of a mill.
A slapshot
The hinged part of a clapperboard, used to synchronise images and soundtrack, or the clapperboard itself.
A person's tongue.
To ring a bell by pulling a rope attached to the clapper.

ety: From clapper + board.

s.def: A device consisting of a board on which information about a film being recorded is noted, and a hinged piece which is brought down on the board with a clap at the start and end of each take of the film; it is used to synchronize picture and sound during editing.
To fight and scratch.
ex: Steady, Birds! present your beaks! in double time, charge and attack, Pounce upon them, smash the potlid, clapperclaw them, tear and hack.

s.def: To abuse with words; to revile; to scold.

ety: Theater slang, c. 1730, from clap + trap, referring to theatrical techniques or gags used to incite applause.

s.def: Empty verbiage or nonsense.
A device for producing a clapping sound in theaters.
A device or trick to gain applause; a humbug.

ety: Borrowed from French claque (“group of people hired to applaud or boo, claque”, literally “a slap; a clap”).

s.def: A group of people hired to attend a performance and to either applaud or boo.
ex: The claque isn't paid. In fact, claqueurs pay to get in. The inducement is that they can buy standing room for half price, without waiting in line.

s.def: A group of fawning admirers.
A group of people who pre-arrange among themselves to express strong support for an idea, so as to give the false impression of a wider consensus.

ety: From Middle English claret, from Middle French claret, from Medieval Latin clārātum vīnum, from clārus. Compare tent (“Spanish red wine”), also from color. Doublet of clairet.

s.def: A dry red wine produced in the Bordeaux region of France, or a similar wine made elsewhere.
A deep purplish-red colour, like that of the wine; Bordeaux.
ex: Honey smiled hugely, so that Alex was shown every one of her claret gums.

s.def: Blood.
ex: He was rejuvenated within a week, thanks to a diet of fresh claret direct from the jugular, while the lawyer slept.

s.def: Of a deep purplish-red colour, like that of claret.
ex: Dhondt drives a claret 1927 Bugatti Royale Type 41, a real spanker, Sixsmith.

s.def: To drink claret.
ex: By night, again, we miss the bright cafe, the brilliantly illuminated offices, and the fringe of guests smoking and clareting […]

der: claret would be port if it could

ety: Borrowed from Middle French clarification, from Latin clārificātiō.

s.def: The act of clarifying; the act or process of making clear or transparent by freeing visible impurities; particularly, the clearing or fining of liquid substances from impurities via the separation of the insoluble particles which prevent the liquid from being transparent.
ex: The clarification of wine.

s.def: The act of freeing from obscurities; disambiguation.
ex: Your ideas deserve clarification.

s.def: An explanatory comment on, or question about, a point of obscurity.
ex: Let me make just one clarification: did he kiss her, or did she kiss him?

s.def: A small piece of writing supplemental to a previously published text, intended to disambiguate, explain away obscurities, but not contradict or emend the text (as would a correction).
Clarity, transparency, mutual understanding; to be clear.
ex: So, just for clarification, you're saying your Chihuahua ate your homework?

ety: From Middle English clarifien, from Old French clarifiier, from Latin clārificō, clārificāre; clārus (“clear”) + faciō, facere (“make”). Semantically clear + -ify.

s.def: To make or become clear or easily understood; to explain or resolve in order to remove doubt or obscurity.
ex: Please clarify what you mean by this.
Over time, the situation gradually clarified.
To clarify his reason, to rectify his will.

s.def: To make or become clear or bright by freeing from impurities or turbidity.
ex: What's the best way to clarify cooking oil?
Leave the wine for 24 hours and it will clarify.

s.def: (intransitive) to become clear or transparent
To glorify.

ety: Borrowed from Italian clarinetto, diminutive of clarino (“trumpet”) (as the first clarinets had a strident tone similar to that of a trumpet), from Latin clarus. Alternatively, the word may come from French clarinette, diminutive form of clarine (“bell”), from clarin, from clair (“clear”), from Latin clarus.

s.def: A woodwind musical instrument that has a distinctive liquid tone whose characteristics vary among its three registers: chalumeau (low), clarion (medium), and altissimo (high).

ety: The noun is derived from Middle English clarion, clarioun (“trumpet with a narrow tube and a shrill sound, clarion; clarion player”) [and other forms], from Old French claron, clarïon (“clarion”) [and other forms], from Medieval Latin clāriōn, clario, clārōn (“clarion; trumpet”), from Latin clārus (“audible; clear, distinct, loud; (visually) bright, clear”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kelh₁- (“to call, summon; to cry”). The adjective is from an attributive use of the noun.

s.def: A medieval brass instrument chiefly used as a battle signal; related to the trumpet, it had a narrow, straight pipe and a high-pitched, piercing sound.
ex: The clarion’s call to action has been heard.
And like a silver clarion rung / The accents of that unknown tongue, / Excelsior!

s.def: The sound of a clarion (sense 1), or any sound resembling the loud, high-pitched note of a clarion.
ex: [K]indling Nations buckle on their mail, / And Fame, with clarion-blast and wings unfurl'd, / To freedom and revenge awakens an injured World!
O chanticleer, / Your clarion blow; the day is near.

s.def: An organ stop consisting of pipes with reeds giving a high-pitched note like that of a clarion (sense 1).
The middle register of the clarinet.
A charge thought to represent a type of wind instrument, a keyboard instrument like a spinet, or perhaps a rest used by a knight to support a lance during jousting.
Of a sound, a voice, a message, etc.: brilliantly clear.
ex: her clarion top notes
And loud that clarion voice replied / Excelsior!
The clarion immediacy of Van Gogh’s painting was echoed by his prose.

s.def: To announce or herald (something) using a clarion (noun sense 1).
ex: His deep voice clarioned the words and he paused, hearing them whisper away into their last faint echoes in the organ loft.
All around me the tamaracks, alder birches and willows would send up amber and golden flares clarioning the winter; […]

s.def: Of a thing: to cause (a place) to echo with a sound like that of a clarion.
To sound a clarion; also, to make a high-pitched, piercing sound like that of a clarion.
ex: [T]hou, young-bodied morn, / In-ushered by the puffed winds clarioning, / No bond can bind.
Grey dawn is over, Chrysilla, and ere now the morning cock clarioning leads on the envious Lady of Morn.

ety: From Middle English claritee, from Old French clarté, from Latin clāritās, from clārus (“clear”); equivalent to clear + -ity.

s.def: The state or measure of being clear, either in appearance, thought or style; lucidity.
ex: She dreamed with great clarity.
The brilliant clarity of his argument could not be faulted.
The clarity of the clean glass was superb.

s.def: The ability to be easily understood.
ex: Lack of clarity on the part of the teacher will cause confusion among the students.

s.def: The ability to think clearly and rationally.
The ability to be easily heard.
ex: The singer was praised for the amazing clarity in her voice.

ety: From Middle English clarie, from Anglo-Norman sclaree, from Late or Medieval Latin sclarēia.

s.def: clary sage (Salvia sclarea)

ety: Of onomatopoeic origin. Compare Saterland Frisian klatskje (“to smack, slap”), West Frisian kletse, kletskje, Dutch kletsen (“to smack, slap, clash”), German Low German klattsen, klatsken (“to smack, splash”), German klatschen (“to clap, smack, slap”) and Klatsch (“a clapping sound; the din resulting from two or more things colliding”), Danish klaske (“to clash, splatter”).

s.def: A loud sound, like the crashing together of metal objects; a crash.
ex: I heard a clash from the kitchen, and rushed in to find the cat had knocked over some pots and pans.
Alone amid clashes of rain against the house.

s.def: A skirmish, a hostile encounter.
match; a game between two sides.
ex: But they ran out of time and inspiration as Les Bleus set up a deserved semi-final clash with Wales.

s.def: An angry argument.
Opposition; contradiction; such as between differing or contending interests, views, purposes etc.
ex: clash of beliefs
culture clash

s.def: A combination of garments that do not look good together, especially because of conflicting colours.
ex: She was wearing a horrible clash of red and orange.

s.def: An instance of restarting the game after a "dead ball", where it is dropped between two opposing players, who can fight for possession.
Chatter; gossip; idle talk.
A heavy fall (of rain); heavy rain.
ex: T' taties offer't ta be a grand crop et forend, bet then seea mitch clash an caald wes again em, an thaev tean up varra smo, […]

s.def: To make a clashing sound.
ex: The cymbals clashed.

ety: Noun dated ca. 1300 and verb dated ca. 1400; from Middle English claspe (“metal catch or hook used to hold things together”), possible metathesis of clapse, which comes from or related to Old English clyppan (“clasp”) (also see clip (verb)). Related to English enclasp (“embrace, hold tightly in one's arms”). Compare hasp, of very similar meaning but older known provenance.

s.def: A device with interlocking parts used for fastening things together, such as a fastener or a holder.
ex: I always have a hard time working the clasp on this necklace!

s.def: A bar or insignia on a medal ribbon, to either indicate an additional award of the medal, or the action or service for which it was awarded.
An embrace, a grasp, or handshake.
ex: He took her hand in a firm clasp.
How few! yet how they creep / Through my fingers to the deep, / While I weep—while I weep! / O God! can I not grasp / Them with a tighter clasp?

s.def: To take hold of; to grasp.
ex: They clasped hands and parted as friends.

s.def: To shut or fasten together with, or as if with, a clasp.
To cling.

ety: Etymology tree English clasp Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Proto-Italic *-āzios Latin -āriusnom. Latin -āriusbor. Proto-Germanic *-ārijaz Proto-West Germanic *-ārī Old English -ere Middle English -ere English -er English clasper From clasp + -er.

s.def: Anything that clasps.
Any of several appendages, in insects, crustacea and fish, that are used to clasp the female during copulation.
The tendril of a plant.

ety: From Middle French classe, from Latin classis (“a class or division of the people, assembly of people, the whole body of citizens called to arms, the army, the fleet, later a class or division in general”), from Proto-Indo-European *kelh₁- (“to call, shout”). Doublet of clas and classis. Displaced Old English ġecynd.

s.def: A group, collection, category or set sharing characteristics or attributes.
ex: The new Ford Fiesta is set to be best in the 'small family' class.
That is one class-A heifer you got there, sonny.
Often used to imply membership of a large class.

s.def: A social grouping, based on job, wealth, etc. In Britain, society is commonly split into three main classes: upper class, middle class and working class.
A group of students in a regularly scheduled meeting with a teacher.
ex: The class was noisy, but the teacher was able to get their attention with a story.

s.def: A group of students who commenced or completed their education during a particular year. A school class.
ex: The class of 1982 was particularly noteworthy.
Thirty years ago there were only a few high schools for boys, and in 1957 the first university class consisted of only 50 young men.

s.def: A category of seats in an airplane, train or other means of mass transportation.
ex: I used to fly business class, but now my company can only afford economy.
The City & South London was also the first British passenger railway to offer only one class.

s.def: A rank in the classification of organisms, below phylum and above order; a taxon of that rank.
ex: Magnolias belong to the class Magnoliopsida.

s.def: A set of objects having the same behavior (but typically differing in state), or a template defining such a set in terms of its common properties, functions, etc.
ex: an abstract base class

s.def: The division of society into classes.
ex: Jane Austen's works deal with class in 18th-century England.

s.def: Admirable behavior; elegance.
ex: Apologizing for losing your temper, even though you were badly provoked, showed real class.

s.def: A series of lessons covering a single subject.
ex: I took the cooking class for enjoyment, but I also learned a lot.

ety: Calque of German Klassenbewusstsein.

s.def: An individual's awareness of their relative place within the class system of society.
A planned event at which members of a past school class meet.
ex: The class of 1986 is having its 20th class reunion before too long.

s.def: Conflict between social or economic classes (especially between the capitalist and proletariat classes); the active expression of a theoretical class conflict looked at from any kind of socialist perspective.
ex: In his letter of 5 March 1852 to Joseph Weydemeyer, Marx declares that it was not he who discovered the existence of classes or the class struggle […]

s.def: Structured by defining classes of objects.
Based on social class.
ex: class-based affirmative action

s.def: Learning delivered in a class either online or in a classroom.
A programming style, where inheritance is achieved by using classes of objects.

ety: From class + -eme.

s.def: A generic or contextual seme, denoting a group of objects.

ety: From French classique, from Latin classic(us) (“relating to the classes of Roman citizenry, especially the highest”), from classis. By surface analysis, class + -ic. Piecewise doublet of classy.

s.def: The author of such a work.
ex: It was the first work to which he had put his name; and it at once raised him to the rank of a legitimate English classic.

s.def: lasting work
Of or relating to the first class or rank, especially in literature or art.
Exemplary of a particular style; defining a class or category; typical; archetypical; epitomic.
ex: He has a classic case of narcissism.

s.def: Exhibiting timeless quality and excellence.
ex: "To Kill a Mockingbird" is a 1960 classic book by Harper Lee.

s.def: Characteristic of or from the past; old; retro; vintage.
ex: watching classic movies as a hobby

s.def: Of or pertaining to the ancient Greeks and Romans, especially to Greek or Roman authors of the highest rank, or of the period when their best literature was produced; of or pertaining to places inhabited by the ancient Greeks and Romans, or rendered famous by their deeds.
ex: 1819, Felicia Hemans, The Widow of Crescentius Though throned midst Latium's classic plains.

s.def: Traditional; original.
ex: Users who dislike the new visual layout can return to classic mode.

s.def: Humorously ironic or apposite.
ex: It was classic—the way she slipped on a banana peel while she was telling us all to be careful!

s.def: A perfect and/or early example of a particular style.

ety: See classic § Etymology for history. By surface analysis, class + -ical or classic + -al or class + -ic + -al

s.def: Conforming to the best authority in literature and art; chaste; pure; refined
ex: classical dance

s.def: Of or relating to the first class or rank, especially in literature or art.
Of or pertaining to established principles in a discipline.
Describing Western music and musicians of the late 18th and early 19th centuries.
Describing art music (rather than pop, jazz, blues, etc), especially when played using instruments of the orchestra.

Of or pertaining to the ancient Greeks and Romans, especially to Greek or Roman authors of the highest rank, or of the period when their best literature was produced; of or pertaining to places inhabited by the ancient Greeks and Romans, or rendered famous by their deeds.
ex: He [Atterbury] directed the classical studies of the undergraduates of his college.

s.def: Knowledgeable or skilled in the classics; versed in the classics.
ex: a classical scholar

s.def: Pertaining to models of physical laws that do not take quantum or relativistic effects into account; Newtonian or Maxwellian.
One that is classical in some way; for example, a classical economist.
Ellipsis of classical music.

A learning process in which a previously neutral stimulus (such as a bell) is paired with a potent stimulus (such as food in the case of a dog), so that the neutral stimulus comes to elicit a conditioned response (salivation) similar to the one elicited by the potent stimulus.

ety: From classical + music.

s.def: Music of the classical period; the music of Mozart, Haydn, etc; the musical period before the romantic.
The more serious forms of music, taught through formal education and performed according to strict rules, as opposed to folk music or popular music.
The study of Ancient Greek and Latin, their literature, history, etc., sometimes inclusive of the study of the ancient Mediterranean generally.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *kelh₁-der. Proto-Italic *klāssis Latin classis Proto-Indo-European *-ikos Proto-Italic *-ikos Latin -icus Latin classicuslbor. French classiquebor. s.def: All the classical traditions of the art and architecture of ancient Greece and Rome, especially the aspects of simplicity, elegance and proportion.
Classical scholarship.
A Latin or Ancient Greek expression used in an English sentence.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *kelh₁-der. Proto-Italic *klāssis Latin classis Proto-Indo-European *-ikos Proto-Italic *-ikos Latin -icus Latin classicuslbor. French classiquebor. Latin -istader. Old French -istebor. Middle English -ist English -ist English clas…

s.def: A classical scholar, especially one who studies ancient Greek and Latin language and culture.
A follower of classicism.

ety: From classic + -ize.

s.def: To make classic.
ex: Another approach is exemplified by the performance group known as Mahligai […] which drew on traditional forms in an attempt to classicize them.

s.def: To conform to the classic style.
ex: Mies' style, for all of its obvious modernity, is essentially rather classicizing […]

s.def: The act of forming into a class or classes; a distribution into groups, as classes, orders, families, etc., according to some common relations or attributes.
ex: Near-synonyms: categorization, classifying, categorizing, typing, sorting

ety: From French classifier. By surface analysis, class + -ify.

s.def: to identify by or divide into classes; to categorize
ex: Should we classify "make up" as an idiom or as a phrasal verb?

s.def: to declare something a secret, especially a government secret
ex: They decided to classify that information.

s.def: To make classy

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *kelh₁-der. Proto-Italic *klāssis Latin classisder. Middle French classebor. English class Proto-Indo-European *-id- Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-idyéti Proto-Hellenic *-íd͏̌d͏̌ō Ancient Greek -ῐ́ζω (-ĭ́zō) Proto-Indo-European *-mos Proto-Indo-European *-mós Ancient Greek -μός (-mós) Ancient Greek -ισμός (-ismós)der. English -ism English classism From class + -ism.

s.def: Discrimination or prejudice that is based on social class, especially against those of lower social class.

ety: From class + -mate.

s.def: A student who is in the same class at school.
ex: Danny and I have been classmates for five years, but I've never spoken to him outside of lessons.
She was your classmate at the village school from first grade.

s.def: A member of a different sort of class, such as locomotives etc.
ex: The Class 87 is the only main line-certified member of the fleet left in the UK, although there are 21 classmates in use overseas [...]

ety: From class + path.

s.def: The path on a file system where the Java virtual machine should look for user-defined classes and packages when running Java programs.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *kelh₁-der. Proto-Italic *klāssis Latin classisder. Middle French classebor. English class Proto-Indo-European *Hrew-? Proto-Indo-European *(H)rewH-der. Proto-Germanic *rūmą Proto-West Germanic *rūm Old English rūm Middle English roum English room English classroom From class + room.

s.def: A room, often in a school, where classes take place.
ex: Secondly, preserved railways are not 24/7 operations. There are closed seasons where they can be turned into open-air classrooms.

ety: From class + -y. Piecewise doublet of classic.

s.def: Elegant, highly stylish or fashionable.
ex: That's a very classy outfit you're wearing.

s.def: Of a superior type; especially, exhibiting admirable personal qualities.
ex: Ignoring his coarse insults was a classy response.

s.def: Obsolete form of khalasi.

ety: From Ancient Greek κλαστός (klastós, “broken in pieces”), from κλάω (kláō, “to break”) + -ic.

s.def: Made up of parts that are easily removable.
Made from fragments of pre-existing rocks.
A rock made from fragments of pre-existing rocks.

ety: From Latin clāthrātus, from clāthrī (“lattice”) + -ātus, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix). The noun is from the clipping of clathrate compound, see -ate.

s.def: A clathrate compound.

ety: From Middle English clatren (“to make a rattling sound”), from Old English *clatrian (attested as the Late Old English gerund clatrung), of onomatopoeic origin. Compare Dutch klateren, kletteren. The noun, derived from the verb, is first attested in the 14ᵗʰ century.

s.def: To make a rattling sound.
ex: When all the bees are gone to settle, / You clatter still your brazen kettle.
Over the cobbles he clattered and clashed in the dark inn-yard, / And he tapped with his whip on the shutters, but all was locked and barred; […]

s.def: To chatter noisily or rapidly.
To hit; to smack.
ex: "I can't watch it because I have to go outside and clatter someone in the nuts!”
“An Orange bitch clattered seven shades of shite out of her,” Padraig eagerly piped up.

s.def: A rattling noise; a repetition of abrupt, sharp sounds.
A loud disturbance.
Noisy talk or chatter.
A large group, especially of sibling children; a lot
ex: a young mother with a clatter of kids told me ... her Catholic doctor refused point-blank to advise other than the rhythm method.
There haven't been any men for years. The last one I can remember was a hairy old ballad singer who, it turned out, had a wife and a clatter of kids.

s.def: Alternative form of clitter; scree.

ety: Borrowed from Latin claudicātiō (“limping”, noun), from claudicō (“to limp, halt, be lame”) + -ātiō (“-ation”, nominal suffix).

s.def: Limping.
A condition in which temporary cramp-like pain in the calf muscles is induced by exercise, typically caused by obstruction of the arteries.
ex: Chronic venous disease includes cosmetically undesirable telangiectasias, varicose veins, venous ulceration, and claudication.

ety: From Middle English clause, claus, borrowed from Old French clause, from Medieval Latin clausa (Latin diminutive clausula (“close, end; a clause, close of a period”)), from Latin clausus, past participle of claudere (“to shut, close”). See close, its doublet.

s.def: A verb along with its subject and their modifiers. If a clause provides a complete thought on its own, then it is an independent (superordinate) clause; otherwise, it is dependent (subordinate). (Independent clauses can be sentences; they can also be part of a sentence. Dependent clauses can only b…
A distinct part of a contract, a will or another legal document.
A group of words that contains a subject and a verb; it may be part of a sentence or may constitute the whole sentence, depending on the syntax in each instance.
ex: Near-synonyms: sentential, sentence

s.def: A verb, its necessary grammatical arguments, and any adjuncts affecting them.
A constituent (component) of a statement or query.
To amend (a bill of lading or similar document).
ex: The question of clausing the bills of lading, so as to avoid "dirtying", which impairs its negotiability, may also be looked into
Any attempt to clause a Bill of Lading will be strenuously resisted by shippers, and they will obtain clean bills in the usual ways
There is little authority in English law dealing with the liability of a carrier who unnecessarily clauses a bill of lading.

ety: Based on Latin claustrum (“cloister”). Doublet of cloistral.

s.def: Of or pertaining to a cloister.
Having cloisters; cloistered.
Relating to the claustrum of the brain.

ety: From Latin claustrum (“a shut-in place”), from Latin claudō (“to shut, close; to imprison, confine”) + -phobia. First attested in the British Medical Journal.

s.def: The abnormal fear of closed, tight places.
ex: She complained of emaciation, nervousness, tenderness of the scalp, weakness of the back, claustrophobia, and other morbid fears.
The first scenes, which take place in a minitheater that keeps shrinking, will be painful for anyone with even a tinge of claustrophobia.
(Editor’s note: Those who suffer from claustrophobia, kabourophobia, arachnophobia or thalassophobia are advised to skip the above trailer.)

ety: From claustrophobia + -ic.

s.def: Suffering from claustrophobia; being scared of being enclosed in a confined space.
Cramped and confined, so as to induce claustrophobia.
ex: ...within the monstrous arrangements of dried flowers on the table-tops, against the Victorian clutter of that claustrophobic room...

ety: First attested in 1661; borrowed from New Latin clāvātus, from Latin clāva (“club”) + -ātus, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix). By surface analysis, clav(a) + -ate.

s.def: Resembling a club, becoming increasingly wide from the base to the distal end.
ex: an organism with clavate antennae

ety: From German Klavichord, from Renaissance Latin clavichordium, from clāvis (“key”) + chorda (“cord, string”).

s.def: An early keyboard instrument producing a soft sound by means of metal blades (called tangents) attached to the inner ends of the keys gently striking the strings.

ety: Borrowed from Middle French clavicule, from Latin clāvicula (“a small key”), diminutive of clāvis (“a key”).

s.def: The collarbone; the prominent bone at the top of the chest between the shoulder and the neck connecting the shoulder and the breastbone.
ex: And you worked a lot too. You were thin from biking around all day; your protruding clavicles collected rainwater.

s.def: A bone in fish.
The upper part of a spiral shell.

s.def: A magnetic or electronic device used to determine the cardinal directions (usually magnetic or true north).
ex: a glance at his compass would have shown him that a northerly course instead of an easterly could not be right

s.def: The range of notes of a musical instrument or voice.
ex: You would sound me from my lowest note to the top of my compass.

s.def: To surround; to encircle; to environ; to stretch round.
ex: And the name of the second river is Gihon: the same is it that compasseth the whole land of Ethiopia.

s.def: A pair of compasses (a device used to draw circular arcs and transfer length measurements).
ex: to fix one foot of their compass wherever they please

s.def: A space within limits; an area.
ex: Animals, in their generation, are wiser than the sons of men but their wisdom is confined to a few particulars, and lies in a very narrow compass.
Clara thought she had never seen him look so small and mean. He was as if trying to get himself into the smallest possible compass.

s.def: An enclosing limit; a boundary, a circumference.
ex: within the compass of an encircling wall

s.def: Moderate bounds, limits of truth; moderation; due limits; used with within.
ex: In two hundred years before (I speak within compass), no such commission had been executed.
"Saints!" she cried, "but what a noise you keep! Can you not speak in compass?"

s.def: Synonym of scope.
ex: the compass of his argument

s.def: Range, reach.
A passing round; circuit; circuitous course.
ex: This day I breathed first; time is come round, / And where I did begin, there shall I end; / My life is run his compass.
They fetched a compass of seven days' journey.

s.def: Any of several plants, the leaves of which become oriented to the morning sun:
Any of the horizontal directions indicated on a compass. There may be 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, or even 128 compass points on a compass, depending on its size and accuracy.

ety: From Middle English compassioun, compassion, from Old French compassion, from Ecclesiastical Latin compassio (“sympathy”), from Latin compati, past participle compassus (“to suffer together with”), from com- (“together”) + pati (“to suffer”); see passion. By surface analysis, com- + passion.

s.def: deep awareness of the suffering of another
Deep awareness of the suffering of others that people have to the point of them being motivated to relieve such states.
ex: Other people's problems, they overwhelm my mind / They say compassion is a virtue, but I don't have the time

s.def: Deep awareness of the individual experiences of suffering of others or themselves that people have to the point of them being motivated to relieve such experiences, as reflected by the psychological term self-compassion.
ex: True leadership lies in compassion, not in coercion.

s.def: To pity.
ex: O heavens, can you hear a good man groan / And not relent, or not compassion him?
The widow's tears flowed wildly. / But Oh! a harbinger of life approached — / God, manifest in flesh — compassioned her, / And bade her weep no more.

ety: Pseudo-Latinism, derived from a pseudo-Latin form of French compassionné, past participle of compassionner (“to feel sorry for”). By surface analysis, compassion + -ate.

s.def: Having, feeling or showing compassion (to or toward someone).
ex: The Compassionate, the All-Compassionate

s.def: Given to someone as an exception because of a family emergency or a death in their family.
ex: compassionate leave; a compassionate visa

s.def: Inviting or asking for pity.
To feel compassion (for someone or with regard to something); to regard (someone or something) with compassion.
ex: […] seeing them die so wofully in the flames, he compassionated them.
“[…] if she were a nice, pretty child, one might compassionate her forlornness; but one really cannot care for such a little toad as that.”
Helen laughed at these sentimental remarks, and wondered that Madame herself did not compassionate her lodger, and console him

ety: Borrowed from New Latin compatibilitās. By surface analysis, compatible + -ity.

s.def: The state of being compatible; in which two or more things are able to exist or work together in combination without problems or conflict.
the capability of two or more items or components of equipment or material to exist or function in the same system or environment without mutual interference.
the ability to execute a given program on different types of computers without modification of the program or the computers. See backward compatibility and forward compatibility.

the capability that allows the substitution of one subsystem (storage facility), or of one functional unit (e.g., hardware, software), for the originally designated system or functional unit in a relatively transparent manner, without loss of information and without the introduction of errors.
the continuity or good fit of material or members or components while being deformed.

ety: Inherited from Middle English compatible, fron Anglo-Norman compatible, from Medieval Latin compatibilis (“in compatibile beneficium, a benefice which could be held together with another one”), from Late Latin compator (“to suffer with”), from com- (“together”) + pati (“to suffer”); see passion.

s.def: Capable of working together without conflict.
ex: This printer isn't compatible with my computer.

s.def: Able to get along well.
ex: My neighbours and I are not very compatible: they're loud and I'm an introvert.

s.def: Consistent; congruous.
ex: His actions were compatible with his sermons.

s.def: Something that is compatible with something else.
ex: a computer company that sells IBM compatibles

ety: Borrowed from French compatriote, itself borrowed from Latin compatriota. By surface analysis, com- + patriot. Displaced native Old English ġelanda.

s.def: Somebody from one's own country.
ex: the distrust with which they felt themselves to be regarded by their compatriots in America
However Russian Pavlyuchenko stunned his compatriots with an unstoppable 25-yard drive into the top corner.

s.def: Of the same country; especially, being countrymen and having a common sentiment of patriotism.

ety: From Middle English comper, from Middle French comper, from Latin compater, compatrem. Doublet of compere as well as compadre and goombah. Influenced by folk-etymological analysis as com- + peer.

s.def: The equal or peer of someone else; a close companion or associate.
ex: And him thus answer'd soon his bold compeer.

s.def: To be equal with; to match.
ex: In my rights, / By me invested, he compeers the best.

Displaced native Old Engli…

s.def: To drive together, round up.
ex: The shepherds compelled the stray sheep into the fold as night began to fall.

s.def: To overpower; to subdue.
ex: She had one of those perfect faces, which irresistibly compel the soul of a man.

s.def: To force, constrain, or coerce.
ex: Logic compels the wise, while fools feel compelled by emotions.
Congratulations, your courage compels respect.
Against my will, / As Pompey was, am I compell’d to set / Upon one battle all our liberties.

s.def: To forcefully or powerfully motivate (a course of action).
ex: As the novel progresses, it picks up a propulsive energy, the kind that compels you to keep reading straight through to the end.

s.def: To have a strong, irresistible force (on someone or something).
To exact, extort, (make) produce by force.
ex: Commissions, which compel from each / The sixth part of his substance.
The Queen has nothing but the power to execute the laws, to adjust grievances and to compel order.

s.def: To force to yield; to overpower; to subjugate.
ex: Easy sleep their weary limbs compell'd.
And I will fetch you forage from all fields, / For I compel all creatures to my will.

s.def: To gather or unite in a crowd or company.
ex: in one troop compell'd

s.def: To call forth; to summon.
ex: She had this knight from far compeld.

ety: By surface analysis, compel + -ing.

s.def: very interesting; able to capture and hold one's attention
ex: The novel was so compelling that I couldn't put it down.

s.def: strong and forceful; that causes one to feel like they must do something
ex: I would need a very compelling reason to leave my job.

s.def: capable of causing someone to believe or agree
ex: He made a compelling argument.

ety: From Old French compendieux, from Latin compendiosus (“advantageous, abridged, brief”), from compendium.

s.def: containing a subset of words, succinctly described; abridged and summarized
briefly describing a body of knowledge

ety: From the Latin compendium (“that which is weighed together; a sparing, a saving, an abbreviation”), from com- (“with”) + pendō (“to weigh”).

s.def: A short, complete summary; an abstract.
A list or collection of various items.

ety: Borrowed from Latin compēnsātus, perfect passive participle of compensō (“to weight together one thing against another, balance, make good”), -ate (verb-forming suffix) for more.

s.def: To pay or reward someone in exchange for work done or some other consideration.
ex: It is hard work, but they will compensate you well for it.

s.def: To make up for; to do something in place of something else; to correct, satisfy; to reach an agreement such that the scales are literally or (metaphorically) balanced; to equalize or make even.
ex: His loud voice cannot compensate for a lack of personality.
To compensate me for his tree landing on my shed, my neighbor paved my driveway.
, Preface The pleasures of life do not compensate the miseries.

s.def: To do (something good) after (something bad) happens.
To adjust or adapt to a change, often a harm or deprivation.
ex: I hate that old car because it steers a little to the left and I'm always compensating for that when I drive it.
To compensate for his broken leg, Gary uses crutches.

ety: From Middle English compensacioun, from Old French compensacion, from Latin compensātiōnem, accusative singular of compensātiō. Equivalent to compensate + -ion.

s.def: The act or principle of compensating.
A recompense or reward for service.
Something which is regarded as an equivalent; something which compensates for loss.
ex: No pecuniary compensation can possibly reward them.

s.def: The extinction of debts of which two persons are reciprocally debtors by the credits of which they are reciprocally creditors; the payment of a debt by a credit of equal amount.
An equivalent stipulated for in contracts for the sale of real estate, in which it is customary to provide that errors in description, etc., shall not avoid, but shall be the subject of compensation.

The relationship between air temperature outside a building and a calculated target temperature for provision of air or water to contained rooms or spaces for the purpose of efficient heating. In building control systems, the compensation curve is defined to a compensator for this purpose.
The ability of one part of the brain to overfunction in order to take over the function of a damaged part (e.g. following a stroke).

ety: From compensate + -or.

s.def: A party or thing which compensates, pays or otherwise provides a compensation
Any device used to compensate for something, notably to achieve a better balance.
ex: Anything that reverses the direction of movement in a length of point rodding will act as a compensator over an equal length on each side of it; […].

s.def: A building control device used to deliver the compensation relationship or curve between the air temperature outside a building and the temperature of water or air provided to spaces or zones within the building for purposes of heating or cooling.
ex: Compensators ensure less heat is provided to a room on a warmer day. They may be implemented mechanically, electronically or in software.

s.def: One of several small magnets placed in the binnacle to neutralize the effect of the ship's metal on the compass

ety: Borrowed from French compensatoire. By surface analysis, compensate + -ory.

s.def: Intended to recompense someone who has experienced loss, suffering, or injury.
Reducing or offsetting the unpleasant or unwelcome effects of something.
That compensates for a deleterious mutation.

ety: Borrowed from Middle French competer, from Latin competere (“to coincide, to be equal to, to be capable of”), from com- (“with”) + petō (“to seek; to aim for, strive for”). Compare Latin competītor (“competitor”).

s.def: To be in battle or in a rivalry with another for the same thing, position, or reward; to contend.
To be in a position in which it is possible to win or triumph.
To take part in a contest, game or similar event.
To strive to achieve or obtain something which another also strives for, whether knowingly or unknowingly.

ety: Borrowed from Middle French compétence, from Late Latin competentia. Doublet of competency.

s.def: The quality or state of being able or suitable for a particular task; the quality or state of being competent for a particular task or skill.
the quality or state of being competent for a general role
The quality or state of being competent, i.e. able or suitable for a general role.
ex: Teachers are now required to teach intercultural communicative competence.

s.def: The system of linguistic knowledge possessed by native speakers of a language, as opposed to its actual use in concrete situations (performance), cf. linguistic competence.
A sustainable income.
ex: Reason's whole pleasure, all the joys of sense, / Lie in three words — health, peace, and competence.

s.def: the legal authority to deal with a matter.
ex: The bill was denied royal assent because the Scottish Parliament does not have legislative competence on the bill's matter.

s.def: The degree to which a rock is resistant to deformation or flow.

ety: From Late Latin competentia. Doublet of competence.

s.def: The ability to perform some task; competence.
ex: The loan demonstrates, in regard to instrumental resources, the competency of this kingdom to the assertion of the common cause.
What professional competencies do science teachers need?

s.def: An individual's capacity to understand the nature and implications of their legal rights and obligations.
Implicit knowledge of a language’s structure.
A sufficient supply of something.
ex: […] it would appear that before taking this precaution Mr. Bree must have had the thrift to remove a modest competency of the gold […]

s.def: A sustainable income.
ex: Superfluity comes sooner by white hairs, but competency lives longer.

ety: From Middle English competent, conpetent, from Old French competent (modern French compétent), from Latin competens, competentem, present participle of competō (“coincide, be equal to, be capable of”). Compare Dutch competent (“competent”), German kompetent (“competent”), Danish kompetent (“competent”).

s.def: Having sufficient skill, knowledge, ability, or qualifications.
ex: He is a competent skier and an expert snowboarder.
I believe in that myself because it has been explained by competent men as the convolutions of the grey matter.
That as a competent keyless citizen he had proceeded energetically from the unknown to the known through the incertitude of the void.

s.def: Having jurisdiction or authority over a particular issue or question.
ex: For any disagreements arising from this contract, the competent court shall be the Springfield Circuit Court.
judicial authority having competent jurisdiction

s.def: Adequate for the purpose.
Functionally in order; functioning adequately.
ex: a competent sphincter; a competent cervix; a competent immune system

s.def: Permeable to foreign DNA.
Resistant to deformation or flow.

ety: Borrowed from French compétition, from Late Latin competītiō, competītiōnem, from Latin competō, from con- + petō. By surface analysis, compete + -ition.

s.def: The action of competing.
ex: The competition for this job is strong.
Several firms are in competition for the contract.

s.def: A contest for a prize or award.
ex: The newspaper is featuring a competition to win a car.

s.def: The competitors in such a contest.
ex: The new stain remover was ten times more effective than the competition.

ety: From Latin competītus (past participle of competere) + -ive.

s.def: Of or pertaining to competition.
Inclined to compete.
Capable of competing successfully.
Relating to the inhibition of the effects of a chemical substance by another substance competing with it for binding or bonding.
ex: competitive antagonist

s.def: Cheap, especially used of quality products.

ety: Borrowed from Middle French compétiteur, from Latin competitor.

s.def: A person or organization against whom one is competing.
A participant in a competition, especially in athletics.
Partner, associate, one working with another toward a common goal.

ety: English compile + -ation, from Middle French, from Latin compilatio (“a raking together, a plundering, a collection of documents”).

s.def: The act or process of compiling or gathering together from various sources.
That which is compiled; especially, a book or document composed of materials gathering from other books or documents.
ex: Susie made Jasmine a compilation CD of some of the best songs they'd heard at the festival.

s.def: Translation of source code into object code by a compiler.

ety: From Middle English compilen, from Old French compiler, from Latin compīlō (“to plunder”).

s.def: To make by gathering pieces from various sources.
ex: Samuel Johnson compiled one of the most influential dictionaries of the English language.

s.def: To use a compiler to process source code and produce executable code.
ex: After I compile this program I’ll run it and see if it works.

s.def: To construct; to build.
ex: Before that Merlin dyde, he did intend / A brasen wall in compas to compyle / About Cairmardin […]

s.def: To achieve (a break) by making a sequence of shots.
ex: Steve Davis compiled a 147.

s.def: To be successfully processed by a compiler into executable code.
ex: There must be an error in my source code because it won’t compile.

s.def: To contain or comprise.
To write; to compose.
ex: They are at their leisure much given to poetry; in which they compile the praises of virtuous men and actions , satires against vice

s.def: An act of compiling code.
ex: Any file with an error or warning on it will be added to this smart group until the next compile.

s.def: Programming language requirements that must be met by source code for it to be successfully compiled (the “compile-time requirements”).
Operations performed by a compiler (the “compile-time operations”).
Properties of the program that can be reasoned about during compilation.

ety: From Middle English compilour, from Anglo-Norman compilour, from Old French compileur, from Latin compīlātōrem, equivalent to compile + -er.

s.def: A computer program that transforms source code into object code.
One who compiles.
ex: a compiler of poetry anthologies
my favourite crossword compiler

ety: Late Middle English complacence, from Late Latin complacentia. Compare French complaisance.

s.def: feeling of self-satisfaction
A feeling of contented self-satisfaction, especially when unaware of upcoming trouble.
ex: Others proclaim the infirmities of a great man with satisfaction and complacency, if they discover none of the like in themselves.
"However, incidents such as the derailment at Walton-on-Thames clearly show us that there is no room for complacency."

s.def: An instance of self-satisfaction.
Passivity as a result of contentment with the current situation.

s.def: To express feelings of pain, dissatisfaction, or resentment.
ex: Joe was always complaining about the noise made by his neighbours.

s.def: To state the presence of something negative; to indicate that one is suffering from something; to report (e.g.) a symptom.
ex: The patient complained of headache, nausea, and joint pain.

s.def: To make a formal accusation or bring a formal charge.
ex: They've complained about me to the police again.
Now, Master Shallow, you'll complain of me to the king?
If you get cheated by the Better Business Bureau, who do you complain to?

s.def: To creak or squeak, as a timber or wheel.
ex: the complaining bed-springs

ety: From Old French complaignant, present participle of complaindre.

s.def: One who makes complaint, one who complains.
ex: 1708-1714 Jeremy Collier, Ecclesiastical History of Great Britain Eager complainants […] in the dispute.
Heading the complainants is Sir Edward le Breton, Lord of the Manor of Loders, and a member of Bridport Rural Council.

s.def: The party that brings a civil lawsuit against another; the plaintiff.
An alleged victim in a criminal investigation or trial.

s.def: One who complains, or is known for their complaints.
A complainant (an alleged victim in a criminal trial).

ety: From Middle English compleynte, from Anglo-Norman compleint, from Old French compleindre, eventually from Latin planctus (whence plaint).

s.def: A grievance, problem, difficulty, or concern.
ex: I have no complaints about the quality of his work, but I don't enjoy his company.

s.def: In a civil action, the first pleading of the plaintiff setting out the facts on which the claim is based.
The act of complaining.
ex: customer complaints
noise complaints
file complaints

s.def: In criminal law, the preliminary charge or accusation made by one person against another to the appropriate court or officer, usually a magistrate.
A bodily disorder or disease; the symptom of such a disorder.
ex: Don't come too close; I've got this nasty complaint.

ety: From complaint + -ive.

s.def: Tending to complain, characterized by complaining.

ety: From French. See complaisant. By surface analysis, com- + plaisance.

s.def: The quality of being complaisant, amiable or agreeable.
ex: I see he has premeditated a Denial by the Complaisance of his Features.

ety: From Middle English complement, from Latin complēmentum (“that which fills up or completes”), from compleō (“to fill up; to complete”) (English complete). Doublet of compliment. The verb is from the noun.

s.def: A word or group of words that completes a grammatical construction in the predicate and that describes or is identified with the subject or object.
To complete, to bring to perfection, to make whole.
ex: We believe your addition will complement the team.

s.def: The totality, the full amount or number which completes something.
ex: Some 11 members of Somerton council's complement of 15 stepped down on Tuesday.

s.def: The whole working force of a vessel.
An angle which, together with a given angle, makes a right angle.
Something which completes, something which combines with something else to make up a complete whole; loosely, something perceived to be a harmonious or desirable partner or addition.
ex: History is the complement of poetry.
London's Kings Place, now one year old, established itself as a venue for imaginative programming, a complement to the evergreen Wigmore Hall.

s.def: A phonetic complement is a graphic element that modifies another, such as (in Linear B script) a small syllabogram that is attached to a logogram as an abbreviation of its reading (as opposed to an adjunct that abbreviates an adjective that modifies that logogram).
An interval which, together with the given interval, makes an octave.
The color which, when mixed with the given color, gives black (for mixing pigments) or white (for mixing light).
ex: The complement of blue is orange.

s.def: Given two sets, the set containing one set's elements that are not members of the other set (whether a relative complement or an absolute complement).
ex: The complement of the odd numbers is the even numbers, relative to the natural numbers.

ety: From complement + -ary. Piecewise doublet of complimentary.

s.def: Acting as a complement; making up a whole with something else.
ex: I'll provide you with some complementary notes to help you study.
The two business partners had complementary abilities: one had excellent people skills, while the other had a head for figures.

s.def: Of the specific pairings of the bases in DNA and RNA.
Pertaining to pairs of properties in quantum mechanics that are inversely related to each other, such as speed and position, or energy and time. (See also Heisenberg uncertainty principle.)
A complementary colour.
One skilled in compliments.
ex: the hands of the most skilful and cunning complementaries alive

s.def: An angle which adds with another to equal ninety degrees.

ety: From Middle English compleet (“full, complete”), borrowed from Old French complet or Latin completus, past participle of compleō (“to fill up, to complete”) (whence also complement, compliment), from com- + pleō (“to fill, to fulfill”) (whence also deplete, replete, plenty), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₁- (“to fill”) (English full).

s.def: To finish; to make done; to reach the end.
ex: He completed the assignment on time.
The Tsengwen Reservoir, located at Nanhsi village, Tainan, was completed in 1973.

s.def: To make whole or entire.
ex: The last chapter completes the book nicely.

s.def: With all parts included; with nothing missing; full.
ex: My life will be complete once I buy this new television.
She offered me complete control of the project.
After she found the rook, the chess set was complete.

s.def: To call from the small blind in an unraised pot.
to accomplish every significant achievement within a field
Finished; ended; concluded; completed.
ex: When your homework is complete, you can go and play with Martin.

s.def: Generic intensifier.
ex: He is a complete bastard!
It was a complete shock when he turned up on my doorstep.
Our vacation was a complete disaster.

s.def: In which all small limits exist.
In which every semantically valid well-formed formula is provable.
In which every Cauchy sequence converges to a point within the space.

ety: Etymology tree English complete Middle English -ly English -ly English completely From complete + -ly.

s.def: In a complete manner; thoroughly.
ex: Please completely fill in the box for your answer, using a number “2” pencil.
I will have completely finished my degree by next July, when my thesis has been properly edited.
It should not have been omitted that previous to completely stripping the body of the leviathan, he was beheaded.

s.def: To the fullest extent or degree; totally.
ex: He is completely mad.
Our future may lie beyond our vision, but it is not completely beyond our control.

A forward pass that is successfully caught by the intended receiver.

The space resulting from such an act.

ex: tab completion

s.def: Orgasm.

in mathematics
Made up of multiple parts; composite; not simple.
ex: a complex being; a complex idea

Complexity.

ety: Borrowed from French compliment, itself a borrowing of Italian complimento, which in turn is a borrowing from Spanish cumplimiento, from cumplir (“to comply, complete, do what is proper”) + -miento or Latin complēmentum. Doublet of complement. Displaced Old English ġeswǣsnes.

Misspelling of complement.

Misspelling of complement.

ety: Borrowed from Latin compōnēns, compōnēntis, present participle of compōnō (“assemble, put together”).

ety: From late Middle English comporten, from Old French comporter, from Latin comportare (“to bring together”), from com- (“together”) + portare (“to carry”).

ety: From Middle English composen, from Old French composer (“to compose, compound, adjust, settle”), from com- + poser, as an adaptation of Latin componere (“to put together, compose”), from com- (“together”) + ponere (“to put, place”).

ety: First attested in 1548; borrowed from Latin congrātulātus, the perfect active participle of Latin congrātulor (“to wish joy, rejoice (with); to congratulate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from con- + grātulor, from grātus (“grateful, pleasing, agreeable, beloved”) + -or. By surface analysis, con- + gratulate.

ex: Remind me to congratulate Dave and Lisa on their wedding.

ex: I congratulated myself on the success of my plan.

ety: From Middle English congratulacion, from Middle French congratulation or its etymon Latin congrātulātiō, from congrātulor (“to congratulate”). By surface analysis, congratulate + -ion.

ex: May I present my warmest congratulations?
a short speech of congratulation

s.def: Expressing praise and approval, expressing approbation.
ex: Warm congratulations on your newborn boy!

ety: The adjective is first attested in 1400–1450, in Middle English, the verb c. 1513; from Middle English congregat(e) (“(of people) banded together; (of liquids) accumulated; (of muscles) contracted; (of wounds) closed up”), borrowed from Latin congregātus, perfect passive participle of congregō (“to congregate”) (see -ate (etymology 1, 2 and 3), from con- (“with, together”) + gregō (“to collect into a flock”), from grex (“flock, herd”). s.def: To collect into an assembly or assemblage; to bring into one place, or into a united body.
ex: Any multitude of Christian men congregated may be termed by the name of a church.
The great receptacle Of congregated waters he called Seas.
Cold congregates all bodies.

ex: Even there where merchants most do congregate.

ex: VVith all the Gods about him congregate:

s.def: Collective; assembled; compact.
Assembled persons.

ety: From Middle English congregacioun, from Old French congregacion, from Latin congregātiō, itself from congregō (“to herd into a flock”). Adopted (1520s) by the English Bible translator William Tyndale, to render the Ancient Greek ἐκκλησία (ekklēsía, “those called together, (popular) meeting”) (hence Latin ecclēsia) in his New Testament, and preferred by 16th century Reformers instead of church. By surface analysis, congregate + -ion.

s.def: A gathering of faithful in a temple, church, synagogue, mosque or other place of worship, especially those present at a devotional service or who regularly attend such services, particularly in contrast to the leadership, choir or others.
The act of congregating or collecting together.
A Roman Congregation, a main department of the Vatican administration of the Catholic Church.
A corporate body whose members gather for worship, or the members of such a body.
Any large gathering of people.
A flock of birds.
ex: "Oh! I wasted most of my morning crawling to a murmuration of starlings, which I foolishly mistook for congregation of plover."
I was excited to ramp up our cave-diving efforts, and to see my first big congregation of penguins.
There was a congregation of pigeons inside the shack, he realized, pushing their beaks through the wooden lattice at the front.

s.def: A group of alligators or crocodiles.
ex: A congregation of crocodiles will communicate with body language and behavior and are also extremely territorial predators.
This explained what had been a puzzle to the most knowing of the party-that wonderful congregation of crocodiles.

s.def: The main body of university staff, comprising academics, administrative staff, heads of colleges, etc.

ety: From Latin congress(um), the past participle of congredior (“to go, come together”), itself from con- + gradior (“to go, step”). The verb is from the noun. Compare typologically coven, convent, convention, omitting several steps, from con- + veniō, Russian сход (sxod), схо́дка (sxódka), akin to сходи́ться (sxodítʹsja), ходи́ть (xodítʹ). Also compare Czech sjezd, Russian съезд (sʺjezd), akin to съезжа́ться (sʺjezžátʹsja), е́здить (jézditʹ). Also compare conference.

An association, especially one consisting of other associations or representatives of interest groups.

the National Congress of American Indians

s.def: To assemble together.
To meet in a congress.

The Kingdom of Poland created in 1815 by the Congress of Vienna as a sovereign state of the Russian part of Poland connected by personal union with the Russian Empire under the Constitution of the Kingdom of Poland until 1832.

ety: From Middle English congruence, from Latin congruentia (“agreement”), from congruēns, present active participle of congruō (“meet together, agree”).

The quality of being isometric — roughly, the same measure and shape.
Matrix similarity by an orthogonal matrix.
Any equivalence relation defined on an algebraic structure which is preserved by operations defined by the structure.
A well-adjusted state or condition in which people are not lying to themselves or in denial.

An instance or point of agreement or correspondence; a resemblance.

ety: From Middle English [Term?], from Latin congruus, from congruō (“to coincide with; to agree”).

Harmonious.

Shaped like a cone.
Describing a map projection in which meridians are mapped to equally spaced lines radiating out from the apex and parallels of latitude are mapped to circular arcs centred on the apex.

ety: From Ancient Greek κώνειον (kṓneion, “hemlock”) + -ine.

ety: Etymology tree English conjecture Proto-Indo-European *h₂el- Proto-Indo-European *-is Proto-Indo-European *h₂élisder.? Proto-Italic *-ālis Latin -ālisbor. s.def: In the nature of a conjecture, or based on a conjecture.
ex: In conjectural statements, the French often use the Future or the Conditional, instead of the Perfect or the Pluperfect used in English.

s.def: Something that is conjectural; a conjecture.
ex: Let us not assume such previous conjecturals, but rather consult and expostulate death, since death is the wages and the reward of sin.

ety: From Old French, from Latin coniectūra (“a guess”), from coniectus, perfect passive participle of cōniciō (“throw or cast together; guess”), from con- (“together”) + iaciō (“throw, hurl”); see jet. Compare adjective, eject, inject, project, reject, subject, object, trajectory, deject, abject, surjection, bijection, interject. Compare typologically Russian прики́дывать (prikídyvatʹ) (akin to кида́ть (kidátʹ)).

s.def: A statement or an idea which is unproven, but is thought to be true; a guess.
ex: I explained it, but it is pure conjecture whether he understood, or not.

s.def: A supposition based upon incomplete evidence; a hypothesis.
ex: The physicist used his conjecture about subatomic particles to design an experiment.

s.def: A statement likely to be true based on available evidence, but which has not been formally proven.
Interpretation of signs and omens.
To guess; to venture an unproven idea.
ex: I do not know if it is true; I am simply conjecturing here.
What could have been done by such a machine downhill can only be conjectured, for the maximum speed was restricted rigidly to 80 m.p.h.

s.def: To infer on slight evidence; to guess at.
ex: February 22, 1685, Robert South, All Contingences under the Direction of God's Providence (sermon preached at Westminster Abbey)

ety: From Old French conjoindre, from Latin coniungo, from con- (“together”) + iungo (“join”). Equivalent to con- + join.

ex: They are representatives that will loosely conjoin a nation.

One of the words or phrases that are coordinated by a conjunction.
A reassembled bone, stone or ceramic artifact.

ety: The adjective (as “combined, united”) and noun are first attested in 1471, in Middle English, the verb in 1530; partly from Middle English conjugat(e) (“combined, united”), partly directly borrowed from New Latin coniugātus, the perfect passive participle of Latin coniugō (“to yoke together, combine; (New Latin) to conjugate, decline, inflect”) (see -ate (etymology 1, 2 and 3)), from con- (“with”) + iugō (“to join”). In Classical Latin, the word for conjugate (grammar) was dēclīnō, coniugō is a…

s.def: To inflect (a verb) for each person, in order, for one or more tenses; to list or recite its principal parts.
ex: In English, the verb 'to be' is conjugated as follows: 'I am', 'you are', 'he/she/it is', 'we are', 'you are', 'they are'.

To join together, to unite; to juxtapose.
ex: The effects of hunger were often conjugated with epidemic disease.

A type of pelvic measurement.
A word agreeing in derivation with another word, and therefore generally resembling it in meaning.
ex: 17th c, John Bramhall, We have learned in logic, that conjugates are sometimes in name only, and not in deed.

A complex conjugate.

Given a field extension L / K and an element α ∈ L, any other element β ∈ L that is another root of the minimal polynomial of α over K.

ety: Borrowed from Latin coniugātiō (“combining, connecting; conjugation”), from coniugō (“join, unite together”). Equivalent to conjugate + -ion.

s.def: The temporary fusion of organisms, especially as part of sexual reproduction.
In some languages, one of several classifications of verbs categorized into distinct classes based on the specific inflectional patterns they exhibit.

Sexual relations within marriage.
The product of that act: the conjugated forms of a verb, collected into a list or recitation.

A function which negates the non-real part of a complex or hypercomplex number; a complex conjugation.

ety: From Latin conjunctus, the perfect past participle of conjungō. Doublet of conjoint. See conjoin.

An adjunct that supplements a sentence with information, connecting the sentence with previous parts of the discourse. Not considered to be an essential part of the propositional content.
Conjoined.

s.def: Acting together; collaborative.

ety: From Old French conjonction, from Latin coniūnctiō (“joining”), from coniungere (“to join”).

ex: The spectacular conjunction of Venus and Mars gave rise to a myriad of mythical interpretations.

The proposition resulting from the combination of two or more propositions using the ∧ ( and ) operator.
A place where multiple things meet.

s.def: Sexual intercourse.
ex: Certaine Nations (and amongst others, the Mahometane) abhorre Conjunction with women great with childe.

ety: From 1540s late Middle English, borrowing from Medieval Latin conjūnctīva (“serving to connect, connective”, feminine), ellipsis of membrāna conjūnctīva (“conjunctive membrane”).

ety: From Latin coniunctivus (“serving to connect”), from coniunctus, past participle of coniungere; compare conjoin. From late 15th c; grammatical sense from 1660s.

Connected: being joined, united, connected.

Relating to a conjunction (part of speech).

Closely united.

s.def: A conjunction.

ety: Borrowed from French conjoncture.

ety: From Middle English conjuracioun, from Middle French conjuration, from Old French conjuracion, from Latin coniuratio (“a swearing together, a conspiracy”).

ety: From Middle English conjuren, from Old French conjurer, from Latin coniūrō (“to swear together; conspire”), from con- (“with, together”) + iūro (“to swear or take an oath”).

ex: Both roads have the same name, but they don't connect: they're on opposite sides of the river, and there's no bridge there.

ex: When that roundhouse kick connected with his temple it sent him flying across the room.

ex: The new railroad will connect the northern part of the state to the southern part.

ex: I connected the printer to the computer, but I couldn't get it work.

ex: I'm flying to London where I connect with a flight heading to Hungary.

The tissue which connects the locules of an anthers together.
A connective tissue.

A type of tissue found in animals whose main function is binding other tissue systems (such as muscle to skin) or organs and consists of the following three elements: cells, fibers and a ground substance (or extracellular matrix).
A framework within something, with which the whole may be cohesively reconstructed or reflected.

ety: Since 1833, from American English. Unknown origin, possibly a fanciful alteration of corruption, or maybe related to captious. Alternatively an arbitrary pseudo-Latinism coinage.

s.def: A fit of anger or panic; conniption fit.
ex: When she came downstairs and saw what her children were eating, she had a conniption.

[…]threatened by the conniptions gripping Wall Street

ex: The joke was not that funny, but he went into conniptions laughing.

ety: From early 18th c., replaced earlier form connivence (late 16th c.), from Latin connīventia, from connīvēns (“winking”).

ety: From French conniver (“to ignore and thus become complicit in wrongdoing”), or directly from its etymon Latin con(n)īvēre (“close or screw up the eyes, blink, wink; overlook, turn a blind eye, connive”) (perhaps alluding to two persons involved in a scheme together winking to each other), from con- (prefix indicating a being or bringing together of several objects) + *nīvēre (related to nictō (“to blink, wink”), from Proto-Indo-European *kneygʷʰ- (“to bend, droop”)).

s.def: To secretly cooperate with other people in order to commit a crime or other wrongdoing; to collude, to conspire.
ex: I might say, / That who despairs, acts; that who acts, connives / With God's relations set in time and space; [...]
This very Law of Libel provides that "if any one connives with a guilty man and alleges him to be innocent, he renders himself liable to punishment."

s.def: Of parts of a plant: to be converging or in close contact; to be connivent.

ex: Out of reverence to Cato, he for a while connived her impurity and immodesty, but at length dismissed her.

s.def: To open and close the eyes rapidly; to wink.
ex: The artist is to teach them how to nod judiciously, and to connive with either eye, and, in a word, the whole practice of political grimace.

ex: connivent justice
his legal justice cannot be so fickle and variable , sometimes like a devouring fire , and by and by connivent in the embers

connivent wings of an insect

ety: Borrowed from Medieval Latin connotātiō, from connotō (“to mark in addition”), from Latin con- (“together, with”) + notō (“to note”); equivalent to connote + -ation.

s.def: A meaning of a word or phrase that is suggested or implied, as opposed to a denotation, or literal meaning. A characteristic of words or phrases, or of the contexts that words and phrases are used in.
ex: The word "advisedly" has a connotation of "wisely", although it denotes merely "intentionally" and "deliberately."
The word "happy" has a positive connotation, while "sad" has a negative connotation.

s.def: The attribute or aggregate of attributes connoted by a term, contrasted with denotation.
ex: The two expressions "the morning star" and "the evening star" have different connotations but the same denotation (i.e. the planet Venus).

ety: From Medieval Latin connotō (“signify beyond literal meaning”), from com- (“together”), + notō (“mark”).

s.def: To signify beyond its literal or principal meaning.
ex: Racism often connotes an underlying fear or ignorance.

s.def: To possess an inseparable related condition; to imply as a logical consequence.
ex: Poverty connotes hunger.
Doctors should be reminded that absence of evidence does not connote a mental illness …

s.def: To express without overt reference; to imply.
To require as a logical predicate to consequence.

ety: 1650s, from Latin connūbiālis, from connūbium (“marriage, wedlock”) (variants of cōnūbiālis (“pertaining to wedlock”), from cōnūbium (“marriage, wedlock”)) from com- (“together”) (English com-) + nūbō (“marry, to take as husband”) (from which nubile) from Proto-Indo-European *snewbʰ- (“to marry, to wed”).

By the end of the season, he had conquered the sport of baseball.

ex: In 1453, the Ottoman Empire conquered Constantinople.

to conquer difficulties or temptations

ety: From Middle English conscience, from Old French conscience, from Latin conscientia (“knowledge within oneself”) (a calque of Ancient Greek σῠνείδησῐς (sŭneídēsĭs)), from consciens, present participle of conscire (“to know, to be conscious (of wrong)”), from com- (“together”) + scire (“to know”).

ex: Your conscience is your highest authority.

Consciousness; thinking; awareness, especially self-awareness.
ex: Thus conscience does make cowards of us all; And thus the native hue of resolution Is sicklied o'er with the pale cast of thought.

ety: From Middle English consecucioun (“attainment”), from Latin cōnsecūtiō (“effect, proper sequence, attainment”), from past participle of cōnsequor (“to follow, result, reach”).

A succession or series of any kind.

The relation of consequent to antecedent.

ety: Borrowed from Latin cōnsēnsus (“agreement, accordance, unanimity”), from cōnsentiō (“feel together; agree”); see consent.

s.def: A process of decision-making that seeks widespread agreement among group members.

Average projected value.

s.def: To seek consensus; to hold discussions with the aim of reaching mutual agreement.
ex: None of this consensusing was done with the Manual. There were no national workshops, forums, etc.

ety: Recorded in Middle English since circa 1225, borrowed from Old French consentir, from Latin cōnsentīre (“to agree; to assent, consent”), itself from com- (“with”) + sentiō (“to feel”) (whence con-).

s.def: Advice; counsel.

ety: Learned borrowing from Latin consentaneus + English -aneous. Consentaneus is derived from consentire (“to agree”).

Agreeing; in accord.

conclusion, deduction or inference; the thing concluded.

ety: Borrowed from Middle French conséquent, from Latin consequens, consequentem, present participle of consequi (“to follow”), from con- + sequi (“to follow”). Compare French conséquent.

ety: From consequent + -ial.

ety: From consequential + -ism, coined by British analytic philosopher G. E. M. Anscombe in 1958.

The ethical study of morals, duties and rights with an approach that focuses consequences of a particular action or cause.

ety: From Middle English consequentely, consequentliche, consequently; equivalent to consequent + -ly.

lack of change in a measurable property of an isolated physical system (conservation of energy, mass, momentum, electric charge, subatomic particles, and fundamental symmetries)

ety: Either irregularly from conservative + -ism or from conservate + -ism; ultimately from Latin cōnservāre (“to conserve; to keep, guard, observe”).

A risk-averse attitude or approach.

ety: Borrowed from Middle French conservatif, from Latin cōnservō (“to preserve”). Equivalent to conserve + -ative.

s.def: A person who favors maintenance of the status quo.
political conservative
One who seeks to promote or preserve traditional values or institutions.
One who seeks to promote traditions in a particular domain (e.g. a fiscal conservative or a social conservative).
Cautious, moderate.

ety: From Medieval Latin cōnservātōrius directly and via French conservatoire, from cōnservāre (“to conserve, to preserve”) + -torius (“-atory: forming related adjectives”) and/or conservator (“conservator, preserver, protector”) + -ius (“-y: forming related adjectives”).

s.def: A greenhouse, a glass-walled building for cultivating delicate plants.

ex: Considering they are newcomers, they've accomplished a lot.

ety: From Middle French consister, from Latin consistō (“stand together, stop, become hard or solid, agree with, continue, exist”), from com- (“together”) + sistō (“to cause to stand, stand”).

ex: Why doe they cover with so many lets, one over another, those parts where chiefly consisteth [translating loge] our pleasure and theirs?
District number twenty-five (25) shall consist the counties of Tompkins, Seneca and Yates.

s.def: To exist or be compatible.
ex: [Homer] allows their characters such estimable qualities as could consist, and in truth generally do, with tender frailties.
First, because it is granted by all divines, that hypothetical necessity, or necessity upon a supposition, may consist with liberty.
All things do not consist by Christ today, and all the way back to Adam all things have not consisted by Christ.

s.def: A lineup or sequence of railroad carriages or cars, with or without a locomotive, that form a unit.
ex: The train's consist included a baggage car, four passenger cars, and a diner.

ety: By surface analysis, consistent + -cy, consistence + -y or consist + -ency.

s.def: Local coherence.
Correspondence or compatibility.
Reliability or uniformity; the quality of being consistent.
ex: They want to achieve a high degree of consistency in their process and their product.
That consistency of behaviour whereby he inflexibly pursues those measures which appear the most just.

s.def: The degree of viscosity of something.
ex: Mix it until it has the consistency of a thick paste.

s.def: Freedom from contradiction; the state of a system of axioms such that none of the propositions deduced from them are mutually contradictory.
Firmness of constitution or character; substantiality; durability; persistency.
ex: His friendship is of a noble make and a lasting consistency.

der: a foolish consistency is the hobgoblin…

ex: The consistent use of Chinglish in China can be very annoying, apart from some initial amusement.

s.def: Compatible, accordant.
Of a set of statements: such that no contradiction logically follows from them.
ex: Part of establishing a foundation for geometry was demonstrating that the axioms were consistent – that they could never lead to contradictions.

s.def: Objects or facts that are coexistent, or in agreement with one another.
A kind of penitent who was allowed to assist at prayers, but was not permitted to receive the holy sacraments.

ety: Etymology tree English consistent Middle English -ly English -ly English consistently From consistent + -ly.

s.def: In a consistent manner.
ex: Thus from October 1 the French National Railways made a number of changes in their services and consistently in the direction of higher speeds.

s.def: constantly; always.

ety: Inherited from Middle English consistorie, from Old Northern French consistorie (“secular tribunal”) (Old French consistoire), and Late Latin consistorium (“waiting room, meeting place of the imperial council”). Meaning "Church council" is from early 14th century. By surface analysis, consist + -ory.

s.def: A solemn assembly or council.
ex: To council summons all his mighty peers, / Within thick clouds and dark tenfold involved, / A gloomy consistory.

s.def: The spiritual court of a diocesan bishop held before his chancellor or commissioner in his cathedral church or elsewhere.
An assembly of prelates; a session of the College of Cardinals at Rome.
ex: Pius […][was] then hearing of causes in consistory.

s.def: A church tribunal or governing body, especially of elders in a Reformed church.
A civil court of justice.

ety: From Latin cōnsociātus, past participle of cōnsociō (“to associate, unite”).

s.def: An associate; an accomplice.
To associate, partner, or join (with).
To form an alliance, confederacy, or relationship with; to bring together; to join; to unite, usually figuratively.
ex: Join pole to pole, consociate severed worlds.
Under this last section, several persons consociated themselves

s.def: To unite in an ecclesiastical consociation.
