s.def: Affected or contrived to charm; mincingly clever; precious; cutesy.
ex: The actor's performance was too cute for me. All that mugging to the audience killed the humor.
Don't get cute with me, boy!
"This time we aren't interested in anything cute or cryptic. We want the truth."

s.def: Mentally keen or discerning (See also acute)
ex: Then Turpin being so very cute, He hid his money in his boot.
"The police are cute enough, of course, to choose either a Roman Catholic or a materialist as the magistrate."
Cute trick, but can you do it consistently?

s.def: Evincing cleverness; surprising in its elegance or unconventionality (but of limited importance).
ex: There's a cute alternative proof of this using lambda calculus.
Cute solution to pin one Knight by unpinning the other and so force discovered guard for the Bishop: it took me hours to find that Bishop key.

syn: having features mainly attributed to in…
der: cute as a bug in a rug

ety: Learned borrowing from Latin cutīcula (“cuticle, skin”). Doublet of cuticula.

s.def: protective covering outside epidermis
The outermost layer of the skin of vertebrates.
ex: By that time she has pushed back his cuticles, cleaned his nails and painted them with clear polish.

s.def: A noncellular protective covering outside the epidermis of many invertebrates.
ex: Holonym: exoskeleton

s.def: A noncellular protective covering outside the epidermis of many plants.
A thin skin formed on the surface of a liquid.
A protective layer on the shell of a bird's egg.

ety: Etymology tree English cute Proto-Germanic *-j-, *-ij- Proto-West Germanic *-i, *-ī Old English -iġ Middle English -y English -y English -ie English cutie From cute + -ie.

s.def: A cute person or animal.
A clementine: a small, waxy-peeled orange hybrid cultivar that is easy to peel by hand.
Any small mandarin orange variety such as a tangerine or a satsuma.

ety: Etymology tree English cut(is) Proto-Indo-European *-nós Proto-Indo-European *-iHnos Proto-Italic *-īnos Latin -īnusder. Old French -inbor. Middle English -in English -ineclip. English -in English cutin From cut(is) + -in.

s.def: A waxy polymer of hydroxy acids that is the main constituent of plant cuticle.

ety: From Latin cutis (“living skin”).

s.def: The true skin, underlying the epidermis.
ex: The cutis measures in thickness from a quarter of a line to a line and a half (a line is one-twelfth of an inch).

s.def: The peridium of some fungi.

ety: From Middle French coutelas, from Old French coutel (“knife”) + -as (augmentative suffix).

s.def: A short sword with a curved blade, and a convex edge; once used by sailors when boarding an enemy ship.
ex: She could feel Tern’s stare fixed right between her shoulder blades, and knew he was aching to plunge his cutlass there.

s.def: A similarly shaped tool; a machete.
To cut back (vegetation) with a cutlass.

ety: From Middle English coteler (“knife-maker”), from Anglo-Norman cuteler, from Old French coutelier (“knife-maker”).

s.def: One whose business is making or dealing in cutlery.

ety: From Middle English cotellerie, cutleri (“the cutler’s art or craft”), from Old French coutelerie (modern French coutellerie).

s.def: Eating or serving utensils such as knives, forks, and spoons.
ex: a cutlery set
This cutlery comes from Normandy, France.

s.def: Sharp cutting utensils.
ex: Proper maintenance of your cutlery will keep the blades from dulling.

s.def: The business of a cutler.

ety: From French côtelette (recorded in English since 1706), from Middle French costelette (“little rib”), from coste + -elette, from Old French coste (“rib, side”), from Latin costa. Influenced by English cut, as if from cut + -let. Doublet of kotlet and kotleta.

s.def: A thin slice of meat, usually fried.
A chop, a specific piece of meat (especially pork, chicken, or beef) cut from the side of an animal.
A piece of fish that has been cut perpendicular to the spine, rather than parallel (as with a fillet); often synonymous with steak.
A prawn or shrimp with its head and outer shell removed, leaving only the flesh and tail.
A mash of vegetables (usually potatoes) fried with bread.

ety: Deverbal from cut off.

s.def: The point at which something terminates or to which it is limited.
A road, path or channel that provides a shorter or quicker path; a shortcut.
A device that stops the flow of a current.
A device for saving steam by regulating its admission to the cylinder (see quotation at cut-off).
A cessation in a flow or activity.
The player who acts directly before the player on the button pre-flop.
Shorts made by cutting off the legs from trousers.
A sleeveless shirt, especially one made by cutting the sleeves off of a t-shirt.
A horizontal line separating sections of the page.
ex: Light-face type, cutoffs, borders and rules are the universal plan. No black body matter and almost no black headlines appear.

s.def: Constituting a limit or ending.
Alternative spelling of cut-out.
ex: Gastronomes who like tiny cutout cow carrots on the edge of their plates will no doubt flock to be observed at this new Queen Street eateria.

ety: From Middle English cutte-purs; equivalent to cut + purse: originally, purses were worn by a strap at the girdle, which the thief would cut.

s.def: A thief who steals from others' purses or pockets in public.
ex: A cutpurse of the empire and the rule
The Gipsie snap & Pedro are none of Toms Comradoes, yͤ punck I skorne, & yͤ cutpurse sworn & yͤ roring boyes brauadoes

ety: From cut + -able.

s.def: That can be cut.

ety: From Middle English cutter, cuttere, kutter. By surface analysis, cut + -er.

s.def: A single-masted, fore-and-aft rigged, sailing vessel with at least two headsails, and a mast set further aft than that of a sloop.
A person or device that cuts (in various senses).
ex: a stone cutter; a die cutter
In some CNC programs, the diameter of the cutter (such as an end mill) is handled by cutter compensation codes.
Chico Pacheco kept repeating the phrase between clenched teeth, lamenting the wasted days of his youth; he had been a notorious cutter of classes.

s.def: A motorized vessel used in law enforcement purpose
ex: a coastguard cutter.

s.def: A foretooth; an incisor.
ex: the Cutters and Eye-teeth have usually but one Root

s.def: A ship's boat, used for transport ship-to-ship or ship-to-shore.
A ball that moves sideways in the air, or off the pitch, because it has been cut.
A cut fastball.
A ten-pence piece. So named because it is the coin most often sharpened by prison inmates to use as a weapon.
A person who practices self-injury by making cuts in the flesh.
ex: After I got out of the mental institution I was looking at t.v. show I was looking it a teenage girl who was a cutter her arm look just like my arm.

s.def: A surgeon.

ety: From cut + throat.

s.def: A murderer who slits the throats of victims.
An unscrupulous, ruthless or unethical person.
A three-player pocket billiards game where the object is to be the last player with at least one ball still on the table.
Ellipsis of cutthroat compound (“an agentive-instrumental verb-noun compound word”).
ex: Children go through a phase of compound acquisition in which they invent cutthroats spontaneously before dropping the habit again.

s.def: Involving the cutting of throats.
Of or relating to a card game where everyone plays for him or herself rather than playing with a partner.
ex: He found that playing cutthroat Spades was much more difficult than playing with a partner.

s.def: Ruthlessly competitive, dog-eat-dog.
ex: Law is a cutthroat business, you always have to look out to see who is trying to outdo you.
More specifically, Scrabblers are diehard, competitive, and occasionally cutthroat players who treat the game like it's chess or baseball...

ety: From cut + -ing.

s.def: The action of the verb to cut.
ex: How many different cuttings can this movie undergo?

s.def: A section removed from a larger whole.
ex: Extract from "Newspaper Cuttings relating to Sussex," (Sussex Archaeological Collections, 1872, pp. 140, 141.)

s.def: An abridged selection of written work, often intended for performance.
ex: The actor had to make his cutting shorter to fit the audition time.

s.def: An open passage at a level lower than the surrounding terrain, dug for a canal, railway, or road to go through.
ex: We flash across the level. / We thunder thro' the bridges. / We bicker down the cuttings. / We sway along the ridges.
No borrow pit excavation was necessary, and 41,000 cu. yd. were removed from cuttings by excavating machines.

s.def: The editing of film or other recordings.
The process of bringing metals to a desired shape by chipping away the unwanted material.
ex: Boring, drilling, milling, and turning are all different kinds of metal cutting processes.

s.def: The act of cutting one's own skin as a symptom of a mental disorder; self-harm.
That is used for cutting.
ex: I need some sort of cutting utensil to get through this shrink wrap.

s.def: Piercing, sharp.
ex: The weather was atrocious, with bitterly cold wind and cutting sleet—rather appropriate, considering Aunt Fonteyn's temperament.

s.def: Of criticism, remarks, etc.: (potentially) hurtful; curt.
ex: The director gave the auditioning actors cutting criticism.

s.def: A sturdy board, used for cutting and preparing food.
The sharp edge of the blade of a knife or other cutting tool.
The forefront, or position of greatest advancement in some field.
ex: The company prides itself for staying at the cutting edge of technology.

ety: From Middle English cotilbone [and other forms], from cotil, cutil, codel (“cuttlefish; cuttlebone”) (from Old English cudele (“cuttlefish”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gew- (“to bend, to curve; an arch; a vault”)) + bon (“bone”) (from Old English bān (“bone”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeyh₂- (“to hit, strike; to cut, hew”)). The English word is analysable as cuttle (“cuttlefish”) + bone.

s.def: Synonym of cuttlefish bone (“the calcareous, oval-shaped internal shell of a cuttlefish (order Sepiida), originally used in powdered form as an antacid and for absorbing moisture or polishing objects, and now chiefly as a dietary supplement for cage birds”).

ety: From cuttle + fish.

s.def: Any squid-like cephalopods (marine mollusks) of the order Sepiida that have eight arms, two retractable tentacles, and a calcareous internal shell, and can eject a dark ink when threatened.

ety: From cuttlefish + bone.

s.def: The calcareous, oval-shaped internal shell of a cuttlefish (order Sepiida), originally used in powdered form as an antacid and for absorbing moisture or polishing objects, and now chiefly as a dietary supplement for cage birds.

ety: Deverbal from cut up.

s.def: Someone who cuts up; someone who acts boisterously or clownishly, for example, by playing practical jokes.
ex: Near-synonyms: class clown; good-time Charlie; prankster

s.def: A work produced by the aleatory literary technique of cutting up and rearranging a written text to create a new text.
ex: Jeff Lawton's Truck Stop (1969), which read like a William Burroughs cut-up novel and was printed in a skewed, rotated, and oddly spaced type.

ety: From cut + water.

s.def: The wedge of a bridge pier, that resists the flow of water and ice.
The forward curve of the stem of a ship.
A black skimmer; a sea bird of the species Rynchops niger, that flies low over the sea, "cutting" the water surface with its lower mandible to catch small fish.

ety: From Middle English cut-werk, equivalent to cut + work.

s.def: A form of embroidery in which intervening fabric is cut away.

ety: From cut + worm, from the habit of eating through the stem of plants, or possibly from cutty (“short”).

s.def: The larva of any of the many moths of the family Noctuidae, considered an agricultural pest.
Alternative spelling of cwt. (“hundredweight”).

ety: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek κύανος (kúanos), a shade of blue variously described as similar to cornflower, copper carbonate, and lapis lazuli, Mycenaean Greek 𐀓𐀷𐀜 (ku-wa-no), possibly from Hittite [script needed] (kuwannan-, “a precious stone; copper; shade of blue”) - likely from Kuwanniya, all going back to kuwanna (woman), related to "queen" and γυνή. Compare modern Greek κυανός (kyanós), also used for cyan.

s.def: An additive secondary colour midway between green and blue, evoked by wavelengths between ~490 and ~520 nm.

ety: Etymology tree English cyan Proto-Indo-European *-ikos Proto-Italic *-ikos Latin -icuslbor. Old French -iquebor. Middle English -ik English -ic English cyanic From cyan + -ic.

s.def: Of cyanogen or its derivatives
azure-blue
ex: The dark bank of the wall rode up. The deep cyanic sky.

s.def: Containing an anthocyanin

ety: From cyan- + -ide.

s.def: Any compound containing the -C≡N group or the CN⁻ anion.
Sodium or potassium cyanide, used in the extraction of gold and silver or as a poison.
ex: The birdies all try an' hide / But they still go for peanuts / When coated with cyanide

s.def: Hydrogen cyanide, or cyanide gas, a poisonous gas.
To treat or poison with cyanide.

ety: Etymology tree Ancient Greek κῠ́ᾰνος (kŭ́ănos) Ancient Greek -εος (-eos) Ancient Greek κῠᾰ́νεος (kŭắneos)der. English cyano- Ancient Greek βακτηρία (baktēría) Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. s.def: Any of very many photosynthetic prokaryotic microorganisms, of phylum Cyanobacteria.
ex: Photosynthesis was established some billion years ago by ancient bacterial precursors of modern cyanobacteria.

ety: From cyano- + -gen; compare French cyanogène. So called because it produced blue dyes.

s.def: The pseudohalogen (CN)₂; a colorless, poisonous gas used as a rocket propellant, an insecticide and in chemical warfare.
The radical -CN.

ety: Etymology tree Ancient Greek κῠ́ᾰνος (kŭ́ănos) Ancient Greek -εος (-eos) Ancient Greek κῠᾰ́νεος (kŭắneos)der. s.def: A blue discolouration of the skin due to the circulation of blood low in oxygen.
ex: She has real, real deep cyanosis around the eyes and mouth too.

ex: He also points out that if the US does come under cyberattack, we may be powerless to stop the attack.

ety: From Ancient Greek κυβερνήτης (kubernḗtēs, “steersman”), from κυβερνάω (kubernáō, “to steer, drive, guide, act as a pilot”) (whence English govern). The term is attested since at least 1948 in the book Cybernetics by Norbert Wiener, influenced by the cognate term and doublet governor, the name of an early control device proposed by James Clerk Maxwell in 1868. Note also the 1830s French cybernétique (“the art of governing”). Also doublet of Kubernetes.

s.def: The theory/science of communication and control in living organisms or machines.
ex: Near-synonym: control theory (not consistently differentiated)

s.def: The art/study of governing, controlling automatic processes and communication.
Technology that is part of and controlled by a living organism (e.g. a cyborg); cybernetic or bionic technology such as prostheses.
ex: […] he lost both of his arms and his jaw in a previous fight and had them replaced with cybernetics.

s.def: Technology related to computers and the Internet.

ety: From cyber- + -punk, coined by American writer and software developer Bruce Bethke as the title of a 1983 short story, and later popularized by Gardner Dozois.

s.def: A subgenre of science fiction which focuses on computer or information technology and virtual reality juxtaposed with a degree of breakdown or radical change in the social order.
A cyberpunk character, a hacker punk, a high-tech low life.
ex: The film The Matrix redefined what a cyberpunk looked like.

s.def: A writer of cyberpunk fiction.
ex: […] cyberpunks like William Gibson, Lucious Sheperd^([sic]), Bruce Sterling […]

s.def: A musical genre related to the punk movement that makes use of electronic sounds such as synthesizers.
ex: Indeed, 'Mindphaser' (and Tactical Neural Implant more generally) represents a high point of cyberpunk in the industrial music scene.

ety: From cyber- + sex.

s.def: A virtual sexual encounter in which two or more persons connected remotely by means of a computer network send one another sexually explicit messages simulating a sexual experience.
ex: He went to his office and logged online to have cybersex for more than six hours.

ety: Blend of cybernetics + space, equivalent to cyber- + space, coined by American-Canadian speculative fiction writer William Gibson in his short story collection Burning Chrome (1982) and popularized in his novel Neuromancer (1984).

s.def: A world of information accessed through the Internet.
The Internet as a whole.
ex: If, as we knew with increasing certainty, Russia, China, North Korea, Iran, and others were contesting us in cyberspace, it was time to fight back.

s.def: A three-dimensional representation of virtual space in a computer network.

s.def: An Aegean island chain in southeast-central Greece, surrounding the main island Delos, further including the islands of Andros, Amorgos, Irakleia, Kea, Mykonos Naxos, Paros, Santorini, Syra, Tinos and others.

ety: Borrowing from New Latin cyclamen, from Latin cyclamīnos.

s.def: Any of various primulaceous flowering plants, of the genus Cyclamen, widely cultivated as a houseplant, having decorative leaves and solitary flowers.
ex: An expectant mother would avoid cyclamen, stepping over it being an ominous sign.
The root of the cyclamen, sowbread, was used in ancient times as an ingredient in love potions.
An interesting cyclamen was also found here with dark rounded unmarbled leaves, but unfortunately without flowers […]

s.def: A purplish-red colour.

ety: From Middle English cicle (“fixed length period of years”), from Late Latin cyclus, from Ancient Greek κύκλος (kúklos, “circle”), from Proto-Hellenic *kúklos, *kʷókʷlos, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷékʷlos (“circle, wheel”). Doublet of chakra, chakram, charkha, chukker, cyclus, kike, and wheel (see there for more).

s.def: A complete rotation of anything.
A process that returns to its beginning and then repeats itself in the same sequence.
ex: electoral cycle menstrual cycle news cycle

s.def: A programme on a washing machine, dishwasher, or other such device.
ex: Put the washing in on a warm cycle.
the spin cycle

s.def: An interval of space or time in which one set of events or phenomena is completed.
ex: the cycle of the seasons, or of the year

s.def: The members of the sequence formed by such a process.
A series of poems, songs or other works of art, typically longer than a trilogy.
ex: The Ring of the Nibelung is a cycle of four operas by Richard Wagner.

s.def: A single, a double, a triple, and a home run hit by the same player in the same game.
ex: Jones hit for the cycle in the game.

s.def: A closed walk or path, with or without repeated vertices allowed.
A chain whose boundary is zero.
An imaginary circle or orbit in the heavens; one of the celestial spheres.
ex: With centric and eccentric scribbled o'er, Cycle and epicycle, orb in orb
There appears to be no absolute cycle in the universe; all is change and progression. No planet ever revolves twice precisely in the same orbit.

ety: By surface analysis, cycle + -ing.

s.def: The sport of riding and racing cycles, especially bicycles.
ex: In all my years as a cycling fan, I've never seen a breakaway like this.

s.def: The activity of riding cycles, especially bicycles (for transport, sport, physical exercise, recreation, tourism...)
Any cyclic action or process.
ex: The cycling of the water softener in the basement was faintly audible from the kitchen.

ety: From cycle + -ist, 1882.

s.def: A person who rides a cycle, especially a bicycle, or who habitually engages in cycling.
A motorcyclist.
ex: Most of the cyclists were members of the Pagans' Motorcycle Club of Washington.

ety: From cyclo- + -oid.

s.def: The locus of a point on the circumference of a circle that rolls without slipping on a fixed straight line.
A fish having cycloid scales.
Resembling a circle; cycloidal.
Thin and rounded, with smooth edges.
characterized by alternating high and low moods.

ety: From cyclo- + -meter.

s.def: A device that counts the revolutions of a bicycle wheel in order to indicate distance travelled.
An instrument for measuring circular arcs.
A machine used to decrypt Enigma machine ciphers.

ety: Coined by English scientist and merchant captain Henry Piddington, probably in the 1840s, and based on some term in Ancient Greek. Sources disagree on the date and on which Ancient Greek term, though it had to be something derived from either κύκλος (kúklos, “circle, wheel”) or κυκλόω (kuklóō, “go around in a circle, form a circle, encircle”), for example the present active participle κυκλῶν (kuklôn). See cycle and wheel.

s.def: Any weather phenomenon consisting of a system of winds rotating around a centre of low atmospheric pressure; a low pressure system.
ex: Near-synonym: storm

s.def: A tropical cyclone occurring in the South Pacific or Indian Ocean.
ex: Near-synonyms: typhoon, hurricane

s.def: The more or less violent, small-scale circulations such as tornadoes, waterspouts, and dust devils.
A strong wind.
A cyclone separator; the cylindrical vortex tube within such a separator
To separate using a cyclone separator.
ex: The product is cycloned and overflow at 45-50% solids is pumped to primary flotation where 50-70% of the copper is removed as a 21% concentrate.

s.def: To storm as a cyclone.
ex: What difference if it rained, hailed, blew, snowed, cycloned?

s.def: To whirl in spirals as a result of a cyclone or whirlwind-like force.
ex: White dust was cycloning at the bottom of ravines that cut for miles into the red flatness
Pine needles cycloned wildly as Jan swung her car into the Institute's parking lot.
The unicorn stamped and gave him a scornful look as Sally cycloned away from them, but Wulfric laughed to himself a crafty laugh.

s.def: To storm wildly; to be in a frenzy.
ex: The winds of change cycloned around Rhodesia and the debris began to fall within its borders.

ety: From cyclops + -ean.

s.def: Massive in stature.
Suggestive of a cyclops.
ex: Some of the descendants of this cyclopean ancestor left their burrows and started to swim.

s.def: Fitted together of huge irregular stones.
Created by combining two images.
Alternative spelling of cyclopaedia.

ety: Borrowed from Latin cyclōps, from Ancient Greek Κύκλωψ (Kúklōps, “Cyclops ['round eyes']”). The sense for copepods is a semantic loan from translingual Cyclops.

s.def: A one-eyed giant from Greek and Roman mythology.
A one-eyed creature of any species.
A person with only one working eye.
Any copepod in the genus Cyclops.
A small magnifying lens in the crystal of a watch to aid in reading the date.

ety: From cyclo- + -rama (as in panorama).

s.def: A panoramic image displayed on the inside of a cylindrical canvas.
ex: Robert Loo sat, quite content, behind the counter, against a cyclorama of tins of milk and corned beef.

s.def: A building or room designed to show this image.
A large, often concave, backdrop, hung upstage in a theater.

ety: From Middle English cignet, signet, from Anglo-Norman cignet, diminutive of Old French cigne (“swan”), from Latin cygnus, cycnus (“swan”), from Ancient Greek κύκνος (kúknos, “swan”).

s.def: The young of a swan.

ety: Borrowed from Latin cygnus (“swan”), from Ancient Greek κύκνος (kúknos, “swan”).

s.def: A summer constellation of the northern sky, said to resemble a swan. It includes the triple star system HD 188753 and the stars Deneb and Albireo.
A king of the Ligurians and relative of Phaeton who was transformed into a swan and placed in the sky as a constellation.

ety: From Middle French chilindre, cylindre, from Latin cylindrus, from Ancient Greek κύλινδρος (kúlindros), from κυλίνδω (kulíndō) "I roll or wallow" (intransitive). Doublet of calander and calender.

s.def: A surface created by projecting a closed two-dimensional curve along an axis intersecting the plane of the curve.
A solid figure bounded by a cylinder and two parallel planes intersecting the cylinder.
Any object in the form of a circular cylinder.
ex: A big greyish rounded bulk, the size, perhaps, of a bear, was rising slowly and painfully out of the cylinder.

s.def: The space in which a piston travels inside a reciprocating engine or pump.
A cylindrical cavity or chamber in a mechanism, such as the counterpart to a piston found in a piston-driven engine.
A container in the form of a cylinder with rounded ends for storing pressurized gas; a gas cylinder.
An early form of phonograph recording, made on a wax cylinder.
The part of a revolver that contains chambers for the cartridges.
The corresponding tracks on a vertical arrangement of disks in a disk drive considered as a unit of data capacity.

New Latin cȳmabor. English cyma From New Latin cȳma (“young sprout or shoot of cabbage”) (whence the botanic usage of cyme), from Ancient Greek κῦμα (kûma, “swell, wave”, “cyma”, “sprout of a plant”), from κύω (kúō, “to conceive, to become preg…

s.def: The wavelike, curved shape of a cymatium, consisting of a concave and a convex line; (loosely) the cymatium itself.
ex: […] while the double-cyma or classical curve of his mouth was not without a looseness in its close.

s.def: A cyme (opening bud).

ety: From Middle English cymbal, from Old English cimbal, cimbala and Old French cimbale, both from Latin cymbalum (“cymbal”), from Ancient Greek κύμβαλον (kúmbalon), from κύμβη (kúmbē, “bowl”). See also chime.

s.def: A concave plate of metal, usually brass or bronze, that produces a sharp, ringing sound when struck: played either in pairs, by striking them together, or singly by striking with a drumstick or the like.
ex: The trumpets, sackbuts, psalteries and fifes, Tabours and cymbals and the shouting Romans, Make the sun dance.
Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not charity, I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal.
Trumpets and Drums shall fright her from the Throne, As sounding Cymbals aid the lab'ring Moon.

ety: ] Borrowed from French cime, cyme (“top, summit”), from Vulgar Latin *cima, from Latin cȳma (“young sprout of a cabbage”, “spring shoots of cabbage”), from Ancient Greek κῦμα (kûma, “anything swollen, such as a wave or billow”; “fetus”, “embryo”, “sprout of a plant”), from κύω (kúō, “to conceive”, “to become pregnant”; in the aorist “to impregnate”). For considerably more information, see cyma, which is an etymological doublet. Compare also Frankish *kīmō (“sprout”), from Proto-Germanic *kīmô,…

s.def: A “head” (of unexpanded leaves, etc.); an opening bud.
A flattish or convex flower cluster, of the centrifugal or determinate type, on which each axis terminates with a flower which blooms before the flowers below it.
ex: The inflorescence is some form of cyme, and the flowers are usually regular.
The plant bears small groups of two or three yellowish coloured flowers on an axillary cyme.
The flower cluster is a cyme (terminal flower is the most advanced), is terminal within the bud and may contain up to six individual flowers.

s.def: A cyma.
Misspelling of senna.

ety: From Middle English cynike, cynicke, from Middle French cynique, from Latin cynicus, from Ancient Greek κυνικός (kunikós), originally derived from the portico in Athens called Κυνόσαργες (Kunósarges), the earliest home of the Cynic school, later reinterpreted as being derived from κύων (kúōn, “dog”), in a contemptuous allusion to the uncouth and aggressive manners adopted by the members of the school.

s.def: A person whose outlook is scornfully negative.
ex: Well, that's one in the eye for the nay-sayers, the doubters, the cynics and assorted tosspots what make up the media and that.
The cynic surfaced, reminding him that she'd been accused of trying to spring the baby trap on Brad Comfort.

s.def: A person who believes that all people are motivated by selfishness.
Synonym of cynical.
Relating to the Dog Star.
ex: the cynic, or Sothic, year; cynic cycle

ety: Originated 1542, from Classical Latin cynicus (“Cynic/cynic”, adjective) + -al. By surface analysis, cynic + -al. In reference to dogs, with allusion to the ultimate etymology (Ancient Greek κυνικός (kunikós, “doglike”)).

s.def: Of or relating to the belief that human actions are motivated only or primarily by base desires or selfishness.
ex: I hope it is no very cynical asperity not to confess obligations where no benefit has been received.

s.def: Skeptical of the integrity, sincerity, or motives of others.
Bitterly or jadedly distrustful or contemptuous; mocking.
Showing contempt for accepted moral standards by one's actions.
Like the actions of a snarling dog, especially in reference to facial nerve paralysis.
ex: Demetrius Attalicus studied the symptomatologies due to strictura cerebri, characterized by a cynical spasm of the facial nerve.

ety: From Cynicism, cynic + -ism; compare cynism.

s.def: A distrustful attitude.
A scornfully pessimistic comment or act.
An emotion of jaded negativity, or a general distrust of the integrity or professed motives of others, due to belief that people are motivated solely by disguised self-interest.
A school of thought in the philosophy of Ancient Greece.

ety: From cyno- + -phobia. Piecewise doublet of canophobia.

s.def: An irrational fear or hatred of dogs or other canines.

ety: From Middle French Cynosure (“Ursa Minor; Polaris”), from Latin Cynosūra (“Ursa Minor”), from Ancient Greek Κυνόσουρα (Kunósoura, “Ursa Minor”, literally “dog’s tail”), from κυνός (kunós, “dog's”) + οὐρά (ourá, “tail”).

s.def: Alternative letter-case form of Cynosure: Ursa Minor or Polaris, the North Star, used as a guide by navigators.
That which serves to guide or direct; a guiding star.
ex: let faith be your cynosure to walk by

s.def: Something that is the center of attention; an object that serves as a focal point of attraction and admiration.
ex: Towers, and battlements it sees Bosom'd high in tufted trees, Where perhaps some beauty lies, The cynosure of neighbouring eyes.
With anglophobia driving out anglophilia, the king – as during the Seven Years War – came to represent the very cynosure of patriotic zeal.

ety: From Middle English cipres, from Old French cipres (French cyprès), from Late Latin cypressus; compare Hebrew גֹּפֶר (gōp̄er), the name of the tree whose wood was used to make the ark (Genesis. vi:14), also κύπρος (relating to aromatic pitch).

s.def: An evergreen coniferous tree with flattened shoots bearing small scale-like leaves, whose dark foliage is sometimes associated with mourning, in family Cupressaceae, especially the genera Cupressus and Chamaecyparis.
Alternative form of Cyprus (“type of fabric”).
Belonging to the suborder Cyprinoidei of the order Cypriniformes.
Resembling the carp.
A fish of that suborder.

ety: From Ancient Greek Κυπριώτης (Kupriṓtēs, “Cypriot”). By surface analysis, Cypr(us) + -iot.

s.def: A person from Cyprus.
A language of Cyprus, a moribund variety of Arabic spoken by the Maronite community.

ety: From Latin Cyprus, from Ancient Greek Κύπρος (Kúpros).

s.def: An island and country in the Mediterranean Sea, normally considered politically part of Europe but geographically part of West Asia. Official name: Republic of Cyprus. Capital: Nicosia.
A suburban area of Beckton, borough of Newham, Greater London, England, named after the Mediterranean island (OS grid ref TQ4380).

ety: From Latin Cȳrenaica, from Ancient Greek Κῡρηναϊκή (Kūrēnaïkḗ), from Κῡρηνᾰῐ̈κός (Kūrēnăĭ̈kós, “Cyrenean, adj.”) + -ή (-ḗ, “-a: forming feminine nouns”), from Κῡρηναῖος (Kūrēnaîos, “Cyrenean, n.”) + -ικός (-ikós, “-ic: forming adjectives”), from Κυρήνη (Kurḗnē, “Cyrene”) + -ιος (-ios, “-y: forming demonyms”). Equivalent to Cyrenaic + -a.

s.def: A geographic region, an and former province of northeastern Libya; in modern usage, extended to the entire eastern portion of Libya.

ety: From Latin Cȳrēnē, from Ancient Greek Κυρήνη (Kurḗnē), of uncertain origin. Classical sources considered the Thessalian demigod the etymon for the Libyan city. Modern scholars variously derive the name from the Libyan spring Κύρα (Kúra) or, noting the myth attested before the spring or city, consider an existing Proto-Berber name to have been conflated with the Thessalian myths by early Greek colonists.

s.def: A former city near Shahhat, Libya.
A Thessalian princess and huntress demigod, companion of Artemis, lover of Apollo, and mother of Aristaeus and Idmon.

ety: From the name Cyril + -ic, from Medieval Latin Cȳrillus, from Ancient Greek Κῡ́ρῐλλος (Kū́rĭllos), denoting Saint Cyril, who devised a predecessor to the Cyrillic script, the Glagolitic alphabet, and whose students later devised the Cyrillic script itself.

s.def: The Cyrillic alphabet or writing system.
ex: Russian is typically written in Cyrillic.
Hidden behind a Cyrillic veil of mystery, it’s one of the harder languages to master, so much so that even many Russians speak it incorrectly.

Old French -ationbor. Middle English -acioun English -ation English -ization English Cyrillization From Cyrillic + -ization.

s.def: putting text into the Cyrillic alphabet
The transliteration of text into the Cyrillic alphabet.
The adoption of the Cyrillic alphabet for a language's writing system.
ex: As far as I know, Cyrillization of Yiddish was never suggested by anyone.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewH-? Proto-Indo-European *ḱewh₁- Proto-Indo-European *-yeti Proto-Indo-European *-éyeti Proto-Indo-European *ḱuh₁éyeti Ancient Greek κῠ́ω (kŭ́ō)? Ancient Greek κύστις (kústis)der. Late Latin cystisder. English cyst From Late Latin cystis, from Ancient Greek κύστις (kústis, “anatomical sac”).

s.def: A pouch or sac without opening, usually membranous and containing morbid matter, which develops in one of the natural cavities or in the substance of an organ.

ety: From Middle French cystique, from Ancient Greek κύστις (kústis).

s.def: Of or pertaining to a cyst.
Of or pertaining to the gall bladder or the urinary bladder.
An inherited condition in which the exocrine glands produce abnormally viscous mucus, causing chronic respiratory and digestive problems.

ety: From Ancient Greek κύστις (kústis, “bladder”), where it was found.

s.def: A nonessential amino acid formed by the oxidation of cysteine; it contains two cysteine residues linked by a disulfide bond.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewH-? Proto-Indo-European *ḱewh₁- Proto-Indo-European *-yeti Proto-Indo-European *-éyeti Proto-Indo-European *ḱuh₁éyeti Ancient Greek κῠ́ω (kŭ́ō)? Ancient Greek κύστις (kústis)der. Late Latin cystisder. English cyst Proto-Indo-European *-tósder. Ancient Greek -της (-tēs)der. Ancient Greek -ῖτις (-îtis)lbor. New Latin -itisder. English -itis English cystitis From cyst + -itis.

s.def: Inflammation of the urinary bladder.

ety: From cysto- + scope.

s.def: A form of endoscope used to examine the ureter and the bladder.

ety: From French cytise (“laburnum”) + English -ine.

s.def: A polycyclic alkaloid whose pharmacological activity is similar to nicotine; used in the treatment of nicotinism.

ety: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek κύτος (kútos, “container, receptacle”).

s.def: cell.
ex: cyto- + pathology → cytopathology

ety: From cyto- + -kine from Ancient Greek κίνησις (kínēsis, “movement”).

s.def: Any of various small regulatory proteins that regulate the cells of the immune system.

ety: From cyto- (“cell”) + -logy.

s.def: biology: the study of cells
The study of cells.
ex: Holonym: cytohistology

ety: Internationalism. Borrowed from taxonomic name Cytomegalovirus, equivalent to cyto- + megalo- + virus.

s.def: Any of several herpes viruses, of the genus Cytomegalovirus, that infect the salivary glands of certain primates, including humans.
ex: The peak period for the development of acute graft-versus-host disease overlaps with the time during which cytomegalovirus infection occurs.
Prophylactic virostatic treatment with aciclovir did not prevent cytomegalovirus infection in an immune suppressed patient.

ety: After German Cytosin, equivalent to Ancient Greek κύτος (kútos) + -ine. Cytosine was discovered and named by the German biochemists Albrecht Kossel and Albert Neumann in 1894 when it was hydrolyzed from calf thymus tissues.

s.def: A heterocyclic base, 4-aminopyrimidin-2(1H)-one, which pairs with guanine in DNA and RNA (by means of three hydrogen bonds).

ety: From Latin Cȳzicus, from Ancient Greek Κύζικος (Kúzikos).

s.def: A former city in Balikesir Province, Turkey, formerly part of the ancient region of Mysia.
Alternative spelling of tsarevich.
Alternative spelling of tsarina.
Alternative spelling of tsarism.

ety: Unadapted borrowing from Polish Czech, from Old Polish Czech, from Old Czech Čech, ultimately a variation and contraction of Proto-Slavic *čelověkъ (“human”).

s.def: Of, from, or pertaining to Czechia, the Czech people, culture, or language.
A person from the Czech Republic (Czechia) or of Czech descent.
ex: By 1963, almost 130,000 Czechs had migrated to this country. They tended to gravitate to the farming communities.

s.def: A Slavic language primarily spoken in the Czech Republic.
The Czech Republic (Czechia).

ety: Calque of Czech Česká republika.

s.def: A country in Central Europe. Capital and largest city: Prague. Until 1993, part of Czechoslovakia.
The Czech Socialist Republic.

ety: Etymology tree English Czech Proto-Indo-European *-(i)yós Proto-Italic *-ijos Proto-Italic *-ios Old Latin -ios Latin -ius Latin -iader. English -ia English Czechia From Czech + -ia.

s.def: A country in Central Europe. Official name: Czech Republic. Capital and largest city: Prague.
Alternative form of Czechoslovakia.

ety: From Czech + -o- + Slovak.

s.def: A native or inhabitant of Czechoslovakia

ety: From Czecho- + Slovakia.

s.def: A former country in Central Europe, now the Czech Republic and Slovakia; Carpathian Ruthenia, at the eastern end, became a part of Ukraine.

ety: From Czech + -o- + Slovak + -ian.

s.def: A person from Czechoslovakia.

ety: From Czechoslovak + -ization, or Czechoslovakize + -ation.

s.def: The process of Czechoslovakizing.

ety: Unadapted borrowing from Polish Częstochowa.

s.def: A city in southern Poland, on the Warta river, with 240,027 inhabitants as of June 2009.

ety: Borrowed from Turkish Çanakkale, from Ottoman Turkish چناق قلعه (Çanak Kalʼe, literally “Fortress of Pots”), so named from the great manufacture of coarse earthenware carried on in and around the town.

s.def: province, district and city of Turkey
A province of Turkey, along the Dardanelles.
A district of Çanakkale Province, Turkey.
A municipality, the capital city of Çanakkale district and Çanakkale Province, Turkey.

ety: From Turkish Çankırı.

s.def: A district of Çankırı Province, Turkey.
A province in northern Turkey.
A municipality, the capital of Çankırı district and Çankırı Province, Turkey.

ety: Borrowed from Turkish Çoruh.

s.def: A river in Turkey flowing north through the Armenian Highland and emptying into the Black Sea in the Adjara region of Georgia.

ety: Unadapted borrowing from Turkish Çorum.

s.def: A district of Çorum Province, Turkey.
A province in southwestern Turkey.
A municipality, the capital of Çorum district and Çorum Province, Turkey.
